Chinese Political & Military Cases — 384 Lines
001 Line H01 Qian Chong’er’s Exile and Return to Jin — Preserve Your Strength Before Taking Action▶

初九｜

001 case_id: XCASE-H01-L1 | global_line_no: 001 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: full_paragraph_translation_pending_QA | publish_status: editorial_review

A succession dispute broke out in the state of Jin. Chong’er left his homeland and spent many years moving among the feudal states. With no Jin government offices on which he could directly rely, he and his followers had to secure a welcome and the resources needed for daily life whenever they arrived somewhere new; only then could they discuss political support.

After leaving Jin, Chong’er traveled through several states and received varying degrees of hospitality and assistance. Ultimately, with support from Qin, he returned to Jin and ascended the throne. His experience shows the position of a political exile who must depend on hosts, followers, and outside resources.

Chong’er received different levels of assistance in different states and at times encountered neglect. Qin later gave him the support that enabled him to return to Jin and become Duke Wen of Jin. His accession resulted from a long exile; it was not a guaranteed plan from the day he left his homeland. The choices of his hosts, the willingness of his followers to remain with him, and changes inside Jin all affected whether he could ultimately return.

In every state he visited, the host decided how honorably to receive the exile, and his followers had to decide whether to continue accompanying him. No single stay automatically meant that his return would succeed. Only when Qin offered assistance and political conditions in Jin were favorable did he gain an opportunity to re-enter his homeland’s political affairs.

Chong’er’s exile among the states and eventual accession in Jin: After leaving Jin, he traveled through several states, receiving different levels of welcome and assistance, before returning to take the throne with Qin’s support. His experience illustrates how a political exile depended on hosts, companions, and external resources. A succession dispute had forced Chong’er from Jin, and he wandered for many years. During his exile he had no stable political foundation; his first tasks were survival and the cultivation of allies. This makes the episode an analogy for a person whose strength remains in a low position and who should not rush to claim supreme authority. The Xiang says, “Do not employ the hidden dragon; yang is still below.” This entry focuses on “preserving strength first.”

The point of this line is to keep one’s strength concealed and build capacity rather than come forward prematurely. The criterion for comparison is preservation and preparation when conditions are not yet mature. The original event and line-specific comparison have recognizable central actions and consequences and are suitable as a retrospective analogy. It must nevertheless not be claimed that the historical participants quoted the Xiang.

002 Line H01 Qian Liu Bang Enters Guanzhong and Announces Three Rules — Use Your Abilities for the Public Good▶

九二｜

002 case_id: XCASE-H01-L2 | global_line_no: 002 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: full_paragraph_translation_pending_QA | publish_status: editorial_review

As Qin rule collapsed, armies from several quarters advanced toward Guanzhong. When Liu Bang reached this former center of Qin government, local residents still faced uncertainty about the garrison and changing laws. If the arriving commander wished to secure their cooperation, people needed to know how his troops would enter the area and which actions would be punished.

After entering Guanzhong, Liu Bang announced three articles of law and explained the army’s arrangements to local elders, seeking to ease the fear caused by Qin’s harsh late-period laws. This was a political measure intended to win local support. Xiang Yu and other forces still possessed considerable strength, and entry into the Pass did not mean Liu Bang had already won control of the realm.

Liu Bang assembled local elders and made the simplified rules public. His soldiers then had to act in accordance with his promises. The arrangement helped reduce local panic, but it did not immediately confer control of the entire government on Liu Bang. Xiang Yu and other military forces were still operating, and conditions beyond Guanzhong remained undecided. The military advance, announcement of the agreement, and ensuing rivalry among the leaders were connected stages; the moment of entering Guanzhong cannot be treated as the endpoint of the struggle for power.

When the people of Guanzhong first heard the rules, armed soldiers were still standing before them. Whether Liu Bang would keep his promises would become apparent only through the actual relationship between the troops and local communities. The continuing contest for control of Guanzhong also meant that this governing arrangement always operated in an unstable political environment.

Liu Bang’s entry into Guanzhong and the agreement on three articles of law: After arriving, he announced the three rules and explained the army’s arrangements to local elders to ease the fear left by Qin’s harsh laws. This was a political measure to obtain local support, while Xiang Yu and others remained powerful; entry into Guanzhong was not equivalent to conquering the realm. As Qin authority collapsed, armies advanced toward the region. Liu Bang restrained harsh punishments and abuses against the populace so that ordinary people could experience the benefit of a political promise. This is comparable to virtue beginning to exert influence beyond its possessor. The Xiang says, “The dragon appears in the field; virtue spreads widely.” The emphasis is on “turning capacity into public benefit.”

The point of this line is the extension of virtuous influence to other people. The criterion is that an achievement must actually benefit others. The original event and line-specific comparison contain recognizable central acts and results and are suitable as retrospective analogy. They do not justify a claim that the participants quoted the Xiang.

003 Line H01 Qian On Protracted War and the Stages of Resistance — Reassess Strategy Continuously▶

九三｜

003 case_id: XCASE-H01-L3 | global_line_no: 003 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: full_paragraph_translation_pending_QA | publish_status: editorial_review

The Sino-Japanese War was still under way in 1938. Victories and defeats on different fronts, together with the mobilization of civilians, produced conflicting assessments of the war’s prospects. Mao Zedong wrote On Protracted War at this juncture to address whether the conflict could be sustained, whether the balance of circumstances might change, and how operations should be arranged across successive stages.

In On Protracted War, written in 1938, Mao analyzed the conditions of the Sino-Japanese conflict and proposed the concepts of prolonged resistance and development through successive phases. It was a strategic analysis of the military situation as it stood at the time, considering the passage of time, changes in the balance of forces, and organized mobilization together.

The essay examined the strengths of both sides and the constraints imposed by time, and advanced a plan for fighting in stages. The later course of the war had not yet occurred when the essay appeared. It was an argument made at that particular historical moment; subsequent events were also affected by developments on different fronts, political forces, and the international situation. The eventual victory should not be used retroactively to claim that the essay had already answered every concrete military problem. Only by starting from the questions of 1938 can one see which conditions the author chose to discuss at the time.

After the work was made public that year, readers and military forces still faced changing front lines. Its account of successive phases offered a framework for organizing time, but individual units still had to deal with supplies, command, and the enemy situation in their own sectors. The strategic judgments of the essay and the particular military outcomes achieved years later cannot be merged into a single decision.

On Protracted War proposes a phased strategy of resistance: In the work he wrote in 1938, Mao Zedong analyzed the conditions of the Sino-Japanese War and proposed prolonged operations unfolding in successive stages. This strategic discussion considered time, changing relative strength, and organized mobilization together. The war was still continuing in 1938; victories and defeats on different fronts, and civilian mobilization, led to divergent assessments of its prospects. On Protracted War viewed the conflict as a continually changing process. It therefore offers an analogy for repeatedly reassessing a situation and adjusting one’s actions, rather than treating a judgment made at one point as permanently valid. The Xiang states, “Diligent throughout the day, one repeatedly returns to the Way.” This entry focuses on “continually reviewing strategy.”

The central concern of this line is diligent vigilance and repeated correction. The criterion is not a single success but repeated scrutiny and verification. The original event and its line-specific comparison contain identifiable principal actions and outcomes and are appropriate as a retrospective analogy. It must not be claimed that the historical participants quoted the Xiang.

004 Line H01 Qian The Northern Expedition and the Capture of Wuchang — Advance When Conditions Permit▶

九四｜

004 case_id: XCASE-H01-L4 | global_line_no: 004 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: full_paragraph_translation_pending_QA | publish_status: editorial_review

In 1926 the Northern Expeditionary Army advanced toward Wuchang, while defending troops still controlled the city and its surrounding defenses. The attackers hoped to capture this city on the Yangtze, but their initial assault failed. They subsequently had to maintain a siege and supply lines outside the walls.

The Northern Expedition did not take Wuchang in a single attempt. Its forces suffered a setback in an assault, maintained a siege, and continued fighting before capturing the city in October 1926. The campaign expanded the political and military influence of the Northern Expedition, but it also caused military and civilian casualties and imposed the costs of a siege on the city.

The campaign continued until October of that year, when the Northern Expeditionary Army finally captured Wuchang. The siege imposed losses on defenders, attackers, and people within the walls, while wartime constraints disrupted urban life. The fall of Wuchang enlarged the expedition’s political and military influence, but that outcome cannot justify removing the earlier failed assault from the account. Capturing the city was the result of successive deployments and sustained combat; new political disputes within the Northern Expedition camp followed afterward.

The defenders could use the city’s fortifications to delay an attack, while the besieging force had to maintain its encirclement and supplies. Fighting lasted into the autumn, and only the transfer of Wuchang in October provided a definite military outcome to the siege. The effects on the city’s residents throughout the encirclement should not disappear from a narrative of victory.

The Northern Expedition captures Wuchang after setbacks in storming the city: The army did not succeed at the first attempt; after a failed assault, a siege, and sustained operations, it took Wuchang in October 1926. The campaign extended the expedition’s political and military influence, but also inflicted military and civilian casualties and the hardships of a siege. As the army advanced toward Wuchang in 1926, defenders continued to hold the city and surrounding defensive positions. The attackers had to contend with encirclement and resistance. In moving from preparation to offensive action, the critical issue was whether they could bear the consequences of the next step, not merely whether they could rise quickly. The Xiang says, “One may leap or remain in the deep; advancing incurs no blame.” This entry emphasizes “advancing only when conditions are right.”

The focus of this line is the ability either to advance or withdraw and to act according to the circumstances. A comparison must show the assessment of conditions and the choice between advancing and holding back. The original event and line-specific comparison contain identifiable principal acts and outcomes and are suitable as retrospective analogies. They do not establish that participants cited the Xiang.

005 Line H01 Qian Liu Xiu Founds the Eastern Han — Leadership Must Create Lasting Order▶

九五｜

005 case_id: XCASE-H01-L5 | global_line_no: 005 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: full_paragraph_translation_pending_QA | publish_status: editorial_review

As Wang Mang’s regime collapsed, armed groups across the country competed with one another. Liu Xiu gradually acquired military and local support, first establishing a political claim of his own and then fighting forces that had not submitted. Even before the war had completely ended, his new regime had to sustain officials and ordinary civilian life in the areas it controlled.

After Wang Mang’s government fell, Liu Xiu founded the Eastern Han amid competition among rival leaders. He gradually brought the principal regions under his rule and then reorganized officials, household registrations, taxes, and labor obligations. Rebuilding a state required both dealing with warfare and restoring the functioning of everyday administration and production.

Liu Xiu ascended the throne in 25 CE and gradually unified the major regions thereafter. Once troops had pacified an area, local officials had to resume the administration of households, levies, and agricultural production, reconnecting day-to-day government with the postwar order. Reusing the dynastic name “Han” marked a definite political turning point, but the time needed to restore governance varied from one locality to another. Many years passed between the rise of rival leaders, the foundation of the Eastern Han, and the consolidation of control over the principal regions.

If local household records were inaccurate after the war, the court had difficulty organizing collections and determining how many troops could be called up. As Liu Xiu’s controlled territory grew, officials had to extend renewed registration and productive activity to newly pacified areas. Unification and administration overlapped in time; they did not suddenly become complete together in a single year.

Liu Xiu establishes the Eastern Han and restores the order of government: After Wang Mang’s regime collapsed, Liu Xiu founded the Eastern Han amid competing leaders, gradually unified the main regions, and reorganized officials, households, taxation, and labor services. Reconstituting government required both dealing with warfare and restarting everyday production and administration. As the Wang Mang regime broke down, armed factions struggled for control. Liu Xiu progressively gained military and local support, established his political authority, and then fought the forces that had not yet submitted. His establishment of the Eastern Han and gradual consolidation of unity illustrate the role leadership can play in creating order. This helps explain why someone occupying high office should produce tangible achievements. The Xiang states, “The flying dragon is in heaven; the great person brings things into being.” This entry focuses on “leaders creating a viable order.”

The emphasis of this line is accomplishing results from a position of high authority. The criterion is that those who hold power must produce concrete public or organizational outcomes. The original event and line-specific comparison contain recognizable central acts and consequences and are suitable as retrospective analogies. This must not be represented as evidence that historical participants quoted the Xiang.

006 Line H01 Qian Fu Jian’s Defeat at the Fei River — Even Great Power Has Limits▶

上九｜

006 case_id: XCASE-H01-L6 | global_line_no: 006 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: full_paragraph_translation_pending_QA | publish_status: editorial_review

Fu Jian of Former Qin controlled large areas of northern China and prepared a major attack on Eastern Jin. His extensive realm allowed him to mobilize armies, but also required troops drawn from different backgrounds to act in concert throughout a distant campaign. Eastern Jin, meanwhile, had to confront the pressure of a powerful southward offensive in the Jianghuai region.

Fu Jian launched a major campaign against Eastern Jin, only to suffer a rout when Jin forces counterattacked in the area of the Fei River. Former Qin’s apparent advantage in troop numbers did not automatically produce dependable organization and command. After the battle, the divisions within the territory under Fu Jian’s rule became more pronounced.

The two armies fought near the Fei River in 383 CE, and Former Qin’s army collapsed after a counterattack. Fu Jian failed to complete the southern expedition. Forces previously held together under his regime reassessed their situations after the defeat, and divisions emerged in succession. Ancient histories offer dramatic descriptions of the battle, and the number of troops cannot necessarily be established precisely. The clear sequence of events is large-scale mobilization, defeat at the Fei River, and the decline of Former Qin’s ability to maintain control.

Before its advance southward, Former Qin had to supply food and military orders for a distant expedition; after defeat, it also had to preserve routes of retreat for troops of different origins. The collapse at the Fei River rapidly affected the existing political structure. Groups that had previously accepted Fu Jian’s command began to make different choices as the military situation changed.

Fu Jian’s southern expedition ends in defeat at the Fei River: He marched against Eastern Jin with a major army but was routed by a Jin counterattack near the Fei River. Former Qin’s apparent numerical superiority did not automatically provide stable organization or superior command, and internal fragmentation became more visible after the defeat. Fu Jian had controlled broad regions of northern China and could mobilize troops, but still had to coordinate forces of different origins during a distant campaign. His defeat despite the advantage of numbers makes the episode an analogy for an overextended dragon: power and scale cannot guarantee that an advantage will last indefinitely. The Xiang states, “The overreaching dragon has cause for regret; fullness cannot endure.” The focus is on “the limits of apparent strength.”

This line concerns the difficulty of sustaining power at its peak and the regret produced by excess. The criterion is to explain how overexpansion causes adverse consequences. The original event and line-specific comparison present identifiable principal acts and outcomes, making them suitable for retrospective analogy. They do not justify claiming that historical participants cited the Xiang.

007 Line H02 Kun From Tianbao Prosperity to the An Lushan Rebellion — Small Cracks Can Become a Crisis▶

初九｜

007 case_id: XCASE-H02-L1 | global_line_no: 007 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: full_paragraph_translation_pending_QA | publish_status: editorial_review

“Treading on frost, hard ice is coming”: the initial condensation of yin foretells what will follow if the same course continues.

During Emperor Xuanzong’s reign, the Tang court had enjoyed prosperity and governed an extensive territory. At the same time, commanders of frontier garrisons were gaining ever greater military power. An Lushan controlled frontier forces, and the political tension between the central government and regional authorities became increasingly difficult to manage as power accumulated in their hands.

Xuanzong’s reign had seen prosperity and expansion, but problems involving the military power of frontier commands and their relationship with the central court continued to build. In 755, An Lushan raised a rebellion that shattered the court’s control over events. The prolonged conflict affected the population, state finances, and regional political authority.

When An Lushan rebelled in 755, the Tang’s established order came under attack, and Emperor Xuanzong left Chang’an. The war continued for years, disrupting population movements, fiscal revenue, and the balance of local military and political power. The outbreak of rebellion can be assigned a date, but the underlying relationship between military commands and the central court had developed over a much longer period. A narrative confined to anecdotes from the palace would fail to explain why the extended war transformed the way the Tang state was governed.

Regional military governors controlled soldiers and local resources. The court’s prosperity did not, by itself, guarantee its control over those commands. After An Lushan’s uprising, his forces advanced along their route, while the court faced decisions about defense and withdrawal. The long war also increased the degree to which local authorities handled their own finances and military affairs; its effects extended far beyond the events of 755.

From prosperity in the late Tianbao era to the An Lushan Rebellion: Xuanzong’s reign included prosperity and expansion, but tensions between military authority in the frontier commands and the politics of the central court continued to accumulate. An Lushan rebelled in 755, disrupting the court’s grip on events, and the ensuing long war affected the population, finances, and regional power. During Xuanzong’s reign, the court had maintained prosperity and a broad territory, even as frontier commanders gradually acquired greater military strength. Well before the rebellion, the concentration of military authority on the frontiers presented structural risks. Just as frost gradually becomes solid ice, accumulating changes must be recognized early instead of being addressed only once rebellion erupts. The Xiang says: “Treading on frost, hard ice approaches: yin has begun to congeal. By following that course gradually, hard ice is reached.” This entry focuses on “small cracks becoming a crisis.”

The central point of this line is the accumulation of minor warning signs. The comparison must show the passage from early indications to a subsequent crisis. Both the original event and its line-specific comparison identify central actions and consequences and are suitable for a retrospective analogy. It must still not be claimed that the historical participants quoted the Xiang.

008 Line H02 Kun Emperor Wen of Han Abolishes the Land Tax — Make Governance Practical▶

九二｜

008 case_id: XCASE-H02-L2 | global_line_no: 008 | editorial_grade: B | translation_status: full_paragraph_translation_pending_QA | publish_status: editorial_review

“The movement of the second six is straight and square”: upright action needs no artifice; the way of the earth becomes evident.

During Emperor Wen’s reign, the imperial court paid attention to agriculture and the burdens borne by ordinary people. Farmers obtained their harvests through cultivation, while the state drew revenue from land taxes and other levies. If the court reduced one source of taxation, it also had to consider how much less the treasury would subsequently collect.

The “Basic Annals of Emperor Wen” in the Records of the Grand Historian records that, in the thirteenth year of his reign, Emperor Wen ordered the abolition of the land tax out of concern for agriculture and the burden on the people. The measure reduced part of the revenue the state collected from agricultural production and illustrated a ruler’s choice between fiscal income and the livelihood of the population.

The Records of the Grand Historian states that Emperor Wen ordered the land tax abolished in his thirteenth year. The edict concerned one particular category of revenue collected from land. Other taxes and labor services remained in various localities; it would therefore be incorrect to say that the state ceased to obtain any resources whatsoever from the people. Once the policy was announced, local officials had to adjust collections in accordance with the edict before residents could experience the change. This historical episode provides a specific measure and year, but whether different farming households benefited equally requires further study.

Upon receiving the tax-exemption edict, local officials had to make new arrangements for revenue formerly obtained from agricultural land. Farm households were relieved of this particular levy, but whether they still owed other taxes or labor services must be examined separately. The actual scope of the policy must not be exaggerated merely because the word “exemption” was used.

Emperor Wen of Han orders the abolition of the land tax: According to the “Basic Annals of Emperor Wen” in the Records of the Grand Historian, in the thirteenth year of his reign Emperor Wen abolished the land tax because he was concerned about agriculture and the burdens borne by the people. The measure reduced a portion of the revenue collected by the state from agricultural production, showing a ruler making a choice between public finances and popular livelihood. During Emperor Wen’s reign, the court gave attention to agriculture and the people’s burdens. His reduction of the land tax directly changed what the population was required to bear. This can be compared with the straight and square conduct of government: measures should be clear, practical, and capable of implementation in everyday life. The Xiang says: “The movement of the six in the second place is straight because it is square. Without contrivance, nothing is unfavorable; the way of the earth shines forth.” This entry focuses on “making government work in practice.”

The emphasis of this line is upright, principled conduct and the capacity to support others with generous virtue. The comparison must focus on clear and upright standards together with sustained support. The original case may be retained, but the analogy covers only part of the conditions expressed by the line. The inference should therefore be narrowed, with its applicable scope and whatever the historical evidence does not establish stated directly.

Grade B: single-round revision — complete translation

Using “E41 — Emperor Wen of Han Issues an Edict Abolishing the Land Tax” as its historical setting, the key ideas of this line are upright conduct and generous, sustained support. The event can suggest a relevant situation, but the analogy is more complete only where upright standards and continuing support are central. Here the comparison is restricted to identifiable actions, limitations, and consequences. Later outcomes must not be treated as if they were known at the time, nor should it be asserted that the participants acted on the basis of the Zhouyi or the Xiang.

009 Line H02 Kun Xiao He Sustains the Chu–Han Campaigns from the Rear — Work Behind the Scenes Can Succeed▶

九三｜

009 case_id: XCASE-H02-L3 | global_line_no: 009 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: full_paragraph_translation_pending_QA | publish_status: editorial_review

“Concealed excellence may be maintained with integrity”: its strengths emerge when the moment is appropriate; service need not entail taking personal credit.

During the Chu–Han conflict, the armies led by Liu Bang at the front constantly needed provisions and new recruits. Guanzhong, which was under his control, offered the means to transport supplies and maintain household registration. If local administration came to a halt, even short-term successes on the battlefield would be difficult to sustain.

During the struggle between Chu and Han, Xiao He remained mainly in Guanzhong, managing the population, military provisions, and the replenishment of troops so that Liu Bang’s front-line forces could continue receiving support. Historical works including the Book of Han describe these rear-area operations as an important condition enabling the Han army to carry on fighting.

Xiao He stayed in Guanzhong and organized local government, sending personnel and grain to the front. Whenever an army exhausted its resources, the rear had to recruit and transport more supplies again. In describing the Han army’s victories, the Book of Han and other records also note Xiao He’s administrative and logistical work. Such duties do not appear in the spectacle of a pitched battle, yet they are carried out between one engagement and another. The assessment of military merit therefore involves more than the position of a front-line commander.

Replenishing troops meant more than writing a number on a register: people had to be organized locally, grain supplies maintained, and both sent to the front. Xiao He’s administrative responsibilities were connected to each successive demand placed on Liu Bang’s forces, enabling the Han army to retain the manpower and supplies to fight again after repeated engagements.

Xiao He supports the Chu–Han conflict from Guanzhong: While Chu and Han contended for power, Xiao He stayed largely in Guanzhong, managing population records, supplies, and troop reinforcements so Liu Bang’s forces at the front could receive sustained support. The Book of Han and other historical records regard these rear-area operations as an important condition for the Han army’s continued fighting. During the Chu–Han War, Liu Bang’s front-line troops continually needed provisions and fresh recruits. Xiao He supported the front from the rear without needing to demonstrate his value in battle. His example helps explain how one may use personal strengths in an appropriate position and thereby contribute to the success of the larger undertaking. The Xiang says: “Concealing one’s brilliance and remaining steadfast means bringing it forth at the right time. Perhaps serving in the king’s affairs reveals the breadth of one’s wisdom.” The focus is on “work behind the scenes can also achieve results.”

The point of this line is to retain one’s talents and virtues inwardly and put them to use when the time is right. The comparison must be supported by evidence both of preserving ability and of using it at an appropriate moment. The event and the line-specific analogy contain identifiable central actions and outcomes and are suitable as retrospective comparisons. It must not be claimed that the historical participants quoted the Xiang.

010 Line H02 Kun King Wen’s Traditional Imprisonment at Youli — Exercise Caution Under Threat▶

九四｜

010 case_id: XCASE-H02-L4 | global_line_no: 010 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: full_paragraph_translation_pending_QA | publish_status: editorial_review

“A tied sack brings no blame”: self-restraint and care prevent harm.

In the closing years of the Shang, the influence of the Zhou people was growing. Later historical writings portray the relationship between Xibo Chang and the Shang royal house as one of mounting pressure. The “Basic Annals of Zhou” in the Records of the Grand Historian says that the Shang ruler imprisoned Xibo Chang at Youli, requiring his retainers to find ways to sustain Zhou activities while seeking his release.

The “Basic Annals of Zhou” in the Records of the Grand Historian records that Xibo Chang was imprisoned at Youli by the Shang ruler and that his retainers sought to have him freed. This traditional account portrays a powerful ruler suppressing a political rival. The subsequent rise of the Zhou must not be read backwards as proof that every action at the time was already predetermined.

His retainers attempted to rescue him, and Xibo Chang eventually left Youli. The story survives in historical narratives compiled much later; its chronology and reported conversations cannot be verified point by point in the way modern documents can. After his release, Zhou power developed through subsequent events; he did not gain control of the realm on the day he emerged from prison. Later traditions that he “elaborated the Changes while imprisoned” require additional evidence if they are introduced into the story. The imprisonment and the release already possess a clear narrative sequence of their own.

While Xibo Chang was imprisoned, his retainers continued to maintain Zhou’s external relations and sought to persuade the Shang ruler to agree to his release. Only after being freed could he return to his former political activities. Posterity knows that the Zhou dynasty later rose to power, but people at that time could not have known that outcome in advance; the period of imprisonment was marked by genuine uncertainty.

Traditional accounts of King Wen’s imprisonment at Youli: The “Basic Annals of Zhou” in the Records of the Grand Historian records that the Shang ruler imprisoned Xibo Chang at Youli and that his retainers sought to secure his freedom. The account depicts a strong ruler repressing a political rival; Zhou’s later development should not be read back as proof that every step was predetermined at the time. Toward the end of the Shang, Zhou power was growing, and later historical works present Xibo Chang’s relationship with the Shang royal house as fraught with pressure. Traditional accounts of King Wen’s captivity at Youli can be read as an example of cautious self-preservation under intense pressure. This interpretation does not assume that he followed the specific wording of this commentary or used any particular technique to avert disaster. The Xiang says: “A tied-up sack brings no blame: through caution one avoids harm.” This entry focuses on “acting carefully in dangerous circumstances.”

The key to this line is restraint in speech and conduct, and caution in avoiding harm. The required evidence is action that demonstrates prudent self-restraint in a high-risk situation. The event and line comparison identify central actions and consequences and are suitable as retrospective analogies. It must not be claimed that the participants quoted the Xiang.

011 Line H02 Kun Feng Yi, the General of the Great Tree — Inner Character Outweighs Display▶

九五｜

011 case_id: XCASE-H02-L5 | global_line_no: 011 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: full_paragraph_translation_pending_QA | publish_status: editorial_review

“The yellow lower garment brings supreme good fortune”: true refinement resides within and respects its proper place.

In the early Eastern Han, commanders accumulated military achievements while taking part in campaigns to establish the regime. Every result was connected with honors conferred by the court, and colleagues inevitably discussed who had achieved what and where. Feng Yi himself led troops and carried out assignments; he was not an onlooker standing outside the army.

The Book of the Later Han records that, when commanders discussed their achievements, Feng Yi would often withdraw beneath a tree, earning the epithet “General of the Great Tree.” The text also describes his modest, retiring demeanor and his reluctance to compete with others. The episode concerns how men with military achievements interacted with colleagues during the founding of a new regime.

According to the Book of the Later Han, Feng Yi often withdrew beneath a tree when the generals gathered to discuss their achievements, and so was called the “General of the Great Tree.” He continued to carry out military duties; avoiding disputes about credit did not mean withdrawing from the founding of the regime. The historian included his movement toward the tree in his biography, and later readers remembered his humility. Only when this depiction of character is read alongside his actual military accomplishments does the context in which the nickname arose become visible.

As the Eastern Han regime was being founded, generals had different theaters of operations and troops under their command. The achievements they discussed bore upon their future political positions. Feng Yi’s move beneath the tree took place on specific occasions when others gathered to contest credit for military victories. His refusal to compete verbally for rank did not amount to denying his participation in the fighting or his acceptance of appointments from the court.

Feng Yi avoids competing for military credit and is called the General of the Great Tree: According to the Book of the Later Han, when generals spoke of their own accomplishments, Feng Yi would often withdraw beneath a tree, giving rise to his nickname. The book also depicts his modest refusal to contend with others, offering a portrait of how a figure with military merit dealt with his colleagues during the foundation of a regime. In the early Eastern Han, generals built up achievements through their campaigns. Feng Yi’s withdrawal to a tree while others discussed their merits offers a historical portrait that can be compared with remaining centered and observing one’s proper place: ability and virtue are expressed through everyday conduct. The Xiang says: “The yellow lower garment brings supreme good fortune; refinement lies within.” This entry focuses on “inner cultivation matters more than outward display.”

The emphasis of this line is inner refinement, balanced judgment, and knowing the bounds of one’s role. The comparison should emphasize inward character and a sense of proportion, not simply public benefit. The event and line-specific comparison contain identifiable central actions and outcomes and are suitable as retrospective analogies. It must not be claimed that the historical participants quoted the Xiang.

012 Line H02 Kun The KMT–Communist Alliance Collapses in 1927 — A Broken Alliance Turns into Confrontation▶

上九｜

The two parties envisioned future allocations of power and forms of social mobilization differently, and disagreements within the alliance gradually accumulated.

The First United Front experienced conflicts over interests, political direction, and power during the Northern Expedition. The 1927 party purge in Shanghai and the subsequent split with the Communists in Wuhan destroyed the cooperation, accompanied by extensive political violence. Following the break, the sides moved toward a prolonged military struggle. The events in Shanghai and Wuhan occurred at different times, involved different actors, and harmed different victims; they must not be collapsed into an abstract “disagreement” with no concrete course of events.

Political organizations that had operated within the same city during the alliance now faced one another’s memberships, registers, and armed personnel as the partnership broke apart. Shanghai and Wuhan took different steps in succession, while those involved risked flight, imprisonment, and death. The ensuing long-term confrontation made restoration of the former relationship even more difficult.

The KMT–Communist alliance breaks down in 1927: During the Northern Expedition, the first cooperation between the Kuomintang and Communist Party encountered conflicts of interest, political direction, and power. The 1927 party purge in Shanghai and the split with the Communists in Wuhan shattered the alliance and involved extensive political violence. Long military confrontation followed. During the First United Front, both parties had participated in the Northern Expedition, but the advance of the front brought problems involving the army, municipal governments, and workers’ and peasants’ movements to the surface. The breakdown in 1927 turned political disagreement into violent confrontation. The regret of being trapped in ignorance arises from remaining alone and distant from reality.

Historical narrative — four original paragraphs translated in order

In 1900, Boxer activity, foreign intervention, and decision-making within the Qing court became entangled, while the diplomatic and military situation in Beijing deteriorated rapidly. The court’s approach to foreign troops and regional officials’ judgments about the security of their own jurisdictions had already begun to diverge.

After the Boxer movement and foreign military intervention intensified, the Qing court issued an edict declaring war on foreign powers, further widening the crisis. Allied troops entered Beijing, the court fled, and the Boxer Protocol was signed the following year. Some regional officials pursued the Mutual Protection of Southeast China, also showing that central and regional authorities did not share the same judgment.

The Qing government issued its declaration of war; hostilities spread, allied forces entered Beijing, and the court fled. Some officials in the southeast pursued mutual-protection arrangements, revealing that different regions did not respond uniformly. The Boxer Protocol was signed the next year, imposing serious consequences on the court and population. Any discussion of mistakes made by the central government must also explicitly acknowledge the armed incursion by foreign powers. The transition from local movements to international war resulted from more than one person’s decision.

After the war edict, not all officials across the empire responded in the same way: the southeastern mutual-protection arrangements highlight the difference between central and regional choices. The allied occupation of Beijing and treaty indemnities transformed a crisis in political judgment into military and fiscal consequences. Different actors made decisions and bore costs at each stage.

The Qing court’s loss of control over foreign-war decisions in 1900: as the Boxer movement and foreign military intervention escalated, the government declared war, further expanding the crisis. Some regional officials pursued southeastern mutual protection, demonstrating conflicting assessments between center and regions. Boxer activity, foreign intervention, and court decision-making had together produced a rapidly worsening situation. Treating complex international and military circumstances as though one-sided expectations could determine the outcome had severe consequences. The episode illustrates how distance from reliable facts can trap decision-makers in misconceptions. The Xiang attributes the plight of ignorance to being far removed from reality. This entry emphasizes the danger of judging without access to the facts.

The line addresses being trapped because one is removed from actual circumstances. The test is evidence of informational isolation and departure from reality. The good fortune of the youthful learner comes from being receptive and modest.

Historical narrative — four original paragraphs translated in order

When Sun Quan governed Jiangdong, Lü Meng was already serving as a military officer, but battlefield experience could not replace knowledge of earlier political and military events. Lü Meng cited the pressure of military duties; Sun Quan nevertheless urged him to study historical accounts while continuing his work. The advice was meant to broaden a commander’s resources for judgment, not to make him resign his commission and specialize in classical scholarship.

According to the Jiangbiao Zhuan, quoted by Pei Songzhi in his annotations to the Records of the Three Kingdoms, Sun Quan encouraged Lü Meng to read in order to understand history and practical experience, not to become a scholar devoted exclusively to the classics. After Lü Meng followed this advice, his knowledge grew, and Lu Su’s assessment of him also changed.

Lü Meng began to read and later discussed affairs of state with Lu Su. Lu Su discovered that he could now address questions formerly unfamiliar to him and revised his opinion. This account survives in material quoted in the annotations to the Records of the Three Kingdoms; the polished dialogues commonly presented in classrooms underwent subsequent retelling. What the historical account permits us to identify is encouragement to learn, acceptance of advice, and a change in a colleague’s judgment. Their meeting did not guarantee the outcome of every campaign Lü Meng would later undertake.

Sun Quan did not transfer Lü Meng’s military post to someone else: he wanted him to gain useful experience through reading while continuing his existing responsibilities. Lu Su’s later reaction came in conversation, not as the result of a single formal examination. Historical judgments concerning a figure’s growth coexist with the concrete military responsibilities that the person continued to shoulder.

Sun Quan encourages Lü Meng to deepen his learning: in the Jiangbiao Zhuan passage quoted by Pei Songzhi in the Records of the Three Kingdoms annotations, the aim was to gain historical understanding and practical insight rather than specialize in the classics. Lü Meng’s learning developed, and Lu Su revised his assessment. Already an experienced officer, Lü Meng needed more than battlefield experience to judge past political and military affairs. His willingness to accept encouragement is an example of a political and military figure acquiring knowledge. The Xiang speaks of the good fortune of an inexperienced learner who responds with deference. This entry emphasizes willingness to learn as the starting point for change.

It is advantageous to ward off raiders because those above and below act in harmony.

The southeastern coast of Ming China suffered raids by wokou forces, and local troops faced difficulties in recruiting men, training them, and fighting effectively. At Yiwu, Qi Jiguang stressed selection, discipline, and coordinated action. In campaigns against coastal raiders he employed formations and weapons designed to support one another. His military-training writings repeatedly stressed turning instruction into actions and standards that troops could actually carry out.

After being assigned to their units, the men practiced coordinating different weapons, positions, and movements. From recruitment and unit formation to drill, it took time for men to learn how to cover and support one another. If recruits never trained together in peacetime and first tried to cooperate only when they encountered an enemy, differences in weapon length and unit positions could interfere with one another. Qi required soldiers to drill repeatedly under a common set of rules so that battlefield commands had a practical foundation. The troops subsequently still had to adapt to changing opponents and conditions in different theaters.

Qi Jiguang’s recruitment and coordinated training at Yiwu: he emphasized the selection of soldiers, discipline, and cooperation, and employed mutually supporting weapons and formations in campaigns against coastal raiders. His training manuals likewise stressed translating rules into executable movements. The southeast coast of Ming China faced incursions, and local armed forces struggled with recruitment and preparation. Qi’s training brought individual capacities together into organized units. As a retrospective comparison, the episode suggests that repelling aggression depends on cooperation between commanders and their troops, and it also underscores the need for a clearly defensive purpose in the use of force. 025 Line H05 Xu Zhou Yafu Waits for an Opening during the Rebellion of the Seven States — Waiting Can Be a Strategy▶

初九｜

025 case_id: XCASE-H05-L1 | global_line_no: 025 | event_id: E05 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective comparison) | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: complete_paragraph_translation | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang commentary — full English translation

Waiting on the outskirts means not venturing rashly into difficulty. Perseverance is beneficial and without blame because the usual standards have not been abandoned.

Received Traditional Chinese explanation — full English translation

“Waiting outside the city, it is appropriate to maintain constancy and thus avoid misfortune.” The Xiang explains this as not recklessly entering danger. “Maintaining constancy is beneficial and without blame” means that established standards have not been lost.

Original review focus — English translation

Avoid reckless action and maintain a steady course.

Historical narrative — four original paragraphs in order

In 154 BCE, seven kingdoms raised forces against the Han, and the armies of Wu and Chu advanced, leaving the kingdom of Liang in urgent need of relief. The court sent Zhou Yafu to command its army. He had to weigh both Liang’s immediate peril and the supply situation of the principal rebel army. If the Han army reacted immediately to every enemy movement, it might be forced to fight under conditions chosen by its opponent.

After the rebellion began, Zhou Yafu did not constantly seek a direct, decisive engagement. He held his position and sent troops to cut the Wu–Chu army’s supply lines. He waited until the enemy encountered difficulties obtaining provisions and then exploited the moment of its retreat. Liang meanwhile endured pressure, making this deployment politically contentious.

Zhou Yafu maintained his own positions while dispatching other forces to interrupt the Wu–Chu supply routes. The danger facing Liang did not disappear, and Zhou was criticized politically for failing to come to its immediate rescue. Only after the enemy’s provisions were disrupted and its offensive became unsustainable did he strike during its withdrawal. Both the victory over the rebels and the risks borne by Liang belong to the outcome. This campaign illustrates how interference with supplies in the rear could alter conditions on the battlefield.

Zhou Yafu’s decision meant that Liang could not immediately receive comprehensive support, much to the displeasure of the Liang court. At the same time, the Han army still had to defend its own positions and prevent the enemy from readily redirecting its attack. Cutting supply lines was not passive observation: it was intended to make the offensive previously sustainable for the Wu–Chu forces progressively harder to maintain.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

Zhou Yafu’s waiting for an opening during the Rebellion of the Seven States: after the uprising began, he did not continually seek a frontal decision. He maintained his positions, disrupted the Wu–Chu supply lines, waited until the enemy faced shortages, and attacked as it withdrew. Liang endured pressure, making the deployment politically controversial. In 154 BCE, seven kingdoms rose against the Han, and Liang urgently needed assistance as the Wu–Chu armies advanced. Zhou did not immediately relieve Liang through a frontal battle as requested; he instead sought to cut the rebels’ supplies. This can be compared with keeping one’s distance and waiting without taking needless risks, rather than doing nothing. The Xiang states that waiting outside avoids a rash approach to danger and that perseverance does not abandon proper standards. This entry focuses on the lesson that waiting can itself be strategic.

Editorial suitability assessment — full translation

A — retain. The example shows a recognizable analogy in its actions and outcomes to avoiding rash danger while maintaining a steady course. It remains a retrospective comparison, not evidence that the historical figure cited the Yijing.

Interpretive boundary: This is a retrospective comparison, not evidence of an historical quotation of the Yijing.

Historical narrative — four original paragraphs in order

After victory in the War of Resistance against Japan in 1945, both the Nationalist government and the Chinese Communist Party faced questions of military reorganization, the takeover of local administrations, and the form of the national government. To avoid a wider internal war, they needed to write down principles both sides could accept while also addressing which forces actually controlled troops on the ground.

Following the war, representatives of the Nationalist government and the Communist Party negotiated in Chongqing and produced the Summary of Talks between the Government and Representatives of the Chinese Communist Party, commonly known as the Double Tenth Agreement. They articulated principles for a peaceful reconstruction of the country, but such central issues as the armies and control of local governments were not fully resolved.

Representatives held talks in Chongqing and publicized the Summary of Talks, or Double Tenth Agreement. The document set out aims concerning peaceful nation-building, but the fundamental questions of military forces and local authority remained unsettled. After publication, disputes over effective control and military clashes continued to develop. Talks, an agreed text, and the implementation of that text are three related stages that do not take place simultaneously. Issuing the agreement must not be described as if peace had already been secured.

What could be written at the negotiating table did not necessarily correspond to territories already controlled by the respective armies. After representatives published the agreement, their organizations still had to communicate the commitments internally and decide whether to implement them. The difficulty of sustaining peace after the war must also be understood through the sequence of, and gaps between, these practical actions.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

The Chongqing negotiations and the Double Tenth Agreement: representatives negotiated after the war, producing a document setting out principles for peaceful nation-building, while the central disputes over armies and local government remained unresolved. After victory against Japan in 1945, both sides also faced military reorganization, territorial takeovers, and the problem of establishing a political system. The talks unfolded in an atmosphere of mutual distrust. They can illustrate the value of keeping channels of communication open amid disagreement, but signing an agreement does not prove that further war can be prevented. The Xiang says that one may wait on the sand and encounter criticism while seeking a favorable conclusion. This entry emphasizes continuing negotiations despite criticism.

Editorial suitability assessment — full translation

B — partial fit. The agreement did not bring lasting peace. The favorable ending suggested by the line can be applied only to the immediate production of a negotiated document, and the difficulties of implementing it must be explained.

The agreement failed to produce lasting peace; a favorable outcome applies only to the moment when the talks yielded a document. Obstacles to implementation must be acknowledged. Readers should distinguish historical facts from editorial analogy and from unsupported claims about consequences.

Revised line-specific comparison — full translation

Fundamental divisions over armies and local political authority remained, and conflict continued afterward. A temporary agreement must not be portrayed as permanent peace.

Historical narrative — four original paragraphs in order

In 1449, the Ming emperor Yingzong personally led troops north against the Oirats. A vast marching force required coordination of provisions, transport, and orders. Neither the advance northward nor the return journey could succeed on troop numbers alone. If deployments during the return were obstructed, losses at the front could directly affect the central government.

Emperor Yingzong led the army north against the Oirats, but during the return it suffered a devastating defeat near Tumu and the emperor was captured. The court faced a severe crisis. The episode involved decisions, movement, logistics, and command, and the defense of Beijing subsequently had to be reorganized.

The Ming army was struck heavily near Tumu and Yingzong was captured. On receiving the news, officials in Beijing had to reorganize military defense and affairs connected with the imperial succession to prevent a battlefield defeat from spreading into a wider catastrophe. Historical sources differ on troop numbers and the responsibility of some individuals, but the sequence is clear: departure on campaign, difficulties on the return, capture of the emperor, and emergency measures in the capital. Beijing’s defense had to begin while the emperor was still a prisoner.

The capture of the emperor immediately had consequences beyond an ordinary military retreat. Officials had to decide how the court would continue to exercise authority, and troops defending the city needed to know whose orders to follow. The capital’s emergency defense was organized with incomplete information from the front. Information carried from the Tumu battlefield to the capital tightly linked the military disaster to political decisions in Beijing.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

The Tumu Crisis exposes fragility in expedition planning: Emperor Yingzong led an army north against the Oirats, suffered a devastating defeat near Tumu during the return, and was captured, plunging the court into crisis. Decisions, marching arrangements, supplies, and command all formed part of the problem, and Beijing’s defenses had to be reorganized. In 1449 the emperor himself accompanied the army. The hurried campaign and troubled withdrawal exposed problems of planning and logistics. The case can prompt reflection on how one’s own decisions increase danger, rather than attributing every disaster solely to an outside enemy. The Xiang speaks of danger outside and of inviting an attacker through one’s own actions; it calls for alert caution. This entry focuses on being especially careful as risk grows.

Editorial suitability assessment — full translation

A — retain. The example shows a recognizable analogy in the actions and outcomes concerning self-created risk and a cautious response. It remains a retrospective interpretation and cannot be used as evidence that the historical actors cited the Yijing.

Both the people who survived and the losses suffered on the spot were part of the withdrawal.

031 Line H06 Song Song and Liao End the Immediate War with the Chanyuan Treaty — Do Not Prolong a Dispute Indefinitely▶

初九｜

031 case_id: XCASE-H06-L1 | global_line_no: 031 | event_id: E06 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective comparison) | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: complete_paragraph_translation | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English rendering

Do not prolong the undertaking, because litigation and contention cannot continue indefinitely. Although there may be some criticism, the issues in dispute become clear.

Received Traditional Chinese interpretation — full English translation

“Do not allow litigation to continue; even if there is minor criticism, ultimately there is good fortune.” The Xiang Commentary explains that a state of contention must not persist indefinitely. “Although there is some criticism” means that the arguments become clear.

Original review focus — English translation

Do not prolong contention.

Historical narrative — four source paragraphs, translated in order

After Liao forces marched south, the Song court had to decide whether fighting on the frontier should expand further. Emperor Zhenzong reached Chanzhou, confronting decision-makers directly with conditions at the front and enabling envoys from both states to travel back and forth over ceasefire terms. Both Song and Liao possessed military forces; neither could dispense with subsequent practical arrangements simply by saying that the two sides were now reconciled.

After the Liao advance and Emperor Zhenzong’s arrival at Chanzhou, negotiations led to the Treaty of Chanyuan in 1005. Song undertook to provide annual payments to Liao, while each government retained its authority and an established order along the frontier. The arrangement carried a fiscal cost, but it also reduced large-scale warfare for a considerable period thereafter.

The negotiations culminated in the Treaty of Chanyuan: both states kept their own governments and Song undertook annual payments. After the agreement, the major campaign then under way ceased and the border had a framework both sides could invoke; the annual payments simultaneously became a recurring item of court expenditure. Warfare on a comparable scale was avoided for a long period, but diplomatic negotiations and frontier friction did not vanish. Military and fiscal consequences of the treaty both persisted.

The treaty settled the immediate fighting and also provided agreed terms that subsequent envoys could cite. Once the armies halted their advance, the court still had to prepare the annual payments on schedule; people in frontier communities meanwhile lived under the new arrangements. The direct benefits of the ceasefire and the continuing costs were not the same for every participant.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

Song and Liao end the immediate war through the Treaty of Chanyuan: after Liao troops advanced south and Emperor Zhenzong arrived at Chanzhou, the sides negotiated and concluded the treaty in 1005. Song supplied annual payments to Liao while the two governments maintained their respective authority and frontier order. This arrangement imposed a financial cost while reducing major clashes for a considerable time. The treaty ended the immediate Song–Liao military confrontation through negotiation. It can illustrate the need to bring a dispute to a close; nevertheless, treaty terms must still be assessed against security and resource burdens at the time. The Xiang Commentary states, “Do not prolong the undertaking, because contention cannot last; though some criticism arises, the arguments are clarified.” The focus is “Do not prolong a dispute indefinitely.”

Editorial suitability assessment — full translation

A — retain. The historical actions and outcome provide a recognizable analogy to not prolonging contention. This remains a retrospective interpretive comparison, not evidence that the historical actors actually quoted the Yijing.

Interpretive boundary: The case is an editorial retrospective comparison; it is not evidence of a historical quotation of the Yijing.

032 Line H06 Song Liu Bei Regroups after the Defeat at Changban — Avoid a Frontal Clash When Outmatched▶

九二｜

032 case_id: XCASE-H06-L2 | global_line_no: 032 | event_id: E33 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective comparison) | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: complete_paragraph_translation | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English rendering

When one cannot prevail in a dispute, one returns and withdraws into concealment. To contend from a subordinate position against those above invites trouble upon oneself.

Received Traditional Chinese interpretation — full English translation

“Unable to prevail in litigation, return to one’s proper place, change one’s intention, and remain steadfast in what is right; then there is good fortune.” The Xiang Commentary explains the return as withdrawal and escape; contending from below against those above invites trouble.

Original review focus — English translation

Limit contention when the balance of power is unfavorable.

Historical narrative — four source paragraphs, translated in order

As Cao Cao advanced south into Jingzhou, Liu Bei could no longer readily maintain his former position there. He led his troops and accompanying people southward. Not everyone in the column was a soldier capable of rapid marching, and the distances separating the pursuing force from the column and its potential sources of assistance kept changing.

When Cao Cao entered Jingzhou, Liu Bei retreated south. His forces were pursued and routed at Changban. He subsequently joined forces with Guan Yu, Liu Qi, and others, and sought cooperation with Sun Quan. Withdrawal enabled some forces to survive, but it was neither smooth nor free of severe losses.

Liu Bei’s army suffered a major blow under pursuit by Cao Cao’s troops at Changban. He later brought forces together with Guan Yu, Liu Qi, and others, gradually recovering some usable military strength and seeking cooperation with Sun Quan. The alliance that followed did not turn the rout at Changban into a successful withdrawal perfectly calculated from the outset. Departure from Jingzhou, pursuit, partial regrouping, and external alliance were separate stages, while the people accompanying the army faced immediate danger.

Civilians traveled with the column, so Liu Bei’s withdrawal could not proceed at the pace of a purely military movement. After the pursuers scattered his forces at Changban, separated groups had to find each other again before talks with outside allies became possible. The people who survived and the losses sustained on the spot were both parts of the retreat.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

Liu Bei regroups after the defeat at Changban: when Cao Cao advanced into Jingzhou, Liu Bei withdrew south, was pursued and routed at Changban, and later joined Guan Yu, Liu Qi, and other forces before seeking cooperation with Sun Quan. The retreat preserved some strength but entailed severe losses. Liu Bei could no longer hold his position in Jingzhou and moved south with troops and accompanying people. His withdrawal after Changban can illustrate preserving a force when one lacks the strength to confront an adversary directly. This is a strategic analogy; hierarchical language about superiors and subordinates must not be used to restrict modern rights. The Xiang states that one who cannot win a dispute withdraws, while contention from below against those above invites misfortune. This entry emphasizes avoiding a head-on clash when outmatched.

Editorial suitability assessment — full translation

A — retain. The case provides a recognizable analogy to limiting contention under an imbalance of strength. The analogy is retrospective; it does not demonstrate that the participants actually cited the Yijing.

Interpretive boundary: The case is an editorial retrospective comparison; it is not evidence of a historical quotation of the Yijing.

033 Line H06 Song Feng Yi Declines to Compete for Credit and Becomes the Great Tree General — Fulfill Your Role Even after Achievement▶

九三｜

033 case_id: XCASE-H06-L3 | global_line_no: 033 | event_id: E15 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective comparison) | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: complete_paragraph_translation | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English rendering

Living upon the virtue inherited from earlier times, it is auspicious to follow the person above.

Received Traditional Chinese interpretation — full English translation

“Inheriting earlier virtue, there is still danger even when remaining upright, yet ultimately good fortune; when serving in royal affairs, do not claim the achievement as your own.” The Xiang Commentary explains that it is auspicious to follow one’s superior.

Original review focus — English translation

Inherit existing virtues and observe the responsibilities of one’s position.

Historical narrative — four source paragraphs, translated in order

During the establishment of the Eastern Han, commanders accumulated military achievements through campaigns. Each victory was connected with honors and rewards from the court, so colleagues naturally discussed who had earned which successes and where. Feng Yi himself commanded soldiers and carried out assignments; he was not an onlooker standing outside the army.

The Book of the Later Han records that when generals discussed their respective merits, Feng Yi often withdrew beneath a tree; hence he became known as the “Great Tree General.” The history also portrays his modesty and reluctance to compete. The account shows how men who had won military credit related to their colleagues during the building of a new regime.

According to the Book of the Later Han, whenever commanders gathered to recount their achievements, Feng Yi would often retire beneath a tree, thereby earning the epithet “Great Tree General.” He continued carrying out military duties; avoiding arguments over credit did not mean withdrawing from the process of establishing the regime. By including the episode beneath the tree in the biography, the historian preserved a picture of his modesty. Only by viewing that portrayal alongside his actual military service can we understand how the sobriquet arose.

During the founding of the Eastern Han, commanders held different fronts and forces; the merits they discussed could affect future political standing. Feng Yi’s withdrawal beneath the tree occurred on specific occasions when others gathered to claim credit. Declining to compete verbally for rank did not mean denying his participation in battle or rejecting appointments from the court.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

Feng Yi avoids arguments over credit and is called the Great Tree General: the Book of the Later Han says he often withdrew under a tree while other commanders discussed their achievements, and describes his modest, uncompetitive character. This account concerns relations among military men during the establishment of a dynasty. Their contributions brought honors and status, but Feng Yi did not rely on continued quarrels over merit to sustain his reputation. Military contribution and political position must nevertheless be considered separately. The Xiang states that living on earlier virtue and following one’s superior is auspicious. This case emphasizes fulfilling one’s proper role despite prior achievement.

Editorial suitability assessment — full translation

A — retain. A recognizable analogy can be made between the case and inheriting virtue while observing one’s proper role. This remains a later comparison, not evidence that Feng Yi invoked the Yijing.

Interpretive boundary: The case is an editorial retrospective comparison; it is not evidence of a historical quotation of the Yijing.

034 Line H06 Song Negotiations End the Detention Crisis of the Xi’an Incident — Change the Way a Conflict Is Handled▶

九四｜

034 case_id: XCASE-H06-L4 | global_line_no: 034 | event_id: E40 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective comparison) | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: complete_paragraph_translation | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English rendering

Return and accept the mandate; change course, remain secure and steadfast, and nothing essential will be lost.

Received Traditional Chinese interpretation — full English translation

“Unable to prevail in litigation, return to one’s proper place, change one’s intention, and remain firmly on the right path; this brings good fortune.” The Xiang explains that one does not lose what matters.

Original review focus — English translation

Redirect a conflict and remain steadfast in what is right.

Historical narrative — four source paragraphs, translated in order

In 1936, pressure to resist Japan was intensifying, while armed conflict continued between the Nationalist government and the Communist Party. Dissatisfied with Chiang Kai-shek’s policies, Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng detained him in Xi’an. An existing political disagreement suddenly became an immediate personal and military crisis.

Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng detained Chiang Kai-shek in Xi’an, triggering a political and military crisis. Negotiations among several parties led to Chiang’s release. The incident brought calls to end the civil war and jointly resist Japan into sharper focus, but commitments, subsequent measures, and the terms of cooperation remained contested.

The parties entered negotiations in the hope of ending the detention without further expanding the military conflict. Chiang Kai-shek was eventually released, and the questions of ending internal warfare and resisting Japan together became more prominent. Securing his release did not mean every condition of cooperation had been settled. Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng subsequently faced differing political consequences. The detention, negotiations, release, and arrangements that followed must be understood as successive but distinct stages.

After the detention became known to political and military groups, the parties had to assess Chiang’s safety and the possibility of new fighting. Negotiation enabled him to leave Xi’an, but it did not turn future cooperation among different factions into a long-term agreement that would implement itself. The circumstances of the individuals involved remained different after the incident.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

The Xi’an Incident’s detention crisis is ended through negotiation: Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng detained Chiang Kai-shek, generating a political and military emergency. Negotiations led to his release, while discussions about ending the civil war and jointly resisting Japan gained prominence. Yet the content of commitments and future cooperation remained disputed. With the pressure to resist Japan rising in 1936, conflict between the Nationalists and Communists had continued. Moving from forcible detention to multiparty talks can illustrate redirecting a conflict in time. The point is the change in method, not a justification of detention itself. The Xiang says to change course while remaining steadfast; this entry focuses on changing how conflict is handled.

Editorial suitability assessment — full translation

A — retain. The change in the method of handling the conflict offers a recognizable analogy to redirecting contention while observing a proper course. The analogy is retrospective, not evidence that the participants quoted the Yijing.

Interpretive boundary: The case is an editorial retrospective comparison; it is not evidence of a historical quotation of the Yijing.

035 Line H06 Song Bao Zheng Opposes Zhang Yaozuo’s Promotion through Palace Ties — Judge Appointments by Public Standards▶

九五｜

035 case_id: XCASE-H06-L5 | global_line_no: 035 | event_id: E21 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective comparison) | editorial_grade: B | translation_status: complete_paragraph_translation | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English rendering

In contention, there is supreme good fortune when decisions are guided by balance and rectitude.

Received Traditional Chinese interpretation — full English translation

“When a dispute is decided by someone impartial, there is great good fortune.” The Xiang Commentary explains that this is because the decision is balanced and upright.

Original review focus — English translation

Handle disputes with impartiality and principled judgment.

Historical narrative — four source paragraphs, translated in order

During the Northern Song reign of Emperor Renzong, Zhang Yaozuo gained promotion through family ties to the palace, drawing the attention of court officials. For remonstrance officials responsible for advising the throne, this was more than an individual change of office: it raised the question of whether appointments would be influenced by the relatives of imperial consorts.

Zhang Yaozuo’s rise through palace connections drew objections from Bao Zheng and other remonstrance officials. They presented memorials and argued with the court, asking the emperor to reconsider the appointment. The central issue is how officials attempted to place checks on the power to make personnel decisions.

Bao Zheng and others submitted memorials stating their objections and asking the emperor to reconsider Zhang Yaozuo’s appointments. The court disputed the respective roles of appointment authority and the right to remonstrate, and opinions were conveyed through formal documents and court audiences. This episode belonged to the procedure of appointing officials; it must not be recast as the fictional Judge Bao conducting a criminal trial of Zhang Yaozuo. The issues were who should hold office, on what grounds, and how the emperor should answer officials’ objections.

Remonstrance officials could not directly appoint or dismiss officials in the emperor’s place. They could submit opinions and continue making their case at court. Zhang Yaozuo’s appointments also have to be distinguished by post and date, rather than collapsing every dispute into a simple accusation that a palace relative was criminally guilty. What Bao Zheng left was a formal objection to a personnel decision.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

Bao Zheng opposes Zhang Yaozuo’s advancement through palace ties: Zhang was promoted because of his relationship with the imperial household, provoking objections from Bao Zheng and other remonstrance officials. Through memorials and debate at court, they asked the emperor to reconsider. The issue is how officials could check appointments. Bao Zheng’s opposition illustrates raising objections as part of a public duty, but he was a remonstrance official, not a neutral judge delivering a court verdict. The Xiang says that contention brings supreme good fortune through balance and rectitude. This entry focuses on handling disagreements according to public standards.

Editorial suitability assessment — full translation

B — partial correspondence. Bao Zheng was a remonstrance official rather than an impartial adjudicator. Public objection must be distinguished from a balanced and impartial judicial decision.

B-grade partial-fit assessment and single-revision guidance

One-time revision recommendation, adding a supplementary comparison rather than deleting the original: this example corresponds only in a limited way to settling disputes through balance and rectitude. Bao Zheng was a remonstrance official, not a neutral judge; public objection and impartial adjudication must be kept distinct. Readers must separate historical fact, editorial analogy, and inferences about effects unsupported by evidence.

Revised line-specific comparison — full translation

Revised line-specific comparison: Bao Zheng’s opposition to Zhang Yaozuo’s appointment was a public objection raised through the recognized remonstrance procedures, not a trial conducted by an impartial judge. The case can invite discussion of using public standards for personnel decisions, but it does not directly establish that the just resolution implied by “contention, supreme good fortune” had actually been achieved.

Single recheck — full translation

Single recheck: B — reasonable but limited, retain. The original narrative, case ID, and original evidence category are unchanged. Do not repeatedly seek an A grade.

Interpretive boundary: The case is an editorial retrospective comparison; it is not evidence of a historical quotation of the Yijing.

Even when one gains ceremonial distinction through contention, this is still not worthy of respect.
