Winning a title through conflict does not necessarily command respect.

Historical narrative — four source paragraphs, translated in order

During the reign of Tang Gaozu, Crown Prince Li Jiancheng and Li Shimin each had political standing and supporters. Li Shimin possessed military achievements and connections in the army, but the succession arrangements had already designated a crown prince. Distrust between the two camps over the future distribution of power deepened.

Li Shimin killed Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji in the coup at Xuanwu Gate, gained political and military advantage, and later became emperor. This was a succession dispute resolved through violence; later favorable judgments of the Zhenguan reign cannot erase the cost of that violence.

In 626, Li Shimin launched an armed operation at Xuanwu Gate, in which Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji were killed. He thereby gained military and political advantage and eventually ascended the throne, breaking the earlier succession arrangements. Policies during the later reign of Emperor Taizong have been judged in different ways, but that history came after the coup; it does not undo the deaths on the day. Because chronicles were often compiled after the victor had established a new order, their narrative perspective also deserves attention.

Xuanwu Gate was an important passage into the palace. By choosing to use force there, Li Shimin brought military action directly to bear on the court’s succession arrangements. Once Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji were killed, the former crown prince could no longer succeed. The later actions of Emperor Taizong must be distinguished from the loss of life and transfer of power on the day of the coup.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

The Xuanwu Gate Incident changes succession by force: Li Shimin killed Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji during the coup at Xuanwu Gate, gained political and military superiority, and later became emperor. Violence determined the succession dispute, and later assessments of the Zhenguan reign cannot erase its cost. Under Tang Gaozu, Li Jiancheng was the designated heir, while both he and Li Shimin commanded supporters. The coup changed the distribution of power at the beginning of the Tang and entailed killing within the imperial family. The analogy warns that political victory does not make the method worthy of respect. The Xiang says that distinction gained through contention is not sufficient to earn respect. The focus is that gaining power still carries a cost.

A — retain. The case offers a recognizable analogy to obtaining high rank through conflict without thereby deserving respect. It is a retrospective comparison, not evidence that the actors cited the Yijing.

When an army goes forth, it must be governed by discipline; the failure of discipline brings disaster.

Existing Traditional Chinese interpretation — translated

“An army must set out according to military discipline; if that discipline fails, misfortune follows.” The Xiang commentary explains the danger of failed discipline.

Line-specific interpretive focus

Military operations require military discipline.

Historical narrative — complete four source paragraphs

As the Jin and Chu armies faced one another near Bi, the Jin commanders had not agreed on whether to cross the river or how to deploy their forces. Xian Hu led his contingent across first, changing the commander-in-chief’s disposition of the army. Other Jin units then had to decide whether to follow or remain in place, making the original command arrangements harder to carry out.

The Zuo Zhuan records that Xian Hu disobeyed his commander and crossed the river with his troops. Zhi Zhuangzi cited the phrase “an army must set out according to discipline” from the line of Shi changing to Lin, warning that an army was in peril when it had a commander but its officers refused his orders. The Jin army nevertheless continued forward and was subsequently defeated by Chu at Bi.

At the military council, Zhi Zhuangzi quoted “an army must set out according to discipline” to identify the problem of officers refusing the orders of an appointed commander. This was a consultation recorded in the Zuo Zhuan that cited the Changes; it was not a record of anyone performing a fresh divination at that moment. Despite the warning, the Jin army did not halt its advance and later lost at Bi. The account traces, in order, an officer’s unauthorized action, a colleague’s warning, the army’s continued advance, and the defeat. Readers can therefore distinguish between a warning being issued and its being heeded.

Once Xian Hu’s contingent crossed the river, the other Jin commanders had to decide how to support those already on the opposite bank. Zhi Zhuangzi’s objection was therefore urgent: could the original common plan still bind the different units? Only after the battle between Jin and Chu did historians incorporate this exchange into the narrative leading up to the defeat.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

Before the Battle of Bi, the Zuo Zhuan records that Xian Hu violated his commander’s judgment and crossed the river with his troops. Zhi Zhuangzi cited the phrase “an army must set out according to discipline” from Shi changing to Lin, warning that refusing orders despite having a commander endangered the army. Jin continued forward and was defeated by Chu at Bi. The opposing Jin and Chu armies had been facing each other near Bi without a shared Jin decision about crossing the river or how to fight. Jin’s fragmented command during the battle is a counterexample illustrating the breakdown of orders and coordinated action. Although the Zuo Zhuan explicitly records a quotation from a line of Hexagram Shi, that does not establish that anyone quoted this particular passage of the Xiang commentary. The Xiang says, “When an army sets out according to discipline; if discipline fails, disaster results.” This case focuses on the lesson “An army must first have discipline.”

Editorial assessment and limitations

Grade A — Retain. The case supplies a recognizable analogy in actions and consequences to the principle that military operations require discipline. It remains a retrospective comparison and must not be treated as evidence that a historical participant actually cited the Xiang commentary.

Meaning of the Xiang

To occupy the center of an army is auspicious because one receives Heaven’s favor; the king’s threefold conferment of command expresses care for the myriad states.

“Commanding competently from within the army is auspicious and without blame; the king repeatedly bestows commissions and rewards.” The Xiang explains these through receiving Heaven’s favor and caring for the many states.

A commander entrusted with authority must be able to exercise command.

Historical narrative — complete four source paragraphs

In 154 BCE, seven kingdoms rose against the Han, and Wu and Chu attacked, leaving the state of Liang in urgent need of aid. The court sent Zhou Yafu to command the army. He had to weigh Liang’s immediate danger against the principal rebel armies’ supply lines. If he merely followed the enemy’s offensive movements, the Han army risked fighting a decisive battle under conditions chosen by its opponents.

After the Rebellion of the Seven States broke out, Zhou Yafu did not continually seek a direct pitched battle. He held his position, sent troops to cut the Wu–Chu forces’ grain routes, and waited until their supply difficulties emerged before seizing the moment of their retreat. The pressure borne by Liang also made this operational plan politically controversial.

Zhou Yafu maintained his defensive position while dispatching units to sever the Wu–Chu grain supply. The assault on Liang did not thereby cease, and Zhou faced political criticism for not relieving it immediately. Once the enemy’s supplies were obstructed and its offensive was difficult to sustain, he attacked as it began to withdraw. The victory over the rebels coexisted with the risks Liang had borne: this campaign illustrates how manipulating food supplies behind the front could change battlefield conditions.

Because Zhou Yafu chose this course, Liang could not receive comprehensive assistance immediately, and its court was dissatisfied. At the same time the Han forces had to maintain their own position so that the enemy could not easily redirect its assault against them. Cutting supply lines was not passive observation; it aimed to make the Wu–Chu armies’ initially sustainable offensive progressively untenable.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

During the Rebellion of the Seven States, Zhou Yafu refrained from constantly seeking frontal battle. He held his position, disrupted the grain supplies of the Wu–Chu armies, and struck when their logistics failed and they retreated. Liang remained under pressure, which caused political controversy over his deployment. In 154 BCE, when seven kingdoms rebelled against the Han and Wu and Chu attacked, Liang urgently sought assistance. Zhou’s responsibility for the campaign can be compared with a commander’s duties and the sovereign’s delegation of authority. “Heaven’s favor” is an ancient expression, not a supernatural explanation for victory. The Xiang reads, “To be in the midst of the army is auspicious, receiving Heaven’s favor. The king bestows commands three times, embracing the myriad states.” The focus here is “Give the commander clear trust.”

Grade B — Partially applicable. Zhou Yafu’s appointment to command provides a connection, but the story does not directly support the “king’s threefold conferment” or “embracing the myriad states.”

Revision recommendation (supplement the comparison without deleting the original): the case corresponds to the line only in the limited aspect of a commander being entrusted with an army and exercising command. His appointment is relevant, but no evidence in this episode directly supports three royal conferments or embracing the myriad states. Readers must distinguish historical facts, editorial analogy, and effects unsupported by evidence.

Revised line-specific comparison

Revised line-specific comparison: Zhou Yafu was appointed to suppress the Rebellion of the Seven States. His command responsibilities and the court’s support can illuminate “auspicious in the midst of the army,” but there is no record in this episode of three separate royal commendations or an event corresponding to “embracing the myriad states.” The analogy is therefore limited to sovereign authorization and the commander’s responsibility.

One-time reassessment

One-time reassessment: B (reasonable with limitations; retained). The original story, case ID, and original evidence classification remain unchanged; no further attempt is made to force an A grade.

Interpretive boundary: the comparison is editorial and retrospective. Unless expressly supported by the source, it must not be described as a historical participant directly using the Xiang commentary.

In 1449, the Ming emperor Yingzong led an expedition north against the Oirats and personally accompanied the army. Emperor Yingzong led Ming forces north against the Oirats, but on the return march the army suffered a devastating defeat near Tumu and the emperor was captured. The court faced a severe emergency. The episode involved problems of judgment, movement, supply, and command, and Beijing’s defense then had to be reorganized.

After the crushing defeat of the Ming army at Tumu and the capture of Yingzong, officials in Beijing had to reorganize military defenses and affairs relating to the throne to prevent the frontline disaster from spreading. Historical records differ on troop numbers and the responsibility of some participants, but the succession of events is plain: an expedition, a failed return, the emperor’s capture, and emergency measures in the capital. The defense of Beijing had to begin while the emperor was still captive.

The consequences of an emperor’s capture immediately went beyond an ordinary withdrawal after defeat: officials had to settle the formal authority of the court, and defenders had to know who could issue orders. The capital’s defense was organized urgently while information from the front remained incomplete. The reports traveling from the battlefield at Tumu to the offices in Beijing linked military disaster directly to political administration.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

Emperor Yingzong led the Ming campaign north against the Oirats but suffered catastrophic losses near Tumu during the return march. He was taken prisoner, and the court faced a severe crisis involving decisions, marching, supplies, and command; Beijing’s defenses had to be reorganized. In 1449 the emperor had personally traveled with a large force. The Tumu Crisis cost the army heavily and resulted in the emperor’s capture. It demonstrates that failed leadership in war does more than spoil a plan: large numbers of people bear the consequences. The Xiang says, “The army may carry corpses: a great failure.” The focus is “Disordered command costs lives.”

Retreating to the left without blame means that accepted norms have not been violated.

Existing Traditional Chinese interpretation — translated

“The army withdraws and takes up a position to the left, prudently avoiding combat; there is no blame.” The Xiang explains that this does not abandon what is proper.

Line-specific interpretive focus

Orderly withdrawal and avoidance of unnecessary harm.

Historical narrative — complete four source paragraphs

During Zhuge Liang’s first Northern Expedition into Longyou, Jieting was a crucial location affecting further operations. Ma Su was charged with its deployment, and the main force’s ability to sustain the offensive depended directly on defending Jieting.

In the first Northern Expedition, Ma Su lost Jieting. Zhuge Liang withdrew and submitted a memorial asking to be demoted, acknowledging his own poor judgment in selecting personnel. The memorial linked defeat to the commander’s responsibility for appointments rather than placing all blame on officers at the front.

After Ma Su lost Jieting, Zhuge Liang brought the army back instead of advancing along the intended route. He submitted a memorial to the court seeking demotion and accepted responsibility for his staffing decision. This statement publicly accounted for his judgment after military failure; it does not justify overlooking other factors on the battlefield. Appointment, battle at Jieting, withdrawal, and the memorial seeking demotion followed a discernible sequence. The fictional “Empty Fort Strategy” is not part of the historically supportable account of this episode.

The defeat at Jieting deprived the Shu army’s subsequent deployment of support; withdrawing could not undo the earlier investment of resources. Zhuge Liang’s memorial was a political accounting to the court, while the soldiers still had to leave the combat zone and arrange defenses anew. Battlefield action was followed directly by responsibility for its consequences.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

After Ma Su lost Jieting during the first Northern Expedition, Zhuge Liang withdrew and petitioned to be demoted for his mistake in choosing personnel. The memorial related failure to the commander’s staffing responsibility rather than solely blaming subordinates. Jieting had been a key point for the expedition’s continuation in Longyou. Zhuge Liang’s withdrawal can be compared with a prudent decision to pull back under adverse conditions. Such a retreat should be judged by whether it preserves the force, not only by whether an army advances. The Xiang says, “Taking up a position to the left is without blame; normal practice has not been abandoned.” The lesson is “Withdrawal is not necessarily dereliction of duty.”

Editorial assessment and limitations

Grade A — Retain. The case illustrates orderly withdrawal and the avoidance of harm as a retrospective comparison. It is not evidence that historical actors quoted the Xiang.

Interpretive boundary: the comparison is editorial and retrospective. Unless expressly supported by the source, it must not be described as a historical participant directly using the Xiang commentary.

041 Line H07 Shi Qi Jiguang Recruits and Trains at Yiwu — Appoint People to Fit the Mission▶

九五｜

041 case_id: XCASE-H07-L5 | global_line_no: 041 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: paragraph_translated_review_pending | publish_status: editorial_review

Full paragraph-level English translation — Traditional Chinese source V4.3.3

Meaning of the Xiang

An elder son commands the army because he acts in due measure; a younger son carries corpses because the appointment is unsuitable.

Existing Traditional Chinese interpretation — translated

“There is game in the fields; one may announce a justified punitive expedition without blame. An able senior should lead the troops; appointing someone unready and returning with the dead is disastrous, even if the cause seemed justified.” The Xiang explains this through proportionate conduct and unsuitable appointment.

Line-specific interpretive focus

Appoint suitable people and avoid placing the unready in command.

Historical narrative — complete four source paragraphs

During the Ming dynasty, the southeastern coast suffered raids by wokou forces, and local units faced difficulties in recruitment, training, and battle. Qi Jiguang recruited soldiers at Yiwu, seeking men willing to obey discipline and undergo training. Individual bravery could not, by itself, ensure that a squad moved in coordination on the battlefield.

At Yiwu, Qi Jiguang emphasized selecting recruits, military discipline, and cooperation among units. In operations against the coastal raiders he employed mutually supporting weapons and formations. His military training writings repeatedly stressed translating instruction into actions and rules that soldiers could actually carry out.

Once recruits were assigned to units, they practiced cooperation among different weapons, positioning, and movement. These arrangements were used in fighting against coastal raiders, and Qi also set down training standards in writing. Selection, organization, and drilling took time so that different men knew how to cover one another. Combat effectiveness also depended on terrain, supplies, and opponents; it cannot all be credited to the striking name of any single formation.

If recruits did not practice together in peacetime and first attempted coordination only when facing the enemy, weapons of differing lengths and the soldiers’ positions could obstruct one another. Qi required repeated exercises according to common rules, giving commands issued in action a practical basis. The units still had to adapt to changing enemy methods across different theaters.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

Qi Jiguang recruited soldiers at Yiwu and emphasized selection, discipline, and cooperation, employing complementary weapons and unit organization in campaigns against the raiders. His training writings stressed translating instruction into executable actions and regulations. Ming coastal forces faced challenges in recruiting, preparing, and fighting. Qi’s practice shows how military effectiveness relies on personnel suited to their responsibilities and on organization. Here the image of an “elder son” is used only as a metaphor for fitness to assume responsibility, not an endorsement of appointments based on blood relationship. The Xiang says, “The elder son commands the army, acting with proper balance; the younger son carries corpses, because the appointment was inappropriate.” This case focuses on “Assign people according to the mission.”

Editorial assessment and limitations

Grade A — Retain. The historical case provides a recognizable analogy for appropriate and inappropriate appointments. It remains a retrospective comparison, not evidence of anyone’s direct citation of the Xiang.

Interpretive boundary: the comparison is editorial and retrospective. Unless expressly supported by the source, it must not be described as a historical participant directly using the Xiang commentary.

042 Line H07 Shi The Early Song Reorganizes Military Command — Settle Authority after Victory▶

上九｜

042 case_id: XCASE-H07-L6 | global_line_no: 042 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: paragraph_translated_review_pending | publish_status: editorial_review

Full paragraph-level English translation — Traditional Chinese source V4.3.3

Meaning of the Xiang

The great ruler issues commands to put achievements in proper order; petty men should not be employed, lest they disorder the state.

Existing Traditional Chinese interpretation — translated

“The ruler issues orders granting lands and offices; unworthy people should not be employed.” The Xiang explains this as properly recognizing achievement and preventing disorder in the realm.

Line-specific interpretive focus

Recognize merit and fault, and make appointments with care.

Historical narrative — complete four source paragraphs

After Emperor Taizu of Song came to power, the court faced the excessive control of troops held by senior generals. The new regime’s military foundations lay in existing forces, and abruptly breaking ties with their commanders might itself disrupt the army. The central government therefore gradually adjusted posts and command authority.

After establishing the Song dynasty, Taizu progressively changed senior generals’ appointments and the system of controlling armed forces to reduce the risk of military commanders becoming independent powers. Posterity often describes this as “releasing military authority over cups of wine,” but historians differ over the banquet conversation, its timing, and the precise course of events.

Some generals left their former military posts, while authority over armed forces was redistributed toward the center. Later accounts called this “releasing military authority over cups of wine,” adding an exchange between ruler and ministers at a banquet. The exact conversation, date, and documentary basis are disputed. What can be observed historically is a change in offices and the control of armed forces; it is not necessary to assume all adjustments were agreed upon on a single evening. After new arrangements were established, the court still had to ensure the military operated under the new command relationships.

When generals’ offices changed, troops needed to know from which institution new orders would come. The court also had to find an acceptable standing for those leaving command. Concentrating military authority therefore involved more than curtailing one person’s power; it also entailed reconnecting the army’s everyday chain of command.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

After taking power, Emperor Taizu of Song gradually adjusted generals’ duties and the organization of military command to reduce the risk that commanders would establish independent military power. Later generations often describe this through the story of “releasing military authority over cups of wine,” but the banquet dialogue, timing, and details remain disputed. The Song court inherited the problem of senior generals holding considerable armed strength. Changing their authority was part of creating a new political order and illustrates why the distribution of rewards must be followed by safeguards against imbalanced power. The Xiang says, “The great ruler commands, assigning credit properly; do not employ petty men, for they will disorder the state.” The case focuses on “Responsibilities and authority must still be organized after war.”

Editorial assessment and limitations

Grade A — Retain. The measures provide a recognizable historical analogy for assessing merit and appointing personnel carefully. The banquet scene involves disputed sources; the comparison remains retrospective rather than proof of anyone citing the Xiang.

Interpretive boundary: the comparison is editorial and retrospective. Unless expressly supported by the source, it must not be described as a historical participant directly using the Xiang commentary.

043 Line H08 Bi Shang Yang Demonstrates Trust by Moving a Log — Trust Begins with Credible Action▶

初九｜

043 case_id: XCASE-H08-L1 | global_line_no: 043 | editorial_grade: A | translation_status: paragraph_translated_review_pending | publish_status: editorial_review

Full paragraph-level English translation — Traditional Chinese source V4.3.3

Meaning of the Xiang

At the outset of joining with others, there is additional good fortune.

Existing Traditional Chinese interpretation — translated

For the initial six of Bi, the Xiang commentary explains that additional good fortune is possible.

Line-specific interpretive focus

Establish cooperation through trustworthiness.

Historical narrative — complete four source paragraphs

As Shang Yang prepared to introduce new laws in Qin, he needed ordinary people to believe that official promises of rewards and punishments would actually be carried out. Before the formal provisions took effect, he chose a small undertaking whose outcome residents could see immediately, so verification would not have to be postponed.

According to the Records of the Grand Historian, before promulgating the new laws Shang Yang placed a wooden pole at a city gate and announced a reward for moving it. Someone eventually did so, and Shang Yang paid as promised. The account uses a small, verifiable action to illustrate how an official promise could begin to gain credibility.

The Records of the Grand Historian recounts that nobody initially trusted the posted reward for moving the pole. When a person finally moved it, Shang Yang did in fact pay the money. Residents saw that the announcement and payment matched, and the new laws were subsequently announced. Historians use this story to portray the establishment of credibility in government orders. Fulfillment of one reward did not guarantee that all subsequent laws would be fair or free of harshness; their effects still depended on local enforcement.

When the pole was actually moved, Shang Yang immediately paid the sum announced. Bystanders could directly compare the promise with the action. This small demonstration preceded enforcement of the new laws and let residents see one reward order fulfilled. The legislation itself would still face a much broader test in practice.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

Shang Yang wins confidence by moving the wooden pole: the Records of the Grand Historian relates that, before introducing new laws, he posted a reward for moving a pole at the city gate and actually paid the person who complied. This verifiable act illustrates how people might come to trust an official promise. Shang Yang wanted Qin residents to see that announced rewards and punishments would be enforced. The historical narrative connects a promise with its fulfillment. It can serve as an example of the initial formation of trust, but the details should not be presented as evidence from a modern experiment. The Xiang reads, “At the first line of Bi, there is additional good fortune.” Here the focus is “Cooperation begins with credible action.”

Editorial assessment and limitations

Grade A — Retain. The acts and outcome offer a recognizable analogy for establishing cooperation through trustworthiness. The comparison remains retrospective and does not establish that the historical participant actually cited the Changes.

Interpretive boundary: the comparison is editorial and retrospective. Unless supported by primary material, it must not be described as a participant directly citing or applying the Xiang.

Form sincere ties without losing independent judgment.

Historical narrative — complete four source paragraphs

When Duke Huan of Qi appointed Guan Zhong, Qi first needed to put its internal administration in order before it could repeatedly send armies, attend meetings of rulers, and honor commitments among the states. Each ruler had separate security concerns and interests. Attendance at a single meeting did not mean surrendering all future decisions to Qi.

Guan Zhong assisted Duke Huan by improving domestic governance and holding interstate meetings, thereby extending Qi’s influence. The Records of the Grand Historian connects Duke Huan’s hegemony with Guan Zhong’s domestic administration and diplomacy. The network of cooperation rested both on shared interests and on Qi’s strength.

Guan Zhong took part in governing Qi while Duke Huan increased his influence through repeated negotiations. The Records of the Grand Historian links their achievements with Qi’s hegemony. Cooperation among states relied on Qi’s strength as well as issues they faced in common. These alliances were not formed in one single meeting: participants and issues changed with circumstances. After becoming a leading state, Qi still had to manage its relationships with other powers continually.

Domestic administration enabled Qi to provision armies and send envoys; diplomatic assemblies translated these resources into dealings with other states. Each common proposal still depended on whether the others would accept it. Duke Huan’s prestige, Guan Zhong’s work, and Qi’s military power supported one another.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

Guan Zhong helps Duke Huan of Qi sustain cooperation among the lords: by reforming domestic administration and arranging interstate meetings, he helped extend Qi’s influence. The Records of the Grand Historian links this diplomatic network with both shared interests and Qi’s strength. Before participating consistently in campaigns and meetings, Qi had to manage its own affairs. Guan Zhong’s coalitions illustrate how an internal political position and external cooperation can reinforce one another; forming an alliance does not require a state to abandon its own judgment. The Xiang reads, “Joining from within, one does not lose oneself.” The focus is “Cooperation still requires an independent position.”

Editorial assessment and limitations

Grade B — Partially applicable. The case shows Guan Zhong maintaining interstate cooperation but does not explicitly establish the personal boundary expressed by “from within” and “not losing oneself.”

Grade B: rationale and revision recommendations

One-time revision recommendation, supplementing rather than deleting the source comparison: the analogy supports only the limited aspect of sincere cooperation without losing one’s position. Guan Zhong’s management of alliances does not itself demonstrate the individual moral boundary evoked by the line. Readers should distinguish documented history, editorial analogy, and supposed effects lacking evidence.

Revised line-specific comparison

Revised line-specific comparison: Guan Zhong’s work to maintain Qi’s alliances shows that cooperation depends on arrangements and a state’s own position. Read through “joining from within, not losing oneself,” the alliances should be understood as resting on each state’s political interests and commitments, not as requiring abandonment of independent judgment merely because one has drawn close to others.

One-time reassessment

One-time reassessment: B (reasonable with limitations; retained). The original story, case ID, and original evidence category are unchanged. No further attempt is made to force an A grade.

Interpretive boundary: the comparison is editorial and retrospective. Unless supported by primary material, it must not be described as a participant directly citing or applying the Xiang.

Harm arises from relying on unsuitable allies.

Historical narrative — complete four source paragraphs

In 1900, Boxer activity, foreign intervention, and decision-making within the Qing court became intertwined. Beijing’s diplomatic and military position deteriorated rapidly. The court’s response to foreign troops and local officials’ judgments about protecting their jurisdictions were already moving in different directions.

As the Boxer movement and foreign military intervention intensified, the Qing government issued an imperial edict declaring war on foreign powers, further widening the crisis. Allied forces entered Beijing, the Qing court fled, and the Boxer Protocol was signed the next year. Some provincial officials pursued the policy known as Mutual Protection of the Southeast, demonstrating that central and local judgments did not coincide.

Following the declaration of war, fighting widened; allied troops entered Beijing and the court fled. Some southeastern officials pursued mutual protection instead of adopting exactly the same course as the center. The Boxer Protocol signed the next year imposed severe consequences on the Qing state and the population. In discussing errors of central policy, one must also expressly acknowledge the armed invasion by foreign powers. The movement from local unrest to international war involved decisions by more than one person.

After the war edict, officials did not all respond alike, as the southeastern mutual-protection arrangements demonstrated. The entry of allied forces into Beijing and subsequent treaty indemnities transformed a crisis of political judgment into military and fiscal consequences. Each stage involved different actors and people who bore the costs.

Line-specific historical comparison — full translation

The Qing court’s foreign-war decisions during the Boxer crisis: once the Boxer movement and foreign military intervention intensified, the court declared war, allied forces entered Beijing, and the court fled; the Boxer Protocol followed in the next year. The separate policy of southeastern mutual protection shows that central and provincial judgments differed. Boxer activity, external intervention, and divided court decisions had already made the situation rapidly worse. The court’s shifting attitude toward Boxer forces illustrates a mistaken assessment of potential partners. This does not mean labeling a complex group as innately good or evil. The Xiang asks, “Joining with the wrong people—is this not harmful?” The focus is “Relying on the wrong people may cause harm.”

Editorial assessment and limitations

Grade A — Retain. The case offers a recognizable analogy for the injury that can follow unsuitable affiliations. It is a retrospective interpretation, not evidence that any actor actually quoted the Changes.

After succession disputes in Jin, Chong’er left his homeland and wandered among other states for many years. Without a Jin government on which he could rely, he and his companions needed hospitality and provisions wherever they went before they could even discuss political support.

Chong’er traveled through several states in exile, receiving differing degrees of hospitality and assistance. Ultimately, Qin’s support enabled him to return to Jin and take the throne. Chong’er received uneven assistance abroad and was sometimes treated dismissively. Later Qin lent its support, allowing him to return and become Duke Wen of Jin. The choices of his hosts, the continued loyalty of his followers, and changes within Jin all shaped his eventual return.

In each state, local hosts decided how Chong’er would be received, and his retainers had to decide whether to continue accompanying him. No single stop automatically assured his return. Only when Qin assisted him and events in Jin also became favorable could he reenter his homeland’s political contest.

Moderation, openness, and restraint in public cooperation.

Historical narrative — complete four source paragraphs

As Qin rule collapsed, several armies advanced toward Guanzhong. When Liu Bang arrived in what had been the core territory of Qin, residents still faced uncertainty over military occupation and changes to the law. To gain their cooperation, an incoming commander had to make clear how the army would enter the region and what behavior would be punished.

After entering Guanzhong, Liu Bang announced three simple legal provisions and explained arrangements to local elders to reduce fear created by Qin’s harsh laws. This was a political measure aimed at gaining local support. Xiang Yu and other powers remained formidable; entry into Guanzhong did not mean Liu Bang had already secured the empire.

Liu Bang assembled the elders and publicly declared the simplified laws; his soldiers then had to honor the promises. The arrangement could reduce local anxiety, but it did not immediately give him all political power. Xiang Yu and other armies were still active, and the situation outside Guanzhong remained unsettled. The advance, publication of the rules, and continued contest among the lords were distinct yet connected phases. Entry into Guanzhong was not the endpoint of the struggle for supremacy.

When Guanzhong residents first heard the rules, armed troops still stood before them. Whether Liu Bang would honor his undertaking could become clear only through their subsequent dealings with the garrison. Competition among the powers for control of Guanzhong also kept this governing arrangement within an unstable political environment.

Liu Bang enters Guanzhong and announces three rules: he publicly simplified the law and explained military arrangements to local elders, seeking to reduce fear of Qin’s harsh legislation. Xiang Yu and rival forces were still active, so taking Guanzhong did not mean he had conquered all China. The announcement offers an analogy for winning acceptance through public, intelligible political conduct. It does not justify claiming that every resident supported him freely and unanimously. The Xiang says, “Open association is fortunate because the position is centered and proper; let the opposing game go and take what follows; the townspeople are not alarmed because those above act moderately.” This case focuses on “Unite support through public rules.”

Liu Bang’s proclamation substantiates the public-rule aspect but not the restraint implied by releasing game in the hunting image. Readers must separate established historical facts, editorial analogies, and unsupported causal claims.

Yet “allowing the game ahead to escape” points toward restraint and nonexcessive pursuit; this episode does not directly demonstrate that image. The comparison therefore remains partial.

One-time reassessment

During their First United Front, the Kuomintang and Chinese Communist Party both participated in the Northern Expedition. The First United Front faced increasing conflicts over interests, political strategy, and control of power during the Northern Expedition. The Shanghai purge and the break at Wuhan in 1927 destroyed cooperation and involved extensive political violence. The events in Shanghai and Wuhan took place at different times, with different actors and victims; they should not be merged into an abstract “disagreement” with no concrete sequence.

Political groups that had worked in the same cities during the alliance now confronted each other’s membership, lists, and armed forces. Shanghai and Wuhan adopted different measures in succession, putting associated individuals at risk of flight, arrest, or death. The long confrontation that followed made a return to the former cooperative relationship even more difficult.

The breakdown of the First United Front in 1927: during the Northern Expedition, competing interests, political strategies, and struggles for authority placed increasing strain on Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. The Shanghai purge and Wuhan split ended the alliance amid political violence, followed by prolonged armed conflict. The parties’ military advances had raised unresolved issues of command, municipal administration, and mass mobilization. This breakdown shows how a partnership lacking a shared political direction may prove hard to sustain. 050 Line H09 Xiao Xu Zhuge Liang Withdraws after the Loss of Jieting and Accepts Responsibility — Return to a Viable Course after Deviation▶

九二｜

050 case_id: XCASE-H09-L2 | suitability_grade: B | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Returning to one’s own proper path is auspicious in principle.

Received interpretation: “Returning to the proper path—how could there be blame? Auspicious.” The Xiang Commentary explains: it is auspicious in principle.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Paragraph 1. When Zhuge Liang’s first Northern Expedition entered Longyou, Jieting was a strategically important position affecting subsequent operations. Ma Su was assigned to direct the local deployment. Whether the main force could preserve the conditions needed to continue advancing was directly related to the defense of Jieting.

Paragraph 2. During the first Northern Expedition, Ma Su lost Jieting. Zhuge Liang withdrew and submitted a memorial requesting a demotion, acknowledging that his appointment of personnel had been inappropriate. This memorial seeking his own demotion connected the defeat to the commander’s responsibility for choosing subordinates, rather than placing all blame on the officers at the front.

Paragraph 3. After Ma Su lost Jieting, Zhuge Liang led his troops back instead of continuing along the previous line of advance. He submitted a memorial to the court requesting demotion and acknowledging his own responsibility for the appointment. The document publicly accounted for the commander’s judgment after a military setback; it cannot be used to set aside other factors on the battlefield. The sequence of appointment, fighting at Jieting, withdrawal, and memorial seeking demotion is clear. The “Empty Fort Strategy” of later fiction is not part of the historical events substantiated here.

Paragraph 4. The defeat at Jieting deprived subsequent Shu deployments of their support. Zhuge Liang’s withdrawal did not mean that resources already committed could be recovered. Taking responsibility in a memorial was a political account rendered to the court; the troops still had to leave the war zone and reorganize their defenses. Battlefield action and subsequent accountability followed one another in this episode.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

Zhuge Liang withdrew after the loss of Jieting and accepted responsibility. During the first Northern Expedition, Ma Su lost Jieting; Zhuge Liang withdrew and submitted a memorial asking to be demoted because he had appointed personnel improperly. The memorial linked defeat to the commander’s responsibility for personnel decisions rather than blaming only frontline subordinates. When the expedition first entered Longyou, Jieting was a key location affecting later operations. Withdrawing and accepting responsibility after its loss can be compared to recognizing that circumstances have changed and returning to actions one can still control, rather than compounding losses to save face. The Xiang Commentary says, “Returning to one’s own path is auspicious in principle.” This entry emphasizes “return to a viable course after deviation.”

Editorial Review Rationale

The event accords with the main direction of action emphasized by “return to a viable course after deviation.” The original historical comparison already provides a concrete event and explains its limits. This is a retrospective interpretive comparison, not evidence that the historical figure actually cited this line.

Revision or Replacement Note

Retain the comparison from the original manuscript; no mandatory revision.

unit_id: XIANG-U-09-03

051 Line H09 Xiao Xu Negotiations Resolve the Detention Crisis of the Xi’an Incident — Changing Course Requires Cooperation▶

九三｜

051 case_id: XCASE-H09-L3 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Being drawn back toward the center, one does not lose oneself.

Received interpretation: “Being drawn back toward the center”: the Xiang Commentary explains that one “does not lose oneself.”

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Paragraph 1. In 1936, pressure to resist Japan was intensifying, while the Nationalist Government and the Communist Party remained engaged in armed conflict. Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng were dissatisfied with Chiang Kai-shek’s policies. They detained him in Xi’an, turning existing political divisions into an immediate personal-security and military crisis.

Paragraph 2. Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng detained Chiang Kai-shek in Xi’an, triggering a political and military crisis. After negotiations among the parties, Chiang was released. The incident gave greater prominence to demands to end the civil war and jointly resist Japan, but the commitments made, subsequent measures, and terms of cooperation remained contested.

Paragraph 3. The parties entered into negotiations in the hope of ending the detention without further enlarging the military conflict. Chiang Kai-shek was ultimately released, and the question of ending the civil war and resisting Japan together became more prominent. Securing his release through negotiations did not settle every condition of cooperation; Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng also subsequently faced different political consequences. Detention, negotiations, release, and later arrangements must be treated as consecutive but distinct stages.

Paragraph 4. News of the detention reached different political and military forces, which had to assess Chiang Kai-shek’s safety and the potential course of further fighting. Negotiations enabled him to leave Xi’an but did not transform future cooperation among the factions into a long-term agreement that would automatically be fulfilled. The people involved continued to face different circumstances after the incident.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

Negotiations resolved the detention crisis of the Xi’an Incident. Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng detained Chiang Kai-shek in Xi’an, creating a political and military crisis. After negotiations among the parties, Chiang was released. Calls to end the civil war and jointly resist Japan gained prominence, although the commitments, follow-up arrangements, and conditions of cooperation remained disputed. In 1936, pressure to resist Japan was intensifying while armed conflict continued between the Nationalist Government and the Communists. The peaceful resolution of the immediate Xi’an crisis required consultation among multiple parties; it can be compared to being drawn toward a more acceptable course by mutual engagement, not to reconciliation achieved simply by one side announcing it. The Xiang Commentary says, “Being drawn back toward the center, one does not lose oneself.” This entry stresses that “changing course requires cooperation from all sides.”

Editorial Review Rationale

The original case illustrates part of what is meant by “changing course requires cooperation from all sides,” but it does not adequately establish the specific position and conditions of action conveyed by the line image. The inference must be limited: the event illustrates only one aspect.

Revised Comparison

The “persuasion toward peace” associated with the Xi’an Incident must be limited to the joint containment of the immediate detention crisis through negotiations among several parties. The negotiations’ success did not make Zhang Xueliang’s and Yang Hucheng’s act of detention legitimate. Chiang Kai-shek’s release did not mean that every party permanently returned to one political course. “Being drawn back toward the center” can only be compared to the mutual pull among the parties that kept the situation from becoming wholly unmanageable. The Xiang Commentary states, “Being drawn back toward the center, one does not lose oneself.” This is a retrospective analogy, not historical proof that the participants based their decisions on this line.

Recheck Decision

Retain the event and the complete original story, narrow the scope of inference, and specify the aspects of the line’s meaning that the event does not match. Retain grade B; there is no requirement to raise every case to A.

Revision or Replacement Note

The manuscript revision treats the historical event, negotiations ending the Xi’an detention crisis, as an analogy drawn by later readers. It sheds light on certain problems involved in “changing course requires cooperation from all sides,” but the incident had its own independent political, economic, and social causes. A resemblance in outcome does not establish that the actors obeyed the line statement. Readers should distinguish information available at the time, actions actually taken, and outcomes known later, and should use the sources cited in the original manuscript to verify the event.

unit_id: XIANG-U-09-04

052 Line H09 Xiao Xu The First United Front Breaks Down in 1927 — Internal Discord Weakens Cooperation▶

九四｜

052 case_id: XCASE-H09-L4 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Husband and wife turn against each other because the household cannot be properly ordered.

Received interpretation: “The spokes of the wheel come loose; husband and wife turn against each other.” Internal discord obstructs action. The Xiang Commentary explains: “the household cannot be properly ordered.”

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Paragraph 1. During the First United Front, the Kuomintang and Communist Party participated together in the Northern Expedition. Yet advances at the front brought successive problems over the armies, municipal power, and worker and peasant movements. The two parties held different views about the future allocation of power and social mobilization, and their differences accumulated within the alliance.

Paragraph 2. The First United Front endured conflicts of interest, political line, and power during the Northern Expedition. In 1927 the purge of Communists in Shanghai and the subsequent split in Wuhan dissolved the alliance, accompanied by large-scale political violence. The two sides thereafter entered a prolonged period of military confrontation.

Paragraph 3. The purge in Shanghai and the split in Wuhan in 1927 dismantled the cooperative relationship and were accompanied by extensive political violence. People previously active within the same camp had to reconsider whether they could remain in their respective organizations. Thereafter the two sides moved toward prolonged military confrontation. Shanghai and Wuhan involved different dates, actors, and victims; they should not be collapsed into a single abstract “disagreement” with no specific course of events.

Paragraph 4. Political organizations that had operated in the same cities during cooperation suddenly faced one another’s members, membership lists, and armed forces when the alliance broke. Shanghai and Wuhan undertook different actions in succession, and those involved risked flight, arrest, or death. The ensuing lengthy conflict made the earlier cooperation still harder to restore.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The First United Front broke down in 1927. During the Northern Expedition, conflicts of interest, political line, and power strained Kuomintang–Communist cooperation. The Shanghai purge and the Wuhan split in 1927 destroyed the alliance amid extensive political violence; the parties then entered a prolonged military confrontation. Their earlier joint participation in the Northern Expedition had raised successive questions about armies, urban government, and the worker and peasant movements. The breakdown of this cooperation illustrates the costs when partners within a common organization lose the ability to coordinate. The marital analogy refers here only to a relationship that has fallen out of balance; it is not a lesson prescribing gender roles. The Xiang Commentary says, “Husband and wife turn against each other; the household cannot be properly ordered.” The focus is “internal discord weakens cooperation.”

Editorial Review Rationale

The event accords with the main course of action conveyed by “internal discord weakens cooperation.” The original historical comparison identifies specific events and explains the limits of the analogy. It is a retrospective reading, not evidence that any actor actually cited this line.

Revision or Replacement Note

Retain the original comparison; no mandatory revision.

unit_id: XIANG-U-09-05

053 Line H09 Xiao Xu Sun Quan and Liu Bei Ally against Cao Cao — Mutual Trust Eases the Anxiety of Cooperation▶

九五｜

053 case_id: XCASE-H09-L5 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

There is trust, and apprehension can be put aside, because one’s aims accord with those above.

Received interpretation: “There is trust; apprehension departs,” indicating that one’s aims are aligned with those of a higher-positioned person.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Paragraph 1. Cao Cao’s southward campaign caused the situation in Jingzhou to change abruptly, leaving Liu Bei and Sun Quan each facing a threat from northern troops. Liu Bei needed a new military backer, while Sun Quan had to decide how to defend the Yangtze. The two already had their own territories and military plans, so contact and coordination were necessary before they could form an alliance.

Paragraph 2. After Cao Cao advanced south, Sun Quan and Liu Bei faced shared military pressure. Negotiations involving Lu Su, Zhuge Liang, and others helped bring them together. Their allied forces resisted Cao’s army at Red Cliffs. After the fighting, however, each side retained its own territorial and political interests; the alliance was not thereafter free of friction.

Paragraph 3. Lu Su, Zhuge Liang, and others took part in the negotiations that brought about cooperation between Sun Quan and Liu Bei. Their combined forces fought Cao Cao’s army around Red Cliffs and achieved a battlefield success, but afterwards they still had to govern their respective territories and troops. Having a common wartime objective did not mean that postwar territorial arrangements had been settled. The relationship passed through military pressure, exchanges of envoys, combined operations, and renewed negotiations after the battle; “a successful alliance” alone cannot describe all that followed.

Paragraph 4. Before the allied forces could be assembled, envoys had to ascertain that both parties were willing to resist Cao Cao together. Afterwards they had to coordinate while each retained its own troops. The end of the Battle of Red Cliffs did not make their objectives identical. Later disputes over Jingzhou arose within this very relationship, despite its earlier history of cooperation in battle.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

Sun Quan and Liu Bei allied against Cao Cao. Facing common pressure from Cao’s southward advance, they formed a partnership through negotiations involving Lu Su, Zhuge Liang, and others. Their allied troops fought Cao’s forces at Red Cliffs, but territorial and political calculations continued on each side afterwards. Cao’s campaign had rapidly transformed the situation in Jingzhou and placed both Liu Bei and Sun Quan under threat from the north. Their alliance created a united front at the time of the threat. It can be compared to how aligned aims help dispel anxiety, although each party retained its interests and later conflicts remained possible. The Xiang Commentary says, “There is trust; apprehension departs; their aims are aligned with those above.” The lesson here is “mutual trust eases the anxiety of cooperation.”

Editorial Review Rationale

The event is consistent with the main direction expressed by “mutual trust eases the anxiety of cooperation.” The original comparison includes identifiable events and limitations. It is a retrospective analogy, not evidence that participants actually cited this line.

Revision or Replacement Note

Retain the original comparison; no mandatory revision.

unit_id: XIANG-U-09-06

054 Line H09 Xiao Xu Xiao He Sustains Liu Bang’s War Effort from Guanzhong — Resources Should Support the Whole▶

上九｜

054 case_id: XCASE-H09-L6 | suitability_grade: B | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Bound together by trust; wealth is not kept for oneself alone.

Received interpretation: “Bound closely together in trust, sharing prosperity with neighbors.” The Xiang Commentary explains: “not wealthy alone.”

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Paragraph 1. During the Chu–Han War, Liu Bang’s armies at the front continuously needed grain, military pay, and fresh recruits. Guanzhong was under his control and had the capacity to transport supplies and maintain population records. If the local administration ceased functioning, even short-term successes on the battlefield could not have been sustained.

Paragraph 2. During the struggle between Chu and Han, Xiao He remained mainly in Guanzhong to administer population matters, provisions, military pay, and replacements for the troops, providing continuing support for Liu Bang’s armies at the front. Historical works including the Book of Han identify this rear-area work as an important condition enabling the Han forces to keep fighting.

Paragraph 3. Remaining in Guanzhong, Xiao He managed local affairs and arranged the dispatch of personnel and grain to the front. After each depletion of the army, the rear had to raise and transport supplies yet again. When texts such as the Book of Han recount the Han army’s victories, they also record Xiao He’s administrative and logistical work. These responsibilities were not visible in scenes of pitched battle, but they were performed between successive engagements. Assessments of military merit therefore had to recognize a role beyond that of frontline commanders.

Paragraph 4. Supplying replacement soldiers meant more than writing a number in the registers: officials had to organize people locally, secure grain, and transport it to the front. Xiao He’s administrative duties were connected with each new demand arising from Liu Bang’s campaigns. As a result, even after several clashes, the Han armies retained the personnel and supplies needed to fight again.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

Xiao He sustained Liu Bang’s war effort from Guanzhong. During the Chu–Han struggle, he remained mainly in Guanzhong, administering people, military provisions, and replacements so that Liu Bang’s frontline forces received continuing support. The Book of Han and other historical works present this work in the rear as an important condition for the Han armies’ continued fighting. Throughout the war, Liu Bang’s forces repeatedly required supplies and fresh soldiers. Xiao He turned local resources into military support. This can be compared to using one’s resources for a shared undertaking rather than hoarding wealth for oneself. The Xiang Commentary says, “Bound together by trust; not wealthy alone.” This entry emphasizes “resources should support the whole.”

Editorial Review Rationale

The event matches the central direction of action expressed by “resources should support the whole.” The comparison in the source manuscript supplies a concrete event and relevant limitations. It is an analogy constructed by later readers, not evidence that any participant cited this line.

Revision or Replacement Note

Retain the original comparison; no mandatory revision.

unit_id: XIANG-U-09-07

055 Line H10 Lu The Korean Armistice Establishes a Mechanism to Stop Fighting — Respect the Boundary after an Armistice▶

初九｜

055 case_id: XCASE-H10-L1 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Once rain has fallen and conditions have settled, virtue has accumulated; for the noble person, advancing on campaign is ill-omened because doubts remain.

Received interpretation: “Rain has already fallen and stores have accumulated; a woman’s persistence may bring danger. The moon is nearly full, and for a noble person an expedition at this point brings misfortune.” The Xiang Commentary explains “virtue has accumulated,” and also “doubts remain.”

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Paragraph 1. After prolonged fighting in the Korean War, the parties negotiated the timing and positions for stopping hostilities as well as questions concerning prisoners of war. Chinese People’s Volunteers had taken part in the fighting. A ceasefire had to be set out in a document accepted by the parties before frontline forces could adjust their operations under its terms.

Paragraph 2. In 1953, the Korean People’s Army and Chinese People’s Volunteers on one side and the United Nations Command on the other concluded a military armistice. The agreement provided for the cessation of hostilities, a military demarcation line, and associated arrangements. It brought extended combat to a temporary halt, but it was not a formal peace treaty.

Paragraph 3. In 1953, the Korean People’s Army and the Chinese People’s Volunteers on one side, and the United Nations Command on the other, signed a military armistice agreement. The document specified a cessation of operations and a military boundary, bringing large-scale combat to a temporary pause. It was a military armistice rather than a formal peace treaty, and the peninsula’s political disputes remained unresolved. The path from lengthy fighting through difficult negotiations to cessation by the frontline forces required several parties to act at the same time.

Paragraph 4. Once armistice terms reached the front, troops on both sides had to confirm the time and location for stopping their fire. Otherwise, a signed document alone could not bring exchanges of fire to an end. Even after a military demarcation line was drawn, political questions concerning territory and sovereignty still remained for subsequent settlement. The agreement therefore had both a clearly defined function and clearly defined limits.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The Korean Armistice established a mechanism for stopping the fighting. In 1953, the Korean People’s Army and Chinese People’s Volunteers on one side and the United Nations Command on the other concluded a military armistice setting out a cessation of hostilities and military boundary arrangements. The protracted combat temporarily ceased, but the agreement was not a formal peace treaty. After years of war, negotiations had dealt with the timing and location of the ceasefire and the question of prisoners. The 1953 armistice placed an effective stopping mechanism on the fighting; it can be compared to resisting a fresh, rash advance once a stage of progress has been achieved. An armistice, however, is not comprehensive peace. The Xiang Commentary states, “Once rain has fallen and conditions have settled, virtue has accumulated. For the noble person, campaigning brings misfortune because doubts remain.” The focus is “respect the boundary after an armistice.”

Editorial Review Rationale

The original case illustrates part of “respect the boundary after an armistice,” but it does not sufficiently reflect all the line image’s specific positions and conditions of action. The inference must be limited to what the event can actually illustrate.

Revised Comparison

The principal achievements of the 1953 Korean Armistice were the cessation of specified military activities and arrangements for a demarcation line, not the establishment of formal peace. When comparing it to “rain has fallen and conditions have settled,” readers should note that a stage of progress had been reached and fresh military action should not be undertaken hastily. The armistice document does not fully substantiate the original text’s meanings relating to the accumulation of virtue and lingering doubts. The Xiang Commentary states, “Once rain has fallen and conditions have settled, virtue has accumulated; for the noble person, campaigning is ill-omened because doubts remain.” This is a retrospective analogy, not historical proof that the parties acted upon the line.

Recheck Decision

Retain the event and full original story. Narrow the inference and make clear which aspects of the line’s meaning are not represented; keep grade B rather than insist on upgrading every case to A.

Revision or Replacement Note

The draft revision uses the historical account of the Korean Armistice’s cessation mechanism as an analogy made by later readers. It illustrates some questions involved in “respecting the boundary after an armistice,” but the event had political, economic, and social causes of its own. Similarities in outcomes cannot establish that the participants followed the line statement. Readers should distinguish the conditions known at the time, the actions actually taken, and the results seen afterwards, and check the event against the original manuscript’s cited sources.

unit_id: XIANG-U-10-02

056 Line H10 Lu Feng Yi Declines to Compete for Credit and Becomes the “Great Tree General” — Act According to Your Principles▶

九二｜

056 case_id: XCASE-H10-L2 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Going forward in plain footwear: one carries out one’s own aspiration.

Received interpretation: “Proceeding in plain footwear”: The Xiang Commentary explains that one acts on one’s own aspiration.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E15

Paragraph 1. In the early Eastern Han period, commanders accumulated merits while helping to establish the new regime. Each victory was linked to court rewards, so colleagues inevitably discussed which achievements belonged to whom. Feng Yi had commanded troops himself; he was not a bystander outside the army.

Paragraph 2. The Book of the Later Han records that when the generals discussed their respective achievements, Feng Yi would often withdraw beneath a tree. He accordingly became known as the “Great Tree General.” The work also portrays him as modest and unwilling to quarrel over credit. The account concerns how men with military merits dealt with one another during the formation of the regime.

Paragraph 3. According to the Book of the Later Han, Feng Yi commonly stood apart beneath a tree when the generals assembled to count their achievements, hence his nickname. He continued to carry out military responsibilities; withdrawing from arguments about credit did not mean withdrawing from the establishment of the regime. The historian included the incident in his biography, leaving posterity with an image of modesty. The origin of the nickname becomes intelligible only when this portrait is read alongside his actual military service.

Paragraph 4. The generals commanded different forces in different theaters, and discussions of military merit were tied to their future political standing. Feng Yi stepped beneath the tree on a specific occasion when others had gathered to claim credit. Refusing to compete verbally did not deny his participation in campaigns or his acceptance of appointments from the court.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The Book of the Later Han says that Feng Yi withdrew beneath a tree as his fellow generals recounted their merits, earning the name “Great Tree General”; it also depicts his modest, noncompetitive manner. Such conduct can be compared with following one’s principles rather than reshaping one’s behavior for display. Yet public duty cannot simply be replaced by yielding to others. The Xiang Commentary states that proceeding in plain footwear is an expression of one’s own aspiration. The comparison emphasizes acting according to one’s principles.

Editorial Review Rationale

The event accords with the principal course of action expressed by the lesson. The source comparison identifies a concrete event and notes its limits. This is a retrospective comparison by later readers, not evidence that the historical people themselves cited this line.

One-Time Revision / Replacement Note

Retain the source comparison; no compulsory revision.

unit_id: XIANG-U-10-03

057 Line H10 Lu Zhou Yafu Waits for the Right Moment in the Rebellion of the Seven States — Maintain Judgment amid Outside Pressure▶

九三｜

057 case_id: XCASE-H10-L3 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

A secluded person’s steadfastness is auspicious; the center is not disordered from within.

Received interpretation: “The road is level; it is auspicious for a person in seclusion to remain steadfast.” The Xiang Commentary says that the inner center is not disturbed.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E05

Paragraph 1. In 154 BCE, seven kingdoms rebelled against the Han, and Wu and Chu forces advanced, leaving the kingdom of Liang in urgent need of help. The court sent Zhou Yafu to command its forces. He had to weigh Liang’s immediate danger against the opposing army’s supply lines. Following the enemy’s attack at once could force the Han army to fight on terms chosen by the enemy.

Paragraph 2. After the revolt began, Zhou Yafu did not continually seek a head-on decision. He held his position and sent troops to sever the Wu-Chu army’s grain route. He waited until the enemy had difficulty obtaining supplies, then seized the opportunity created by its withdrawal. Meanwhile Liang remained under pressure, making this plan politically controversial.

Paragraph 3. Zhou Yafu defended his own position while sending a separate force against the enemy’s supply line. The pressure on Liang did not disappear, and Zhou faced political criticism for failing to come to its immediate aid. Only when the enemy’s supplies had been disrupted and its offensive could no longer be maintained did he strike during its retreat. The successful suppression of the revolt and the danger borne by Liang are both part of the record; the strategy changed conditions at the front by acting against the rear supply of grain.

Paragraph 4. Zhou Yafu’s decision meant that Liang could not receive comprehensive immediate assistance, and its court was dissatisfied. At the same time the Han army still had to preserve its position and prevent the enemy from easily redirecting the attack. Cutting the grain route was not passive observation: it gradually deprived the Wu-Chu forces of the means to sustain their offensive.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

During the revolt Zhou Yafu maintained his original deployment despite demands that he save Liang immediately. He defended his position, cut the Wu-Chu army’s food supply and attacked when its retreat offered an opportunity, although his course imposed real risks upon Liang. The case can illustrate judgment undisturbed by outside clamor. Such steadiness, however, needs a sound assessment of the battlefield; it is not mere obstinacy. The Xiang Commentary says, “A secluded person’s steadfastness is auspicious; the center is not disordered.” The lesson is to maintain judgment amid external pressure.

Editorial Review Rationale

The event accords with the principal course of action expressed by the lesson. The source comparison identifies a concrete event and notes its limits. This is a retrospective comparison by later readers, not evidence that the historical people themselves cited this line.

One-Time Revision / Replacement Note

unit_id: XIANG-U-10-04

058 Line H10 Lu Fu Jian’s Southern Campaign Ends in Defeat at the Fei River — Forcefulness Cannot Make Up for Limited Capability▶

九四｜

058 case_id: XCASE-H10-L4 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Impaired sight does not make for clarity; impaired steps cannot keep pace. The misfortune of being bitten arises from an unsuitable position; the warrior who acts as ruler is rigid in his aims.

Received interpretation: The inherited explanation invokes impaired sight, impaired walking, stepping on a tiger’s tail and being bitten; its Xiang glosses concern inadequate clarity, inability to proceed, an unsuitable position and unyielding purpose.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E34

Paragraph 1. Fu Jian of Former Qin controlled large parts of northern China and prepared a major assault on Eastern Jin. His wide domain enabled him to mobilize armies, but forces drawn from different backgrounds still had to act together on a distant campaign. Eastern Jin, meanwhile, faced strong pressure from the southward advance in the Jiang-Huai region.

Paragraph 2. Fu Jian marched south against Eastern Jin with a great army, but was routed after Jin troops counterattacked near the Fei River. An apparent advantage in numbers did not automatically become stable organization or effective command. Afterward the internal divisions of the territories under his rule became more visible.

Paragraph 3. The armies fought near the Fei River in 383. Former Qin forces collapsed following the counterattack. Fu Jian failed to complete his campaign, and groups previously brought together under his regime reassessed their positions; successive divisions followed. Ancient histories contain dramatic descriptions of the battle, and troop numbers cannot necessarily be verified precisely. The clear sequence is extensive mobilization, defeat at Fei River and the decline of Former Qin’s control.

Paragraph 4. Before moving south, Qin had to supply the expedition and coordinate orders. Once defeated, it also had to preserve routes of withdrawal for forces of different origins. The collapse at Fei River quickly affected the ruling structure: groups that had previously accepted Fu Jian’s authority began to make other choices as the military situation changed.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The defeat at Fei River illustrates the danger of mistaking size and determination for effective control. Fu Jian’s forces possessed an apparent numerical advantage, but not the organizational unity necessary to sustain it. This historical comparison must not use the original text’s bodily images to pass judgment on persons with disabilities. The Xiang Commentary speaks of insufficient clarity and capacity, an unsuitable position and rigid intentions. The focus here is that forcefulness cannot compensate for inadequate capability.

Editorial Review Rationale

The event accords with the principal course of action expressed by the lesson. The source comparison identifies a concrete event and notes its limits. This is a retrospective comparison by later readers, not evidence that the historical people themselves cited this line.

unit_id: XIANG-U-10-05

059 Line H10 Lu Lin Xiangru Goes to Qin and Returns the Jade Intact to Zhao — Proceed Cautiously When Facing a Stronger Power▶

九五｜

059 case_id: XCASE-H10-L5 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Apprehension and caution eventually bring good fortune, for the intention can be carried out.

Received interpretation: “Treading on the tiger’s tail, fearful and cautious, is ultimately auspicious.” The Xiang Commentary explains that the intention can be realized.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E10

Paragraph 1. Qin proposed exchanging cities for Zhao’s He Shi jade. The Zhao court had to choose between handing over the prized object and rejecting a stronger state’s proposal. Lin Xiangru was ordered to take the jade to Qin with no guarantee that an exchange would succeed. Once at court, he had to judge whether Qin truly meant to hand over the promised cities.

Paragraph 2. The Records of the Grand Historian says that Qin’s king offered cities in exchange for the jade. Fearing it might lose the jade without receiving territory, Zhao sent Lin Xiangru to respond. Through negotiation and court ceremony he created room to maneuver and arranged for the jade to reach Zhao ahead of him. The episode depicts diplomacy amid unequal power.

Paragraph 3. When Lin Xiangru realized that the Qin king had taken possession of the jade without seriously preparing to transfer cities, he contrived to recover it and sent someone back to Zhao with it. After the object left Qin’s court, he stayed to negotiate and only later returned himself. The Records of the Grand Historian describes successive acts of diplomatic response, dispatching the jade and confronting the Qin king. The elaborate dialogue in the transmitted account is ancient literary narration and cannot be checked word for word like a recording.

Paragraph 4. Zhao initially sent the jade to avoid relinquishing the possibility of exchange before Qin had openly refused. Observations at court changed Lin Xiangru’s next move: his companion took the jade back first, while he remained to answer the stronger ruler. That diplomatic maneuver did not erase the underlying disparity in power between the two states.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

Lin Xiangru’s careful responses during the jade dispute show how apprehension, when translated into alertness, may support purposeful action. The account in the Records of the Grand Historian relates his use of negotiation and court procedure to return the jade safely, but neither the original offer nor Zhao’s exposure to Qin was without risk. The Xiang Commentary speaks of eventual good fortune through caution and the fulfillment of one’s intention. The lesson is to act carefully when facing a stronger power.

Editorial Review Rationale

The event accords with the principal course of action expressed by the lesson. The source comparison identifies a concrete event and notes its limits. This is a retrospective comparison by later readers, not evidence that the historical people themselves cited this line.
