unit_id: XIANG-U-10-06

060 Line H10 Lu The Xuanwu Gate Incident Changes the Succession by Force — Authority to Decide Does Not Eliminate Danger▶

上九｜

060 case_id: XCASE-H10-L6 | suitability_grade: B | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Decisive treading can be perilous even when one is steadfast, despite a formally appropriate position.

Received interpretation: “Decisive action is dangerous even when it is correct.” The Xiang Commentary explains that the position occupied is properly placed.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E43

Paragraph 1. During the reign of Tang Gaozu, the crown prince Li Jiancheng and Li Shimin each possessed political standing and supporting forces. Li Shimin had military achievements and connections in the army, but the existing succession arrangement recognized his brother as crown prince. Distrust concerning the future distribution of power increased on both sides.

Paragraph 2. At the Xuanwu Gate incident, Li Shimin had Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji killed, securing political and military advantage, and later became emperor. The succession conflict was resolved through violence. Later evaluations of the Zhenguan reign cannot erase the human and political cost of how power was seized.

Paragraph 3. In 626 Li Shimin launched an armed action at Xuanwu Gate, in which Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji were killed. He subsequently gained the political and military advantage and eventually ascended the throne, interrupting the previous succession. Later evaluations of Taizong’s reign belong to the history after the coup; they cannot undo the deaths on that day. Because histories were often compiled after a victor established power, their narrative standpoint also requires attention.

Paragraph 4. Xuanwu Gate was a key access route to the palace. By choosing it as the site for armed action, Li Shimin made military force directly alter the court’s succession. After Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji were killed, the previously designated crown prince could no longer inherit the throne. Taizong’s subsequent accomplishments must be considered separately from the deaths and transfer of power at the coup.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The Xuanwu Gate incident rearranged succession after a violent seizure of power. The possession of rank and decision-making authority does not remove the dangers or moral costs of a decisive act. Li Shimin’s later rule must not be used to erase the political risks and casualties of the coup. The Xiang Commentary links decisive action and danger with a properly situated position. This case emphasizes that having power to decide does not eliminate danger.

Editorial Review Rationale

The event accords with the principal course of action expressed by the lesson. The source comparison identifies a concrete event and notes its limits. This is a retrospective comparison by later readers, not evidence that the historical people themselves cited this line.

unit_id: XIANG-U-10-07

061 Line H11 Tai Beiping Avoids a Major Urban Battle through Negotiation and Reorganization — Assess Actions in Light of Their Results▶

初九｜

061 case_id: XCASE-H11-L1 | suitability_grade: B | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Great good fortune is at the top; this is cause for great celebration.

Received interpretation: “Great good fortune at the top”: the Xiang Commentary explains that there is abundant cause for celebration.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E59

Paragraph 1. The Pingjin campaign in late 1948 and early 1949 made Beiping a possible site of urban assault. Fu Zuoyi’s side controlled the troops in the city, while Communist forces exerted pressure outside. The decision whether to fight affected military arrangements as well as the damage that residents and buildings might suffer.

Paragraph 2. In the Pingjin campaign, Fu Zuoyi’s representatives negotiated with Communist forces. The defenders accepted arrangements to leave the city and be reorganized, and the transfer of control was completed in January 1949. This reduced the destruction that a major battle within the city might have caused, but the agreement was reached under substantial military pressure.

Paragraph 3. The parties negotiated the departure and reorganization of defenders and the transfer of the city. Fu Zuoyi’s side accepted the terms, and the main change of authority in Beiping took place in January 1949, avoiding a large urban battle. The negotiations were driven by clear military pressure and should not be romanticized as unconditional reconciliation. From encirclement and agreement on troop disposition to the actual takeover, each step had to be carried out.

Paragraph 4. After accepting reorganization, the defenders had to leave their former positions as agreed. The incoming authorities had to keep transport, public order and government offices functioning. One meeting could not replace the practical work of transfer. Because troop movements and the order of entry had been arranged, Beiping did not experience the large-scale fighting inside the city that had otherwise been possible.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The Beiping handover followed military encirclement, negotiations and troop reorganization, and avoided a major battle within the city. A review of the result must consider the pressure involved, the bargaining process, the reorganization and the consequences for civilians. It is not enough to call the outcome auspicious merely because an urban battle did not occur. The Xiang Commentary says, “Great good fortune at the top; great cause for celebration.” This is a retrospective analogy, not proof that the negotiators based their decisions on the line.

Editorial Review Rationale

The original case illustrates one aspect of “assessing action through its results,” but it does not fully reproduce the line’s precise position and conditions of action. The inference must be narrowed and described as one facet rather than the whole meaning.

Replacement, Revision or Version Boundary

Revised comparison: Beiping passed through encirclement, negotiation and reorganization, ultimately avoiding a large battle inside the city. Reading this through “examining one’s treading and considering signs of fortune” requires attention to pressure, bargaining, reorganization and residents’ experience; the absence of fighting does not prove that every party’s later outcome was fortunate. The Xiang Commentary reads, “Great good fortune is at the top; this is cause for great celebration.” The comparison is retrospective, not evidence that those involved made decisions on the basis of the line.

One-Time Revision / Replacement Note

Keep the original event and complete historical story; narrow the inference and identify what remains unmatched. Retain grade B rather than force an upgrade to A.

Editorial boundary: A negotiated handover under military pressure is not equivalent to unconditional reconciliation or proof of lasting success.

unit_id: XIANG-U-11-02

062 Line H11 Tai The Northern Expedition Takes Wuchang after a Failed Assault — Collective Action Requires a Shared Direction▶

九二｜

062 case_id: XCASE-H11-L2 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Pulling up the reeds brings auspicious progress; the intention is directed outward.

Received interpretation: “Pulling up the reeds and advancing auspiciously”: the Xiang Commentary explains that the aspiration is directed outward.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E35

Paragraph 1. In 1926 Northern Expedition forces advanced toward Wuchang. Defenders still held the city and its surrounding lines. The attackers hoped to take this city on the Yangtze, but their first assault failed, forcing them to maintain a siege and supplies outside the walls.

Paragraph 2. The capture of Wuchang did not occur in a single strike. The northern expeditionary forces failed in an initial assault, continued the siege and fighting, and took Wuchang in October 1926. The battle extended the political and military influence of the expedition, but entailed civilian and military casualties and the costs of encirclement.

Paragraph 3. The fighting continued until October, when the expeditionary army finally took Wuchang. The siege imposed losses upon defenders, attackers and residents, and restricted daily life inside the city. Wuchang’s fall increased the expedition’s influence but cannot erase the earlier failed assault. Taking the city followed successive deployments and sustained fighting; further political disputes still arose within the expeditionary camp.

Paragraph 4. The defenders used fortifications to delay the attack, while the besiegers had to preserve their encircling positions and supplies. Only when Wuchang changed hands in October did the campaign acquire a clear military outcome. The impact upon the city’s population throughout the siege must not disappear from the narrative of victory.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

After initial assaults failed, the Northern Expedition continued the siege and took Wuchang in October 1926, expanding its influence at the cost of military and civilian losses. The campaign brought several political and military forces into a coordinated effort. This can illuminate the image of interconnected reeds and a shared outward goal; it cannot erase differences among the participants. The Xiang Commentary says, “Pulling up reeds and advancing auspiciously; the aspiration is directed outward.” The lesson is that collective action requires a shared direction.

Editorial Review Rationale

The event illustrates part of the lesson, but the specific position of the line and its requirement of like-minded, upright mutual engagement are not directly established by the fighting. Winning the city does not by itself satisfy those requirements.

Replacement, Revision or Version Boundary

Revised comparison: The Wuchang campaign moved from an unsuccessful assault through continued encirclement to a renewed offensive. The common war effort can illuminate people working toward a shared outward objective. Yet neither the mutual drawing of similar reeds nor the requirement of uprightness is established by the battle details. Victory alone must not substitute for that requirement. This is a retrospective analogy rather than evidence that participants consulted the line.

One-Time Revision / Replacement Note

Keep the event and full story while narrowing the analogy. A siege involving assault, pressure and civilian harm can illustrate an outward military objective, but not every ethical and relational aspect of the reed image; retain B rather than force A.

unit_id: XIANG-U-11-03

063 Line H11 Tai Guan Zhong Helps Duke Huan of Qi Maintain Cooperation among the Lords — Leadership Requires Room for Different Talents▶

九三｜

063 case_id: XCASE-H11-L3 | suitability_grade: B | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Embracing what is broad and following the balanced course allows things to flourish.

Received interpretation: “Embrace the broad and uphold the central course”: the Xiang Commentary explains that this brings expansion and brilliance.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E08

Paragraph 1. When Duke Huan appointed Guan Zhong, Qi first had to govern its own territory before it could repeatedly send troops, convene interstate meetings and fulfill promises. Other rulers had their own security concerns and interests. Even when they attended a meeting, they did not surrender every future choice to Qi.

Paragraph 2. Guan Zhong assisted Duke Huan in enlarging Qi’s influence through domestic reforms and meetings with the other lords. The Records of the Grand Historian links Duke Huan’s hegemony to Guan Zhong’s administration and diplomacy. This network of cooperation rested both on common interests and Qi’s strength.

Paragraph 3. Guan Zhong participated in governing Qi, and Duke Huan expanded influence through repeated negotiations. The Records of the Grand Historian connects their administration and the rise of Qi’s leadership. Cooperation among states drew on Qi’s power but was also motivated by shared problems. The interstate meetings were not all one meeting with unchanging participants and subjects; both changed with circumstances. Even after gaining a leading position, Qi had to keep managing its relations.

Paragraph 4. Domestic administration enabled Qi to provide grain, supplies and envoys; diplomacy converted those resources into relations with other states. Every common proposal still depended on whether the other parties could accept it. Duke Huan’s prestige and Guan Zhong’s work complemented one another, supported by Qi’s military strength.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

Guan Zhong’s appointment and Qi’s interstate cooperation illustrate a leader’s willingness to use talent without excluding people solely because of former grievances. Guan Zhong and Duke Huan coupled internal reforms with diplomacy, but cooperation depended on other states’ interests and on Qi’s strength. Inclusion must be accompanied by judgment about competence and public responsibility. The Xiang Commentary speaks of accommodating broadly and following a central course to achieve greater reach. The focus is on making room for different talents.

Editorial Review Rationale

The event accords with the principal course of action expressed by the lesson. The source comparison identifies a concrete event and notes its limits. This is a retrospective comparison by later readers, not evidence that the historical people themselves cited this line.

One-Time Revision / Replacement Note

Retain the source comparison; no compulsory revision.

unit_id: XIANG-U-11-04

064 Line H11 Tai The End of the Anti-Japanese War Does Not Secure Lasting Peace — Victory Can Be Followed by Reversal▶

九四｜

064 case_id: XCASE-H11-L4 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

What goes does not fail to return; this is the boundary between heaven and earth.

Received interpretation: “No level ground remains without a slope, and no departure without a return. Remaining upright in difficulty is without blame.” The Xiang Commentary refers to the boundary between heaven and earth.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E63

Paragraph 1. After the war against Japan ended in 1945, China had to take over local offices, determine army positions and arrange postwar political authority. The Nationalist Government and the Chinese Communist Party retained separate political and military resources. Ceasefires and negotiations could not automatically decide who would administer every locality.

Paragraph 2. After victory in 1945, China still faced army reorganization, regional takeover and the distribution of political power. Although negotiations and ceasefire efforts took place, conflict between the Nationalists and Communists gradually widened; full-scale civil war broke out in 1946. Ending the war against an external enemy did not automatically establish domestic peace.

Paragraph 3. The Chongqing talks and subsequent consultations attempted to set terms for cooperation, but friction continued in the field and in local communities. In 1946 armed clashes expanded and the country moved toward full-scale civil war. A victory proclamation could date the end of the foreign war; local administration, disarmament and joint government required separate agreements and implementation. The gap between agreements and actions on the ground was a major reason why the postwar order failed to stabilize.

Paragraph 4. Even after ceasefire initiatives, local armed forces and offices continued competing for the right to take over territories. An agreement announced at the center did not mean every garrison immediately moved or stopped fighting. The wider fighting of 1946 exposed the growing gap between hopes for peace and what happened.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

China’s inability to secure peace after 1945 illustrates that a favorable situation need not endure automatically. The end of the war against Japan did not resolve military administration or the competing claims of the Nationalists and Communists. The Xiang Commentary states, “What goes does not fail to return; this is the boundary between heaven and earth.” The later conflict came from definite political conditions, not from a prediction made by the hexagram. The lesson is that a victory can be followed by reversal.

Editorial Review Rationale

The example can be related to the transition of an alliance, but the conditions of cooperation and responsibility for rupture must be distinguished. The outbreak of fighting must not be presented as the unavoidable fulfillment of a single line.

Replacement, Revision or Version Boundary

Revised comparison: After the anti-Japanese war, hopes of peaceful reconstruction diverged from the realities of military and administrative control. The phrase “what goes does not fail to return” may remind readers that a favorable trend is not permanent. It is not a prediction that the postwar period must necessarily lead to renewed war. Negotiations, local takeover and fighting must be analyzed separately. This is a later analogy, not proof of decisions based on the line.

One-Time Revision / Replacement Note

Retain the historical episode and original story, while distinguishing negotiations, the taking over of territories and military clashes; the line offers a warning about change, not a prophecy that renewed war was inevitable.

unit_id: XIANG-U-11-05

065 Line H11 Tai Sun Quan and Liu Bei Unite against Cao Cao — Shared Circumstances Make an Alliance Possible▶

九五｜

065 case_id: XCASE-H11-L5 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

They come lightly and without wealth, for none holds secure resources; trust without warning expresses what the heart desires.

Received interpretation: “Coming readily, not relying on wealth, trusting neighbors without prior warning”: the Xiang Commentary says the parties have lost their separate security and their sincere intentions are aligned.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E13

Paragraph 1. Cao Cao’s advance south rapidly altered the situation in Jingzhou. Liu Bei and Sun Quan each faced a northern army’s threat. Liu Bei needed new military support, while Sun Quan had to settle the defense of the Yangtze. Both sides already possessed their own territories and deployments and had to make contact and coordinate before joining forces.

Paragraph 2. Facing shared military pressure from Cao Cao’s southward campaign, Sun Quan and Liu Bei cooperated after negotiations involving Lu Su, Zhuge Liang and others. Their combined forces resisted Cao at Red Cliffs. Yet each side continued to have territorial and strategic interests afterward, and the alliance was not free from friction.

Paragraph 3. Envoys including Lu Su and Zhuge Liang helped produce cooperation. Their combined forces fought Cao’s troops around Red Cliffs and achieved military results, but each ally still had to govern its territory and armies. A shared wartime objective did not settle later territorial arrangements. The relationship passed through military pressure, diplomacy, joint action and fresh negotiations afterward; “a successful alliance” does not sum up all subsequent events.

Paragraph 4. Before the coalition formed, envoys had to establish whether both sides would resist Cao Cao together. After formation, the armies had to coordinate while retaining their respective strengths. Victory at Red Cliffs did not make the allies’ aims identical. Later conflicts over Jingzhou arose within a relationship that had also involved joint military action.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The Sun–Liu alliance arose from a common threat, not simply from an attempt to buy cooperation with wealth. The parties recognized the need to collaborate while retaining separate interests. The Xiang Commentary speaks of trusting one another without depending on riches, and of genuine wishes within the heart. Shared circumstances made the alliance possible; they did not abolish later disputes.

Editorial Review Rationale

The event accords with the principal course of action expressed by the lesson. The source comparison identifies a concrete event and notes its limits. This is a retrospective comparison by later readers, not evidence that the historical people themselves cited this line.

One-Time Revision / Replacement Note

Retain the source comparison; no compulsory revision.

unit_id: XIANG-U-11-06

066 Line H11 Tai Princess Xijun’s Marriage Alliance with Wusun — Diplomatic Ties Carry Political Aspirations▶

上九｜

066 case_id: XCASE-H11-L6 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Good fortune through auspicious arrangements; one acts on one’s aspiration from the center.

Received interpretation: “Through blessings, great good fortune; one’s aspiration is carried out from the center.”

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Replacement candidate: Princess Xijun marries the ruler of Wusun (historical sources: Book of Han, Western Regions). Superseded event: E31 Zhang Qian’s embassy (archived).

Paragraph 1. During Emperor Wu’s Western Han reign, long rivalry between Han and the Xiongnu led the court to seek Wusun support through diplomacy. Zhang Qian had suggested cultivating Wusun through gifts and marriage ties, combining political interests with a relationship of kinship.

Paragraph 2. According to the Book of Han, “Account of the Western Regions, Part Two,” in the Yuanfeng period the Han court sent Liu Xijun, a daughter of the Prince of Jiangdu, to Wusun as a princess to marry its ruler, the Kunmo. The court arranged clothing, attendants and gifts, using marriage to establish a political connection across state borders.

Paragraph 3. The Wusun ruler also had marriage relations with the Xiongnu. The Han marriage therefore did not immediately produce an exclusive ally, nor did it mean that Princess Xijun alone could decide matters of state diplomacy.

Paragraph 4. The marriage carried the Han court’s political hopes, but the development of trust still depended on Wusun’s internal arrangements and the neighboring powers. This is a marriage-alliance policy recorded in historical sources; it does not establish that the participants acted on Hexagram 11, line five, of the Zhouyi.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The fifth line of Tai invokes “Emperor Yi marrying off his younger sister” and links marriage to political order; the Xiang Commentary adds that one carries out an aspiration from the center. The Han court’s dispatch of Princess Xijun to marry the Wusun ruler supplies a documented marriage agreement, official authorization and political purpose; this is closer to the line than an earlier example confined to Zhang Qian’s diplomatic mission. Both involve concrete arrangements intended to put political wishes into effect. Yet Xijun’s marriage also involved unequal power and her personal circumstances. An auspicious phrase must not be used to idealize it or to assume an alliance’s inevitable success.

Editorial Review Rationale

The prior case of Zhang Qian’s diplomatic contact with Wusun did not sufficiently represent the marriage alliance, hierarchical relationships and central fulfillment of aspirations expressed in this line. An event with an explicit marriage alliance is therefore selected instead.

Replacement, Revision or Version Boundary

SOURCE-VERSION NOTICE: The Traditional Chinese master contains a “C-grade replacement” record and the candidate story about Princess Xijun. It also retains the superseded E31 Zhang Qian mission. The replacement story is translated here as the displayed candidate; the older story remains an archived source and should not be mixed with it in public presentation. The source record’s approval and publish status require separate confirmation.

One-Time Revision / Replacement Note

This entry preserves the former Zhang Qian case as archival material but designates the Princess Xijun marriage-alliance account as the replacement candidate. It requires editorial sign-off; do not silently present the old E31 event as the final historical case.

Archival Event (Superseded; Not for Public Display)

Zhang Qian visited Wusun during Han diplomacy aimed at shifting the balance with the Xiongnu. The Wusun had their own political and security considerations, so an embassy could communicate a proposal but not compel agreement. Subsequent exchanges and marriages unfolded over additional missions and policies; they cannot all be attributed to one visit. This original case is preserved as an editorial archive rather than the replacement narrative.

Archived narrative paragraph 1. Competition between Han and the Xiongnu prompted the Han court to seek relations with other powers of the Western Regions. Zhang Qian traveled again to convey the Han court’s intentions to Wusun and other places. Envoys could bring proposals, but upon arrival they had to await responses determined by the other side’s domestic circumstances.

Archived narrative paragraph 2. On his second journey to the Western Regions, Zhang Qian conveyed the Han court’s wish to cooperate with Wusun and other states, hoping to change the balance of power between Han and the Xiongnu. Diplomatic contacts gradually increased; however, Wusun had its own internal political and security concerns and would not immediately act according to the Han court’s wishes.

Archived narrative paragraph 3. Wusun did not immediately accept every arrangement once the Han court explained the benefits of cooperation. Zhang Qian’s mission opened further exchanges of information and people, while subsequent diplomatic ties developed through other envoys and policies. Later marriage alliances and contacts must not all be retroactively attributed to Zhang Qian’s single mission. The Han invitation and Wusun’s decision on how to respond were separate political choices.

Archived narrative paragraph 4. An envoy had to cross a long route to reach Wusun carrying the Han court’s hopes for relations; the recipients still had to discuss the proposal among their own people. Han’s goal of containing the Xiongnu and Wusun’s willingness to revise existing diplomatic ties were two questions that neither side could settle unilaterally.

Archived historical comparison: Zhang Qian’s second mission conveyed proposals for cooperation intended to shift the balance between Han and the Xiongnu, but Wusun’s internal concerns prevented automatic acceptance. The event can retrospectively illustrate diplomatic aspirations and alliance-building, not a modern general rule that marriages should be used for diplomacy. The Xiang Commentary says, “Through blessings, great good fortune; the center acts upon its aspiration.” This older event does not sufficiently embody the line’s specific marriage-alliance image and therefore remains superseded.

unit_id: XIANG-U-11-07

067 Line H12 Pi Prosperity in the Late Tianbao Era Gives Way to the An Lushan Rebellion — An Order Can Collapse from Within▶

初九｜

067 case_id: XCASE-H12-L1 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

The city wall falls back into its moat, for its commands have become disordered.

Received interpretation: “The city wall falls into the moat; do not use armies, but issue orders from one’s own town; even steadfastness brings regret.” The Xiang Commentary points to disordered commands.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E55

Paragraph 1. Under Emperor Xuanzong, Tang rule enjoyed periods of prosperity and a far-reaching domain, while commanders in frontier garrisons gradually accumulated military power. An Lushan controlled frontier troops, and tensions between the central government and regional authorities grew harder to manage as power concentrated.

Paragraph 2. The reign experienced prosperity and expansion, but unresolved problems accumulated between frontier commands and court politics. In 755 An Lushan rebelled and disrupted the court’s control. The resulting war had long-term effects on population, revenue and regional power.

Paragraph 3. After An Lushan rose in 755, the existing order was shaken and Xuanzong left Chang’an. War continued for years, influencing migration, state finances and local civil-military authority. The uprising has a clear starting date, but the relationship between frontier commands and the center had been developing over a longer period. Focusing only on palace anecdotes would conceal why the prolonged conflict transformed Tang governance.

Paragraph 4. Regional military governors controlled troops and local resources; the court’s prosperity did not guarantee command over them. After the rebellion began, armies advanced and the court made decisions about defense and retreat. Years of war then increased the extent to which regional authorities handled revenue and military affairs themselves. The consequences were not confined to 755.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The An Lushan Rebellion dealt a massive blow to the Tang. The image of a wall falling back into a moat can help readers understand the breakdown of institutions supporting a seemingly prosperous order. This must not be represented as a sudden transfer of heaven’s mandate that explains the rebellion by itself. The Xiang Commentary says that the wall returns to the moat because commands have become disordered. The emphasis is that an order can collapse from within.

Editorial Review Rationale

The event accords with the principal course of action expressed by the lesson. The source comparison identifies a concrete event and notes its limits. This is a retrospective comparison by later readers, not evidence that the historical people themselves cited this line.

One-Time Revision / Replacement Note

Retain the source comparison; no compulsory revision.

unit_id: XIANG-U-12-02

068 Line H12 Pi Bao Zheng Opposes Zhang Yaozuo’s Promotion through Palace Connections — Uphold Public Duty in an Unfavorable Setting▶

九二｜

068 case_id: XCASE-H12-L2 | suitability_grade: B | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Pulling up reeds with steadfastness is auspicious, because the intention is directed toward the ruler.

Received interpretation: “Pulling up reeds and remaining steadfast is auspicious”: the Xiang Commentary explains that the intention is directed toward the ruler.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E21

Paragraph 1. During Emperor Renzong’s Northern Song reign, Zhang Yaozuo received promotions because of his kinship ties to the palace, drawing the attention of court officials. For officials charged with remonstrance and oversight, this was more than one man’s change of position: it raised the question whether kinship with the imperial family would govern appointments.

Paragraph 2. Zhang Yaozuo’s promotion because of his palace connections provoked opposition from Bao Zheng and other remonstrance officials. They submitted memorials and argued the matter at court, asking the emperor to reconsider the appointments. The point is how officials sought to check the exercise of the appointment power.

Paragraph 3. Bao Zheng and others submitted memorials setting out objections and calling for reconsideration of Zhang’s posts. Debate unfolded between the ruler’s personnel authority and officials’ right to remonstrate, with arguments conveyed through formal documents and court audiences. This episode belongs to the appointment process, not to a fictional criminal trial of Zhang presided over by Bao. The question concerned who should receive office, on what grounds, and how the emperor should answer criticism.

Paragraph 4. Remonstrance officials could not appoint or dismiss officials themselves; they could submit advice and keep debating the matter at court. Zhang’s different appointments must also be distinguished by post and date, rather than treating every controversy as a single offense of “guilt by imperial kinship.” Bao Zheng’s contribution was a formal objection to a personnel decision.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

Bao Zheng challenged the appointment of Zhang Yaozuo as an example of continuing to discharge public duties amid a powerful network of palace relationships. The ancient expression of an intention directed toward the ruler is interpreted here as responsibility for public service, not unconditional personal loyalty. The Xiang Commentary speaks of steadfast advance and an intention directed to the ruler. The lesson is to uphold public duty even under unfavorable circumstances.

Editorial Review Rationale

The event accords with the principal course of action expressed by the lesson. The source comparison identifies a concrete event and notes its limits. This is a retrospective comparison by later readers, not evidence that the historical people themselves cited this line.

One-Time Revision / Replacement Note

Retain the source comparison; no compulsory revision.

unit_id: XIANG-U-12-03

069 Line H12 Pi The Traditional Account of King Wen’s Imprisonment at Youli — Do Not Lose Your Principles amid Adversity▶

九三｜

069 case_id: XCASE-H12-L3 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

A great person endures obstruction and prospers without throwing the group into disorder.

Received interpretation: “The great person faces obstruction yet finds a way through; the group is not thrown into disorder.”

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E36

Paragraph 1. As the power of the Zhou grew toward the end of the Shang, later historical writings portray relations between Xibo Chang and the Shang royal house as strained. The Zhou Annals in the Records of the Grand Historian says the Shang king imprisoned Xibo Chang at Youli, forcing his followers to sustain Zhou activities and seek his release.

Paragraph 2. According to that account, Xibo Chang was confined at Youli by the Shang king, and his followers sought to free him. This transmitted story depicts a powerful ruler suppressing a political rival. The Zhou people’s subsequent rise must not be read backward as proof that every step was predetermined.

Paragraph 3. His followers acted to obtain his release, and Xibo Chang eventually left Youli. The account comes from histories compiled much later; its dates and spoken words cannot be checked one by one as modern records might be. The Zhou continued to develop after his release: they did not gain dominion on the day he left prison. Later stories that he “elaborated the Changes in captivity” need their own evidence; the confinement and release already form a coherent historical sequence.

Paragraph 4. While Xibo Chang was held, his followers kept up Zhou’s outside relations and tried to persuade the Shang ruler to release him. Only after being freed could he resume his political activities. Later generations know the Zhou dynasty rose, but people at the time could not foresee this outcome; confinement still involved uncertainty.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The account of King Wen’s confinement at Youli can illustrate maintaining political aims despite being cut off from normal activity. Without adequate historical evidence, one must not invent his precise inner thoughts or the measures he took. The Xiang Commentary says that a great person under obstruction does not throw the group into disorder. The analogy concerns preserving a political community under pressure; it does not imply that every silence is virtuous or that Xibo Chang used this line to protect himself.

Editorial Review Rationale

The case shows only part of “not losing one’s principles amid adversity”; it does not establish every feature of the line’s position and conditions of action. The inference must be narrowed.

Replacement, Revision or Version Boundary

Revised comparison: The transmitted imprisonment narrative invites discussion of how a group might remain coherent without inviting greater danger. “The great person endures obstruction without disturbing the group” is not a blanket endorsement of silence; nor is it evidence that Xibo Chang cited the line. This is a retrospective historical analogy.

One-Time Revision / Replacement Note

Keep the story with a limited analogy. Restraint in a high-pressure situation may help preserve associates and a political community, but silence is not invariably correct; there is no evidence that Xibo Chang acted according to this line.

unit_id: XIANG-U-12-04

070 Line H12 Pi Yuan Shikai’s Imperial Bid Provokes the National Protection Movement — Political Position and Legitimacy Can Diverge▶

九四｜

070 case_id: XCASE-H12-L4 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Concealing shame arises because the position is inappropriate.

Received interpretation: “Harboring shame”: the Xiang Commentary says that the position occupied is unsuitable.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E12

Paragraph 1. After the republic was founded, Yuan Shikai held a central government leadership role but maintained complex relations with regional political forces. In 1915 he pursued restoration of an imperial system, directly altering the republican framework and arrangements of authority. Public displays by supporters could not guarantee acceptance by the military, provincial officials or political groups.

Paragraph 2. Yuan Shikai’s 1915 attempt to establish an empire provoked political opposition and the National Protection War. Some of those who had formerly backed him ceased cooperating, and the imperial plan was abandoned in 1916. Concentration of power did not automatically produce stable political support.

Paragraph 3. Opposition groups launched a national-protection movement, and political protests were increasingly accompanied by armed conflict. Some local leaders who had previously worked with Yuan no longer cooperated, testing central control. Yuan withdrew the imperial plan in 1916, but conflicts over power did not vanish on that date. From preparing for emperorship to public opposition and withdrawal, events involved successive changes in political backing and battlefield pressure.

Paragraph 4. When proponents called for a change of system, provincial officials still had to choose their position between the republic and the new empire. Responses from the provinces reached the center at different times, and Yuan’s orders could not necessarily be implemented as intended. With the National Protection War, political dissent also became troop movements.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

Yuan Shikai’s imperial bid encountered broad resistance, showing that acquiring a title is not the same as gaining legitimacy. The claimed position did not correspond to a political order acceptable to many of those whose support was required. The Xiang Commentary attributes the shame to an unsuitable position. This retrospective example highlights the gap between political position and legitimacy.

unit_id: XIANG-U-12-05

071 Line H12 Pi The Nanjing Provisional Government Establishes Republican Institutions — New Responsibilities Need Institutional Authority▶

九五｜

071 case_id: XCASE-H12-L5 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

Having a mandate brings no blame; the intention can be put into practice.

Received interpretation: “With a mandate there is no blame, and those of the same kind share blessings”: the Xiang Commentary explains that the intention can be realized.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E50

Paragraph 1. After the 1911 Revolution, southern provinces needed an institution able to represent the republic abroad and handle governmental affairs at home. Founding a government required more than declaring an ideal: someone had to manage departments, finances and military orders. Nanjing became the seat of the provisional government, although its actual territorial control was limited.

Paragraph 2. On 1 January 1912, Sun Yat-sen became provisional president in Nanjing. The provisional government established agencies and issued policy statements in an effort to convert the revolution’s political aims into everyday administration. Yet its financial resources and effective nationwide authority remained restricted.

Paragraph 3. Sun took office on 1 January 1912, the government set up offices and promulgated policies, and officials began serving under new institutional titles while still confronting the Qing court and other regional armed forces. During north-south negotiations, appointments and allocations of authority continued to change. Inauguration had a definite date; securing the money and political backing necessary to carry out orders across the country was a separate process.

Paragraph 4. The Nanjing government had to transform revolutionary personal and military connections into offices, assigned responsibilities and official correspondence. Provinces that professed allegiance to a republic did not necessarily surrender taxation and military command at once. Even after Sun took office, the provisional agencies organized everyday government within these constraints.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The Nanjing provisional government used offices and administrative rules to undertake public affairs. Political intentions need assignments of authority and institutions, not solely personal reforming wishes. The Xiang Commentary links action under a mandate to the fulfillment of an intention. This example therefore stresses that a new responsibility requires institutional authority, while acknowledging the provisional government’s limited practical reach.

unit_id: XIANG-U-12-06

072 Line H12 Pi Liu Xiu Establishes Eastern Han and Restores Administration — Build a Stable Center in a Crisis▶

上九｜

072 case_id: XCASE-H12-L6 | suitability_grade: A | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English

The good fortune of a great person comes from occupying an appropriate position.

Received interpretation: “The great person’s good fortune”: the Xiang Commentary explains that the position is properly placed.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E24

Paragraph 1. As Wang Mang’s regime disintegrated, armed groups competed across the country. Liu Xiu gradually won support from troops and local groups, first establishing his own claim to political authority and then fighting those who had not accepted it. Even before the wars ended, the new regime had to keep officials and civilian life functioning in areas it controlled.

Paragraph 2. After Wang Mang’s collapse, Liu Xiu established Eastern Han amid competing regional forces, gradually brought major areas under unified control, and then reorganized officials, population registers, taxes and labor obligations. Reconstruction involved both continued warfare and the restoration of routine government and production.

Paragraph 3. Liu Xiu ascended the throne in 25 CE and unified major regions over subsequent years. When fighting ended in a locality, officials had to restore population registers, tax and labor arrangements and agriculture so that daily government could follow the postwar order. Restoring the name “Han” was a definite political step; rebuilding effective administration took different lengths of time in different places. Several years passed between the rise of rival contenders, the founding of Eastern Han and control over the principal regions.

Paragraph 4. If postwar population records were inaccurate, the court could not reliably organize taxation or determine available recruits. As Liu Xiu’s control expanded, officials had to extend registration and renewed production into recently pacified areas. Territorial unification and administration overlapped in time; they did not suddenly become complete in a single year.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

Liu Xiu’s establishment of Eastern Han and gradual restoration of order can illustrate the need for a stable center of leadership during crisis. Military victories alone did not re-create population records, farming or administration. This historical comparison is not a universal justification for monarchy. The Xiang Commentary speaks of good fortune linked to an appropriate position. The lesson concerns restoring a workable center in uncertain conditions.

unit_id: XIANG-U-12-07

072 Line H12 Pi The 1911 Revolution Brings Qing Rule to an End — Political Change Can Break a Deadlock▶

The 1911 Revolution Brings Qing Rule to an End — Political Change Can Break a Deadlock

Xiang Commentary — English

When obstruction reaches its end it overturns; how could it last indefinitely?

Received interpretation: “At the end of obstruction comes overturning”: the Xiang Commentary asks how such a condition could last.

Historical Event and Narrative — Four Paragraphs

Source event ID: E49

Paragraph 1. After the Wuchang uprising in 1911, provinces successively announced separation from the Qing court. Insurgents, regional armies and political figures did not all have identical aims, but the Qing’s former network of authority was already shaken. Fighting and north-south negotiations proceeded together as the parties contested whether monarchy could continue and who would represent central government.

Paragraph 2. After Wuchang, multiple provinces declared independence from Qing rule. Military confrontation and negotiation between north and south shaped the political settlement. The Qing emperor abdicated in 1912, and a republican form of government replaced the monarchy. The change resulted from several forces, not one leader or one uprising alone.

Paragraph 3. The Qing emperor abdicated in 1912, ending its monarchical system and replacing it with a republic. The abdication edict marked a recognizable transition, but the integration of military units, provinces and fiscal authority into the new government still required negotiations. From the original uprising through provincial responses to the north-south settlement, neither one person nor one city accomplished the entire institutional transformation. Revolutionary military success was not the same as a republic’s sustained operation.

Paragraph 4. After the abdication, troops and officials who had served the Qing still had to decide how they would function under the new political arrangements. North-south talks dealt with the monarch’s title, but could not write all provincial military and financial rules at once. The new republican authorities had to continue negotiating with local actors after the change of system.

Line-Specific Historical Comparison

The 1911 Revolution led to abdication and the establishment of a republic, providing an analogy for ending a prolonged political impasse. Yet the collapse of an old order did not ensure that its successor would immediately be stable. The Xiang Commentary states, “When obstruction reaches its end, it overturns; how could it last indefinitely?” This episode highlights the potential for political change to break a deadlock without treating change itself as a guarantee of good government.

073 Line H13 Tong Ren The 1949 CPPCC Adopts the Common Program — Cooperation Must Extend beyond Familiar Circles▶

初九｜

073 case_id: XCASE-H13-L1 | unit_id: XIANG-U-13-02 | original_event_id: E45 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: B | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'When people associate beyond the gate, who can find fault?'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. In 1949, as a new central government was being formed, the participants needed to discuss governmental institutions, personnel, and principles of administration. With the military situation and control of local areas changing, a shared institutional document could tell participants which arrangements would serve as the basis for establishing the government.

Paragraph 2. The First Plenary Session of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference adopted the Common Program and addressed the organizational arrangements of the central government. The document set basic directions for state-building and political institutions, translating cooperation among participants into an institutional text for the establishment of the new government.

Paragraph 3. The document set directions for institutions and policies during the early years of the new state; government agencies still had to be established and put those directions into practice. Participation was confined to a particular political range: the conference was not a procedure in which all residents voted directly. Additional administrative and political work was needed between a conference resolution and the operation of local institutions according to its provisions.

Paragraph 4. Only after the Common Program was adopted did the new central institutions have a shared text on which to base the assignment of responsibilities. When delegates dispersed, the administrative work was just beginning: appointments, the issuance of orders, and the takeover of local administrations all had to be carried out by institutions. There was a time lag between adopting a document and having it followed in practice in every part of the country.

074 Line H13 Tong Ren The Jingnan Campaign Turns an Imperial Dispute into Civil War — Family Loyalty Cannot Resolve Political Rivalry▶

九二｜

074 case_id: XCASE-H13-L2 | unit_id: XIANG-U-13-03 | original_event_id: E37 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: A | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'Association confined to one's own clan is the way to regret.'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. After the Jianwen Emperor took the throne, the court sought to adjust the powers of imperial princes in different regions. Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, commanded forces in the north, and the reduction of princely fiefs affected whether he could retain his former military and political position. The conflict between the center and the princely houses could not be resolved by agreement and gradually turned into troop movements.

Paragraph 2. Following the Jianwen Emperor's policy of reducing the princely fiefs, Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, raised an army and fought the central government. In 1402, Yan forces entered Nanjing and Zhu Di took the throne. Problems of succession and military power within the imperial family ultimately became a war affecting local communities and ordinary people.

Paragraph 3. Zhu Di rose in arms in 1399 and fought the Jianwen regime. The war continued for several years; Yan troops entered Nanjing in 1402 and Zhu Di became emperor. This was not merely a family quarrel at an imperial gathering: communities along the armies' routes and residents of the cities were affected by civil war. After the victors founded a new regime, their accounts of the reasons for the uprising and of the war could also influence the records available to later generations. Such accounts must be checked separately against specific dates and actions.

Paragraph 4. The measures to reduce princely fiefs initially concerned the central government's adjustment of princes' authority, but after Zhu Di raised troops, large armies and local communities bore the consequences. When Nanjing was taken, the Jianwen regime lost control and the new monarch began organizing the court. Several years of actual warfare separated that outcome from the original dispute over the princes' fiefs.

Original Line-Specific Historical Comparison — English

Historical comparison — The Jingnan Campaign Turns an Imperial Dispute into Civil War: Following the Jianwen Emperor's policy of reducing the princely fiefs, Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, raised an army and fought the central government. The Jingnan Campaign arose from conflict between imperial princes and the central court. It illustrates the limits of treating public authority as a matter to be resolved within a family; kinship cannot be equated with political consensus. The Xiang commentary reads: 'Association confined to one's own clan is the way to regret.' This entry focuses on: Family Loyalty Cannot Resolve Political Rivalry.

Editorial Assessment and Limits

075 Line H13 Tong Ren The Chongqing Negotiations Produce the Double Tenth Agreement — Hostility Can Obstruct Cooperation▶

九三｜

075 case_id: XCASE-H13-L3 | unit_id: XIANG-U-13-04 | original_event_id: E58 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: B | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'Troops lie concealed in the thickets because the adversary is strong. They do not rise for three years: how could they advance?'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. After victory in the War of Resistance against Japan in 1945, both the Nationalist Government and the Chinese Communist Party faced questions about reorganizing the armed forces, taking over local administrations, and the country's political system. To avert a larger domestic war, they needed to write down principles acceptable to both sides while addressing who actually controlled troops on the ground.

Paragraph 2. After the war, representatives of the Nationalist Government and the Chinese Communist Party negotiated in Chongqing and produced the Summary of Conversations between Government and Communist Representatives, commonly known as the Double Tenth Agreement. The sides set out principles for peaceful national reconstruction, but core issues, including the military and local political authority, remained unresolved.

Paragraph 3. Representatives met in Chongqing and issued the Summary of Conversations between Government and Communist Representatives, or Double Tenth Agreement. The document stated objectives such as peaceful national reconstruction, but central questions of control over armies and local government were not fully settled. After its publication, control on the ground and armed conflict continued to evolve. Negotiations, a signed text, and implementation are three connected processes that do not happen simultaneously. Issuing an agreement must not be described as peace having already been secured.

Paragraph 4. What could be written down at the negotiating table did not necessarily match the territories controlled by each side's armies. After representatives announced the agreement, their organizations still had to communicate the commitments and decide whether to carry them out. The difficulty of sustaining postwar peace must also be examined through the sequence of, and gaps between, these practical actions.

Original Line-Specific Historical Comparison — English

First-Round Suitability Review — English

The event E58, “The Chongqing Negotiations Produce the Double Tenth Agreement,” can illustrate “keeping an opponent in view and refraining from action over an extended obstruction,” but the recorded historical actions cover only some aspects of the image. A policy result or later interpretation must not be treated as evidence that the historical participants based their decisions on the Xiang commentary.

V4.3.1 Revised Line Comparison — English

[Retain original case; one limited interpretive revision.] Historical comparison — The Chongqing Negotiations Produce the Double Tenth Agreement: After the war, representatives of the Nationalist Government and the Chinese Communist Party negotiated in Chongqing and produced the Summary of Conversations between Government and Communist Representatives, commonly known as the Double Tenth Agreement. The sides set out principles for peaceful national reconstruction, but core issues, including the military and local political authority, remained unresolved. After victory in the War of Resistance against Japan in 1945, both the Nationalist Government and the Chinese Communist Party faced questions about reorganizing the armed forces, taking over local administrations, and the country's political system. 076 Line H13 Tong Ren The Chanyuan Treaty Ends the Current Song–Liao Fighting — Even at the Edge of Conflict, One Can Turn Back▶

九四｜

076 case_id: XCASE-H13-L4 | unit_id: XIANG-U-13-05 | original_event_id: E06 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: B | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'Climbing the wall but not overcoming it is right; the good outcome comes from reaching an impasse and returning to the rules.'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. After Liao forces moved south, the Song court had to decide whether the frontier conflict should expand further. Emperor Zhenzong's arrival at Chanzhou brought decision-makers face to face with frontline conditions and allowed envoys from both states to travel back and forth to discuss terms for ending the fighting. Both Song and Liao had military strength; neither side could dispense with subsequent arrangements by simply declaring that relations were amicable.

Paragraph 2. After the Liao forces advanced south and Emperor Zhenzong arrived at Chanzhou, the two sides negotiated and concluded the Chanyuan Treaty in 1005. Song agreed to make annual payments to Liao, while each side retained its own government and an agreed frontier order. The arrangement entailed a fiscal cost but also reduced large-scale warfare for a considerable period thereafter.

Paragraph 3. The negotiations culminated in the Chanyuan Treaty: each side retained its government and Song undertook to make annual payments. After the agreement, the current large-scale operations on the front ceased and a framework for the border was established; the payments simultaneously became a continuing expense for the court. Wars on the same scale were avoided for a substantial period, but border negotiations and friction did not disappear. Both the military and fiscal consequences continued under the treaty.

Paragraph 4. The treaty addressed the immediate fighting and provided terms to which later diplomatic missions could refer. Once the armies stopped advancing, the Song court still had to prepare the annual payments, while frontier communities lived under the new arrangements. The immediate effects of peace and the continuing costs were not the same for all participants.

Original Line-Specific Historical Comparison — English

First-Round Suitability Review — English

The event E06, “The Chanyuan Treaty Ends the Current Song–Liao Fighting,” can illustrate “approaching direct conflict yet returning to a proper rule rather than pressing the attack,” but the recorded historical actions cover only some aspects of the image. A policy result or later interpretation must not be treated as evidence that the historical participants based their decisions on the Xiang commentary.

077 Line H13 Tong Ren Sun Quan and Liu Bei Ally against Cao Cao — A Shared Goal Still Requires Practical Cooperation▶

九五｜

077 case_id: XCASE-H13-L5 | unit_id: XIANG-U-13-06 | original_event_id: E13 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: A | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'The beginning of association proceeds from impartial uprightness. The great armies meet and contend with one another.'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. Cao Cao's southward advance rapidly changed the situation in Jingzhou, and Liu Bei and Sun Quan each faced a threat from the northern forces. Liu Bei needed new military support, while Sun Quan had to decide how to defend the Yangtze. Each side already held its own territory and had its own deployments, so contact and coordination had to precede any alliance.

Paragraph 2. Following Cao Cao's southward advance, Sun Quan and Liu Bei faced shared military pressure and established cooperation through negotiations involving Lu Su, Zhuge Liang, and others. Allied forces resisted Cao's army at Red Cliffs, but after the battle each side continued to consider its own territory and interests. The alliance was not free from friction thereafter.

Paragraph 3. Lu Su, Zhuge Liang, and others took part in talks that brought about cooperation between Sun Quan and Liu Bei. Their allied forces fought Cao's troops around Red Cliffs and obtained military gains, after which each side still had to administer its territory and army. Sharing an objective in wartime did not mean that postwar territorial arrangements had already been settled. The relationship passed through military pressure, exchanges of envoys, joint operations, and further negotiations after the battle; 'a successful alliance' alone does not describe all that followed.

Paragraph 4. Before the coalition formed, envoys had to establish whether both parties would jointly resist Cao's army. Afterward, the two sides had to coordinate while retaining their separate forces. The end of the Battle of Red Cliffs did not mean their goals were entirely identical. The later dispute over Jingzhou arose within a relationship whose participants had once fought together.

Original Line-Specific Historical Comparison — English

Historical comparison — Sun Quan and Liu Bei Ally against Cao Cao: Following Cao Cao's southward advance, Sun Quan and Liu Bei faced shared military pressure and established cooperation through negotiations involving Lu Su, Zhuge Liang, and others. The Sun–Liu alliance was more than a profession of goodwill: it required military coordination. A common direction becomes a genuine encounter and cooperation through concrete actions. The Xiang commentary reads: 'The beginning of association proceeds from impartial uprightness.

The sides set out principles for peaceful national reconstruction, but core issues, including the military and local political authority, remained unresolved.

Paragraph 3. Representatives met in Chongqing and issued the Summary of Conversations between Government and Communist Representatives, or Double Tenth Agreement. The document stated objectives such as peaceful national reconstruction, but central questions of control over armies and local government were not fully settled. After its publication, control on the ground and armed conflict continued to evolve. Negotiations, a signed text, and implementation are three connected processes that do not happen simultaneously. Issuing an agreement must not be described as peace having already been secured.

Paragraph 4. What could be written down at the negotiating table did not necessarily match the territories controlled by each side's armies. After representatives announced the agreement, their organizations still had to communicate the commitments and decide whether to carry them out. The difficulty of sustaining postwar peace must also be examined through the sequence of, and gaps between, these practical actions.

After victory in the War of Resistance against Japan in 1945, both the Nationalist Government and the Chinese Communist Party faced questions about reorganizing the armed forces, taking over local administrations, and the country's political system. To avert a larger domestic war, they needed to write down principles acceptable to both sides while addressing who actually controlled troops on the ground. The negotiations yielded an agreement, but full civil war subsequently broke out. This illustrates the distance that may remain between formal association and the actual fulfillment of political aspirations. The Xiang commentary reads: 'Association in the outskirts: the aspiration has not been fulfilled.' This entry focuses on: The Results of Talks May Fall Short of Hopes.

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'The first nine of Great Possession does not involve harm through association.'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. During Emperor Wen's reign, the court was concerned with agriculture and the burden on common people. Farmers obtained harvests by cultivating land, while the state collected revenue through the land tax and other means. Reducing one category of levy also required the court to consider the revenue the treasury would subsequently forgo.

Paragraph 2. The Basic Annals of Emperor Wen in the Records of the Grand Historian record that, in the thirteenth year of his reign, the emperor ordered the abolition of the land tax because of his concern for agriculture and people's burdens. The measure reduced a portion of state revenue taken from agricultural production, illustrating a ruler's choice between fiscal receipts and the livelihood of the population.

Paragraph 3. The Records of the Grand Historian state that the land tax was abolished by imperial edict in Emperor Wen's thirteenth year. The edict concerned one levy on land; other taxes and corvée obligations remained, so it cannot be described as the state ceasing to collect any resources from the people. After the policy was announced, local officials had to adjust collection in accordance with the edict before residents could experience the change. The event has a specific measure and date, but whether different farming households benefited equally requires separate study.

Paragraph 4. When local officials received the tax-remission edict, the revenues formerly collected from land had to be rearranged. Farming households consequently bore less of this particular levy, but whether they still owed other services or taxes must be examined separately. The scope of a policy must not be enlarged without limit merely because the word 'exempt' appears in it.

080 Line H14 Da You Xiao He Supports the Chu–Han War from Guanzhong — Major Responsibilities Require Capacity to Bear Them▶

九二｜

080 case_id: XCASE-H14-L2 | unit_id: XIANG-U-14-03 | original_event_id: E27 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: A | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'The great wagon carries its load, for what has accumulated within does not collapse.'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. During the Chu–Han War, Liu Bang's frontline armies continually needed provisions and fresh soldiers. Guanzhong, under his control, provided conditions for transporting supplies and managing the population. If local administration stopped functioning, even short-term gains on the battlefield would be difficult to sustain.

Paragraph 2. During the struggle between Chu and Han, Xiao He remained chiefly in Guanzhong, managing population records, grain provisions, and the replenishment of soldiers so that Liu Bang's troops received continuing support. The Book of Han and other historical works describe this rear-area work as a significant condition enabling Han forces to keep fighting.

Paragraph 3. Xiao He stayed in Guanzhong, administered local affairs, and supplied personnel and grain to the front. Each time an army exhausted its resources, the rear had to mobilize and transport supplies again. The Book of Han and other historical records, in describing Han victories, also record Xiao He's administrative and logistical work. Those responsibilities are not visible in images of a major battle, yet they took place between successive engagements; assessments of military merit therefore cannot be confined to frontline commanders.

Paragraph 4. Replenishing troops involved more than writing a number on a register: personnel had to be organized locally, grain maintained, and both delivered to the front. Xiao He's administrative work was linked to Liu Bang's recurring battlefield needs, allowing Han troops to retain the manpower and materials to fight again after successive clashes.

Original Line-Specific Historical Comparison — English

Historical comparison — Xiao He Supports the Chu–Han War from Guanzhong: During the struggle between Chu and Han, Xiao He remained chiefly in Guanzhong, managing population records, grain provisions, and the replenishment of soldiers so that Liu Bang's troops received continuing support. Xiao He's organization of personnel and supplies behind the front can be compared to a great wagon carrying a load: sustained action in the field depends on institutions and provisioning capable of bearing the burden. The Xiang commentary reads: 'The great wagon carries its load, for what has accumulated within does not collapse.' This entry focuses on: Major Responsibilities Require Capacity to Bear Them.

081 Line H14 Da You Bu Shi Offers His Wealth for Frontier Defense — Private Resources Can Serve Public Responsibility▶

九三｜

081 case_id: XCASE-H14-L3 | unit_id: XIANG-U-14-04 | original_event_id: E16 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: B | publish_status: editorial_review

Replacement Candidate — English Translation

event_id: NEW-CN-PM-01403 | Event: Bu Shi Voluntarily Contributes His Wealth to Support Frontier Affairs | version_role: replacement_candidate

Bu Shi became wealthy by raising sheep. During Emperor Wu of Han's reign, repeated military campaigns against the Xiongnu increased the state's burdens. Bu Shi submitted a memorial offering to transfer half his family property to the government in support of frontier affairs. An envoy asked whether he sought official appointment; Bu Shi replied that he was not suited to official service and did not seek a post. Chancellor Gongsun Hong suspected that such conduct was unusual, and the court did not initially accept the offer. Later, as campaigns and the resettlement of migrants drained government resources, Bu Shi again gave 200,000 coins to the governor of Henan to assist impoverished migrants. When the emperor learned of this, he rewarded and commended him. This history was not a transaction in which a single donation purchased rank: it was a process in which private wealth, public affairs, and court recognition first encountered delay and only later received a response.

Replacement Line-Specific Comparison

The Xiang commentary's words, 'A duke offers a feast to the Son of Heaven; a petty person would bring harm,' emphasize a fitting relationship between resources and public duty. Bu Shi voluntarily contributed his wealth to help fund frontier affairs and later provided further assistance when official relief was insufficient. These are observable acts of devoting private resources to public purposes. Subsequent commendation by the court gives concrete form to the relationship of responsibility 'toward the Son of Heaven,' rather than leaving it entirely abstract. Bu Shi, however, was not literally a duke or prince as in the line, and the court's praise for his donations must not be treated as a reward guaranteed by the Xiang commentary.

Replacement Source and Limits

Records of the Grand Historian, 'Treatise on Fiscal Equalization' (Pingzhun shu). The main course of events is supported by the cited source; specific psychological states, exact numerical claims, and all textual variants have not been independently verified. Any imperfect correspondence remains within a grade-B limitation in the replacement review. The previous event and comparison are retained for editorial audit only and are not intended for display in the new version.

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'A duke offers a feast to the Son of Heaven; a petty person would bring harm.'

Received traditional-language explanation — English rendering: A duke or prince offers a banquet to the Son of Heaven; a petty person cannot bear such a responsibility. The Xiang commentary explains that a petty person brings harm.

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation (Archived Original)

Paragraph 1. After Emperor Taizu founded the Song dynasty, the court faced the problem of senior commanders holding too much military power. The new state's military foundations came from existing forces, and abruptly severing relations with their commanders could also disrupt the army's operations. The center therefore gradually adjusted appointments and command authority.

Paragraph 2. After establishing his government, Emperor Taizu progressively reorganized senior commanders' positions and the means by which armies were controlled, reducing the risk that generals with their own troops could set up independent power bases. Later generations often describe this as 'Relinquishing Military Command over a Cup of Wine,' but scholars differ on the banquet dialogue, its date, and the precise course of events.

Paragraph 3. Some generals left their former commands, and military authority was redistributed toward the center. Later writers called these changes 'Relinquishing Military Command over a Cup of Wine' and included conversations between sovereign and ministers in a banquet scene; the exact dialogue, timing, and historical sources remain disputed. The observable historical process was a change in offices and in methods of army control. There is no need to assume that every adjustment was settled in one evening. Once the new arrangements were established, the court still had to ensure that armies functioned under the new chain of command.

Paragraph 4. When commanders' positions changed, units still had to know which offices would issue their new orders. The court also had to arrange acceptable roles for those leaving their commands. Centralizing military authority thus involved more than reducing any individual's power; it also meant reconnecting the army's daily chain of command.

Original Line-Specific Historical Comparison — English

Historical comparison — Bu Shi Offers His Wealth for Frontier Defense: After establishing his government, Emperor Taizu progressively reorganized senior commanders' positions and the means by which armies were controlled, reducing the risk that generals with their own troops could set up independent power bases.

082 Line H14 Da You Feng Yi Is Called the General of the Great Tree — Great Achievements Need Not Be Flaunted▶

九四｜

082 case_id: XCASE-H14-L4 | unit_id: XIANG-U-14-05 | original_event_id: E15 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: A | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'Not displaying one's abundance brings no blame; this is clear discernment.'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. In the early Eastern Han, commanders accumulated military achievements through their campaigns. Each victory was connected to honors and rewards from the court, and colleagues naturally discussed who had accomplished what and where. Feng Yi himself commanded troops and carried out assignments; he was not an observer standing apart from the army.

Paragraph 2. The Book of the Later Han records that, when other commanders discussed their achievements, Feng Yi often withdrew to sit beneath a tree, giving rise to his title, 'General of the Great Tree.' The account also portrays his modesty and reluctance to compete. It describes how men whose achievements helped establish a regime related to their colleagues.

Paragraph 3. According to the Book of the Later Han, when commanders gathered to compare achievements, Feng Yi often withdrew beneath a tree, hence his title 'General of the Great Tree.' He continued to undertake military assignments; avoiding arguments about credit did not mean withdrawing from the establishment of the regime. The historian included the movement beneath the tree in his biography, so later readers remembered Feng Yi's modesty. This characterization must be read alongside his actual military achievements to understand the context of the title.

Paragraph 4. The generals who helped establish the Eastern Han commanded different regions and units; the merits they discussed could affect their later political standing. Feng Yi stepped beneath the tree during a specific gathering where others were contending over their achievements. He did not compete for verbal precedence, but he did not deny his service in battle or refuse appointments from the court.

Original Line-Specific Historical Comparison — English

Historical comparison — Feng Yi Is Called the General of the Great Tree: The Book of the Later Han records that, when other commanders discussed their achievements, Feng Yi often withdrew to sit beneath a tree, giving rise to his title, 'General of the Great Tree.' The account also portrays his modesty and reluctance to compete. Feng Yi's reluctance to compete over military credit illustrates the ability to recognize when to restrain oneself. Moderation does not deny one's contribution; it avoids turning prestige into another cause of friction. The Xiang commentary reads: 'Not displaying one's abundance brings no blame; this is clear discernment.' This entry focuses on: Great Achievements Need Not Be Flaunted.
