083 Line H14 Da You Shang Yang Establishes Trust by Moving a Wooden Pole — Credibility Gives Authority Weight▶

九五｜

083 case_id: XCASE-H14-L5 | unit_id: XIANG-U-14-06 | original_event_id: E61 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: A | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'His sincerity is shared; trust gives expression to his intentions. The auspiciousness of awe-inspiring authority comes from ease and the absence of defensiveness.'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. As Shang Yang prepared to introduce new laws in Qin, he wanted residents to know that the government's promises of reward and punishment would be carried out. Before the regulations formally took effect, he selected a small task whose outcome people could see on the spot, so fulfillment of the promise would not require a long wait to verify.

Paragraph 2. The Records of the Grand Historian relate that, before promulgating the new laws, Shang Yang placed a wooden pole at a city gate and announced a reward for anyone who moved it. When someone did so, the reward was actually paid. The story uses a small, verifiable act to show how people might be persuaded to trust official promises.

Paragraph 3. According to the Records of the Grand Historian, Shang Yang set up a pole at the gate and offered a reward for moving it. At first no one believed the offer; later someone complied, and Shang Yang paid the announced sum. Residents saw that the order and payment matched, and the new laws were then published. This is a historian's account of establishing the credibility of commands. Carrying out one promised reward did not guarantee the fairness or leniency of every subsequent law. The effects of the reforms must also be assessed through their implementation in local communities.

Paragraph 4. When someone actually moved the pole, Shang Yang paid the amount he had announced, and onlookers could directly compare words with actions. This small-scale demonstration occurred before the new laws were implemented, allowing residents first to observe one reward order being fulfilled. The formal legislation still had to prove itself over a much wider area.

Original Line-Specific Historical Comparison — English

Historical comparison — Shang Yang Establishes Trust by Moving a Wooden Pole: The Records of the Grand Historian relate that, before promulgating the new laws, Shang Yang placed a wooden pole at a city gate and announced a reward for anyone who moved it. The pole-moving episode connects the fulfillment of promises with later reforms. It invites discussion of how public trust supports authority, but it does not make every harsh penal measure of the subsequent reforms justified. The Xiang commentary reads: 'His sincerity is shared; trust gives expression to his intentions.

084 Line H14 Da You Liu Xiu Establishes the Eastern Han and Restores Governance — Explain Success through Observable Conditions▶

'The highest good fortune of Great Possession comes from Heaven's support.'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. As Wang Mang's regime collapsed, armed groups competed across different regions. Liu Xiu gradually gained support from troops and local communities, established his own political claim, and then fought forces that had not submitted. Even before the warfare had completely ended, his new government had to maintain officials' work and the people's daily lives in the territory under its control.

Paragraph 2. Following the collapse of Wang Mang's government, Liu Xiu founded the Eastern Han amid competition among rival armed groups. He gradually unified the major regions and reorganized officials, household registration, taxes, and labor obligations. Reconstructing political authority required both dealing with war and restoring ordinary administration and production.

Paragraph 3. Liu Xiu took the throne in 25 CE and later gradually unified the major regions. Once troops had subdued an area, local officials had to restore household registration, tax and labor arrangements, and agriculture to connect daily administration to the postwar order. Reviving the dynastic name 'Han' was a clear political milestone, but the time needed to restore governance varied from place to place. Years passed between the rise of competing warlords, the founding of the Eastern Han, and control over the major regions.

Paragraph 4. If population records remained inaccurate after the fighting, the court would struggle to arrange revenue collection or determine the soldiers it could mobilize. As Liu Xiu's territory expanded, officials had to extend registration and the restoration of production into recently pacified areas. Unification and administration overlapped in time; they did not suddenly arrive together in a single year.

086 Line H15 Qian Feng Yi Gives Way to Colleagues and Avoids Claiming Credit — Inner Modesty Should Be Visible in Actions▶

九二｜

086 case_id: XCASE-H15-L2 | unit_id: XIANG-U-15-03 | original_event_id: E61 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: A | publish_status: editorial_review

VERSION CONTROL: a replacement candidate is present in the Traditional Chinese V4.3.1 record. The archived former event is for audit, not the default reader display.

Replacement Candidate — English Translation

event_id: NEW-CN-PM-01502 | Event: Feng Yi Gives Way to Colleagues and Withdraws from Arguments over Credit | version_role: replacement_candidate

In the early Eastern Han, commanders serving under Liu Xiu had long been involved in military operations, and military achievements and status were highly valued. Feng Yi was known among the generals for his modest and retiring manner. Historical sources record that, when he encountered other commanders, he would often yield the road; after the troops had encamped, when the generals gathered to discuss their merits, he generally withdrew beneath a tree. The army therefore called him the 'General of the Great Tree.' His modesty did not mean that he stopped serving: he continued to carry out real military responsibilities. These actions show a manner of conduct expressed not merely in words but in his dealings with others and in occasions when people disputed credit. The historical sources principally record outward words and conduct, not a directly measurable inner state. The phrase 'found within the heart' can therefore only be a bounded retrospective interpretation.

Replacement Line-Specific Comparison

The Xiang commentary's words, 'Modesty expressed openly brings good fortune when steadfast, because it is found within the heart,' call for humility to have an inner basis that becomes visible outwardly. Feng Yi yielded the road when meeting colleagues and withdrew beneath a tree while other generals disputed credit. These observable actions illustrate how modesty may be expressed through repeated conduct rather than loud self-promotion. Historical biographies characterize those acts as modest and retiring; Feng Yi's actual inner feelings cannot be independently verified, nor can one infer that his later military achievements were thereby guaranteed.

Replacement Source and Limits

Dongguan Hanji, 'Feng Yi'; Book of the Later Han, 'Biography of Feng Yi.' The sources support the core event; particular psychological motives, numerical precision, and all textual variants have not been independently verified. An imperfect correspondence, if any, remains a bounded grade-B analogy in the replacement review. The archived event and comparison are preserved only for editorial audit, not for display in the new version.

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'Modesty expressed openly brings good fortune when steadfast, because it is found within the heart.'

Received traditional-language explanation — English rendering: When a reputation for modesty becomes known, steadfastness is auspicious. The Xiang commentary explains that the quality is grounded in the heart.

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation (Archived Original)

Paragraph 1. As Shang Yang prepared to introduce new laws in Qin, he wanted residents to know that the government's promises of reward and punishment would be carried out. Before the regulations formally took effect, he selected a small task whose outcome people could see on the spot, so fulfillment of the promise would not require a long wait to verify.

Paragraph 2. The Records of the Grand Historian relate that, before promulgating the new laws, Shang Yang placed a wooden pole at a city gate and announced a reward for anyone who moved it. When someone did so, the reward was actually paid. The story uses a small, verifiable act to show how people might be persuaded to trust official promises.

Paragraph 3. According to the Records of the Grand Historian, Shang Yang set up a pole at the gate and offered a reward for moving it. At first no one believed the offer; later someone complied, and Shang Yang paid the announced sum. Residents saw that the order and payment matched, and the new laws were then published. This is a historian's account of establishing the credibility of commands. Carrying out one promised reward did not guarantee the fairness or leniency of every subsequent law. The effects of the reforms must also be assessed through their implementation in local communities.

Paragraph 4. When someone actually moved the pole, Shang Yang paid the amount he had announced, and onlookers could directly compare words with actions. This small-scale demonstration occurred before the new laws were implemented, allowing residents first to observe one reward order being fulfilled. The formal legislation still had to prove itself over a much wider area.

Original Line-Specific Historical Comparison — English

Historical comparison — Feng Yi Gives Way to Colleagues and Avoids Claiming Credit: The Records of the Grand Historian relate that, before promulgating the new laws, Shang Yang placed a wooden pole at a city gate and announced a reward for anyone who moved it.

Archived Original — Editorial Audit Only

The original event and the original line-specific comparison are retained solely as an editorial audit trail. The proposed replacement must be reviewed for historical accuracy, suitability, and publication before it becomes a public-facing record.

Archived comparison: The Records of the Grand Historian relate that, before promulgating the new laws, Shang Yang placed a wooden pole at a city gate and announced a reward for anyone who moved it. Feng Yi's repeated practice of giving way to colleagues and avoiding disputes over credit demonstrates modesty through observable behavior rather than through self-advertisement. Yet the actual state of his mind cannot be established from the external record alone. The Xiang commentary reads: 'Modesty expressed openly brings good fortune when steadfast, because it is found within the heart.'

'The hardworking and modest noble person earns the allegiance of the people.'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. During the Chu–Han War, Liu Bang's frontline armies continually needed provisions and fresh soldiers. Guanzhong, under his control, provided conditions for transporting supplies and managing the population. If local administration stopped functioning, even short-term gains on the battlefield would be difficult to sustain.

Paragraph 2. During the struggle between Chu and Han, Xiao He remained chiefly in Guanzhong, managing population records, grain provisions, and the replenishment of soldiers so that Liu Bang's troops received continuing support. The Book of Han and other historical works describe this rear-area work as a significant condition enabling Han forces to keep fighting.

Paragraph 3. Xiao He stayed in Guanzhong, administered local affairs, and supplied personnel and grain to the front. Each time an army exhausted its resources, the rear had to mobilize and transport supplies again. The Book of Han and other historical records, in describing Han victories, also record Xiao He's administrative and logistical work. Those responsibilities are not visible in images of a major battle, yet they took place between successive engagements; assessments of military merit therefore cannot be confined to frontline commanders.

Paragraph 4. Replenishing troops involved more than writing a number on a register: personnel had to be organized locally, grain maintained, and both delivered to the front. Xiao He's administrative work was linked to Liu Bang's recurring battlefield needs, allowing Han troops to retain the manpower and materials to fight again after successive clashes.

Paragraph 4. Remonstrance officials could not themselves appoint or dismiss officials in place of the emperor. They could submit arguments and continue debate at court. Zhang Yaozuo's appointments must also be distinguished by office and date; the controversy cannot be compressed into a simple claim that a relative of the palace was 'guilty.' What Bao Zheng left was a formal objection to a personnel decision.

Results in battle also depended on terrain, supplies, and the opponent; they cannot all be credited to one formation with a memorable name.

If recruits had not practiced in peacetime, their first attempt at coordination upon meeting an enemy could lead to weapons of different lengths and unit positions obstructing one another. Zhou Yafu's choice prevented Liang from receiving comprehensive relief at once, and its court resented this; Han troops meanwhile had to hold their own ground so that the enemy could not easily turn on them. 091 Line H16 Yu Yuan Shikai’s Imperial Bid Provokes the National Protection Movement — Applause Can Conceal a Crisis▶

'Joy proclaimed at the beginning: an exhausted aspiration brings misfortune.'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. After the republic was established, Yuan Shikai occupied a leading position in the central government while maintaining complex relationships with local political forces. In 1915 he moved to establish an imperial system, directly altering the republican designation and the associated distribution of powers. The voices of his supporters could not guarantee that armies, provincial officials, or political parties would accept the new regime.

Paragraph 2. In 1915 Yuan Shikai pursued a return to monarchy, provoking political resistance and the National Protection War. Some forces that had formerly supported him ceased to cooperate, and the monarchy was cancelled in 1916. Concentrating power had not automatically produced durable political support.

Paragraph 3. Opponents launched the National Protection movement, and political protests increasingly accompanied armed conflict. Some provincial forces that had earlier cooperated with Yuan were no longer willing to do so, testing the center's control over the provinces. Yuan cancelled the imperial system in 1916, but the underlying power conflicts did not disappear that same day. The stages from preparations for emperorship, public resistance, and cancellation involved successive changes in political backing and pressure from the battlefield.

Paragraph 4. When supporters proposed the change, local officials still had to decide where they stood between the existing republic and the proposed monarchy. Responses from different provinces reached the central government at different times, and Yuan's orders could not necessarily be implemented as he had expected. After the National Protection War broke out, political opposition also translated directly into troop movements.

In 1926, the Northern Expeditionary Army advanced toward Wuchang, while the defenders still controlled the city and its surrounding lines. The attackers wanted to take this Yangtze city, but the first assault failed. They subsequently had to maintain a siege and supplies outside the walls. The Northern Expedition depended on political mobilization and military organization. Its advance may illustrate momentum once forces have been assembled, but morale alone was not sufficient for success. The Xiang commentary reads: 'Taking the lead in enthusiasm brings great gains, for the aspiration is carried out on a large scale.' This entry focuses on: Shared Momentum Can Move Collective Action Forward.

095 Line H16 Yu Late-Qing Constitutional Preparations Face a Crisis of Credibility — Keeping a System Alive Does Not Resolve Its Problems▶

九五｜

095 case_id: XCASE-H16-L5 | unit_id: XIANG-U-16-06 | original_event_id: E53 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: B | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'The enduring illness of the fifth six comes from riding the strong. Its persistence without death means that the center has not yet perished.'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. In 1906, the Qing court announced preparations for constitutional government to respond to calls for political reform. Supporters of reform hoped that political authority would gradually open up, while the imperial house still wished to preserve its leading role in government. They had different expectations about the preparatory timetable and what the new institutions would actually be empowered to do.

Paragraph 2. The Qing court announced preparations for constitutionalism, later set out annual preparatory tasks, and established new advisory and political-consultative institutions. Yet the reform timetable, retention of imperial authority, and the personnel composition of the 1911 cabinet disappointed supporters. Confidence among constitutional reformers in the court was damaged.

Paragraph 3. The court subsequently published preparatory measures and established institutions including provincial advisory councils and the National Assembly. As these bodies began operating, the retention of imperial power, the speed of reform, and the appointments to the cabinet in 1911 generated disappointment. Some who had originally hoped for constitutional government no longer believed the court was willing to surrender corresponding powers, while revolutionary activity and provincial political change intensified. Several years separated announcement, institutional creation, and the loss of confidence; the Qing collapse cannot be attributed solely to one cabinet appointment.

Paragraph 4. The establishment of the provincial advisory councils and the National Assembly enabled advocates of constitutionalism to operate within the new institutions; they continued to examine whether the imperial house would yield more important powers. When the 1911 cabinet appointments were announced, they could directly compare the current arrangements with earlier promises. Their disappointment did not arise overnight.

Original Line-Specific Historical Comparison — English

The Qing court's constitutional preparations amid internal and external pressures show a system still existing while its crisis remained unresolved. 096 Line H16 Yu Late-Tianbao Prosperity Gives Way to the An Lushan Rebellion — Complacent Enjoyment Cannot Last Indefinitely▶

上九｜

096 case_id: XCASE-H16-L6 | unit_id: XIANG-U-16-07 | original_event_id: E55 | original_evidence_type: B (retrospective analogy) | recorded_grade: A | publish_status: editorial_review

Xiang Commentary — English Rendering

'Darkened enthusiasm reaches the top: how could it last long?'

Historical Event — Complete Four-Paragraph Translation

Paragraph 1. During Emperor Xuanzong's reign, the Tang court had experienced prosperity and held extensive territory, while the military strength of commanders in frontier garrisons also increased. An Lushan controlled frontier troops, and political tensions between center and provinces grew more difficult to manage as power became concentrated.

Paragraph 2. The Xuanzong reign saw prosperity and expansion, but problems involving frontier military power and central politics continued to accumulate. In 755, An Lushan raised a rebellion and shattered the court's control of the situation. The war had long-lasting effects on population, finances, and provincial authority.

Paragraph 3. In 755 An Lushan rebelled, disrupting the established Tang order, and Emperor Xuanzong left Chang'an. The fighting continued for years, affecting population movements, fiscal receipts, and local military-political power. The uprising has a date, but relations between frontier commands and the center had deteriorated over a much longer period. An account limited to palace anecdotes would fail to show why the lengthy war changed the ways in which Tang China was governed.

Paragraph 4. Provincial military governors held troops and local resources; the court's prosperity did not automatically assure its control over frontier commands. After An Lushan rebelled, armies advanced along their routes and the court made decisions about defense and flight. Prolonged warfare increased the extent to which local authorities handled finances and military affairs for themselves; the effects did not end in 755.

Original Line-Specific Historical Comparison — English

Historical comparison — Late-Tianbao Prosperity Gives Way to the An Lushan Rebellion: The Xuanzong reign saw prosperity and expansion, but problems involving frontier military power and central politics continued to accumulate. The profound change surrounding the An Lushan Rebellion invites reflection on whether a prosperous-age mentality impeded recognition of risk. The Tang crisis had institutional causes and must not be attributed solely to indulgence. The Xiang commentary reads: 'Darkened enthusiasm reaches the top: how could it last long?' This entry focuses on: Complacent Enjoyment Cannot Last Indefinitely.

Editorial Assessment and Limits

The inherited case record is graded A for interpretive suitability. The historical event remains a later analogy to the Xiang commentary. The original evidence marking B denotes retrospective comparison, not a direct historical quotation of this line by the participants.

097 Line H17 Sui Sun Quan Encourages Lü Meng to Study — Update Your Abilities as Your Responsibilities Change▶

初九｜

097 case_id: XCASE-H17-L1 | event_id: E04 | grade: A | unit_id: XIANG-U-17-02 | publish_status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — translated paragraphs

Paragraph 1. When Sun Quan governed Jiangdong, Lü Meng was already serving as a military officer, but battlefield experience could not replace knowledge of earlier political and military events. Lü Meng cited the pressure of military duties; Sun Quan nevertheless urged him to study historical accounts while continuing his work. The advice was meant to broaden a commander’s resources for judgment, not to make him resign his commission and specialize in classical scholarship.

Paragraph 2. According to the Jiangbiao Zhuan, quoted by Pei Songzhi in his annotations to the Records of the Three Kingdoms, Sun Quan encouraged Lü Meng to read in order to understand history and practical experience, not to become a scholar devoted exclusively to the classics. After Lü Meng followed this advice, his knowledge grew, and Lu Su’s assessment of him also changed.

Paragraph 3. Lü Meng began to read and later discussed affairs of state with Lu Su. Lu Su discovered that he could now address questions formerly unfamiliar to him and revised his opinion. This account survives in material quoted in the annotations to the Records of the Three Kingdoms; the polished dialogues commonly presented in classrooms underwent subsequent retelling. What the historical account permits us to identify is encouragement to learn, acceptance of advice, and a change in a colleague’s judgment. Their meeting did not guarantee the outcome of every campaign Lü Meng would later undertake.

Paragraph 4. Sun Quan did not transfer Lü Meng’s military post to someone else: he wanted him to gain useful experience through reading while continuing his existing responsibilities. Lu Su’s later reaction came in conversation, not as the result of a single formal examination. Historical judgments concerning a figure’s growth coexist with the concrete military responsibilities that the person continued to shoulder.

Xiang explanation — English

A change in office is auspicious when it follows what is right; productive dealings outside one’s circle are not a loss.

Line-specific historical comparison — expanded English

Lü Meng cited the pressure of military duties; Sun Quan nevertheless urged him to study historical accounts while continuing his work. The advice was meant to broaden a commander’s resources for judgment, not to make him resign his commission and specialize in classical scholarship.

Lü Meng accepted Sun Quan’s invitation to study while retaining his military responsibilities; his interactions with Lu Su offer a concrete parallel to correcting one’s course and learning through contact.

098 Line H17 Sui The Qing Court’s Disastrous Foreign-War Decisions in 1900 — Choosing Whom to Rely On Has a Cost▶

098 case_id: XCASE-H17-L2 | event_id: E62 | grade: B | unit_id: XIANG-U-17-03 | publish_status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — translated paragraphs

Paragraph 1. In 1900, Boxer activity, foreign intervention, and decision-making within the Qing court became entangled, while the diplomatic and military situation in Beijing deteriorated rapidly. The court’s approach to foreign troops and regional officials’ judgments about the security of their own jurisdictions had already begun to diverge.

Paragraph 2. After the Boxer movement and foreign military intervention intensified, the Qing court issued an edict declaring war on foreign powers, further widening the crisis. Allied troops entered Beijing, the court fled, and the Boxer Protocol was signed the following year. Some regional officials pursued the Mutual Protection of Southeast China, also showing that central and regional authorities did not share the same judgment.

Paragraph 3. The Qing government issued its declaration of war; hostilities spread, allied forces entered Beijing, and the court fled. Some officials in the southeast pursued mutual-protection arrangements, revealing that different regions did not respond uniformly. The Boxer Protocol was signed the next year, imposing serious consequences on the court and population. Any discussion of mistakes made by the central government must also explicitly acknowledge the armed incursion by foreign powers. The transition from local movements to international war resulted from more than one person’s decision.

Paragraph 4. After the war edict, not all officials across the empire responded in the same way: the southeastern mutual-protection arrangements highlight the difference between central and regional choices. The allied occupation of Beijing and treaty indemnities transformed a crisis in political judgment into military and fiscal consequences. Different actors made decisions and bore costs at each stage.

Xiang explanation — English

Binding oneself to the immature means one cannot at the same time associate with the more mature.

099 Line H17 Sui The Sun–Liu Alliance against Cao Cao — Choose Partners Who Can Share the Burden▶

九三｜

099 case_id: XCASE-H17-L3 | event_id: E13 | grade: B | unit_id: XIANG-U-17-04 | publish_status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — translated paragraphs

Paragraph 1. Cao Cao's southward advance rapidly changed the situation in Jingzhou, and Liu Bei and Sun Quan each faced a threat from the northern forces. Liu Bei needed new military support, while Sun Quan had to decide how to defend the Yangtze. Each side already held its own territory and had its own deployments, so contact and coordination had to precede any alliance.

Paragraph 2. Following Cao Cao's southward advance, Sun Quan and Liu Bei faced shared military pressure and established cooperation through negotiations involving Lu Su, Zhuge Liang, and others. Allied forces resisted Cao's army at Red Cliffs, but after the battle each side continued to consider its own territory and interests. The alliance was not free from friction thereafter.

Paragraph 3. Lu Su, Zhuge Liang, and others took part in talks that brought about cooperation between Sun Quan and Liu Bei. Their allied forces fought Cao's troops around Red Cliffs and obtained military gains, after which each side still had to administer its territory and army. Sharing an objective in wartime did not mean that postwar territorial arrangements had already been settled. The relationship passed through military pressure, exchanges of envoys, joint operations, and further negotiations after the battle; 'a successful alliance' alone does not describe all that followed.

Paragraph 4. Before the coalition formed, envoys had to establish whether both parties would jointly resist Cao's army. Afterward, the two sides had to coordinate while retaining their separate forces. The end of the Battle of Red Cliffs did not mean their goals were entirely identical. The later dispute over Jingzhou arose within a relationship whose participants had once fought together.

Xiang explanation — English

Binding oneself to the mature expresses the intention to leave what is inferior behind.

100 Line H17 Sui Early Song Reforms of Military Command — Manage Misgivings as Your Influence Grows▶

九四｜

100 case_id: XCASE-H17-L4 | event_id: E16 | grade: A | unit_id: XIANG-U-17-05 | publish_status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — translated paragraphs

Paragraph 1. After Emperor Taizu founded the Song dynasty, the court faced the problem of senior commanders holding too much military power. The new state's military foundations came from existing forces, and abruptly severing relations with their commanders could also disrupt the army's operations. The center therefore gradually adjusted appointments and command authority.

Paragraph 2. After establishing his government, Emperor Taizu progressively reorganized senior commanders' positions and the means by which armies were controlled, reducing the risk that generals with their own troops could set up independent power bases. Later generations often describe this as 'Relinquishing Military Command over a Cup of Wine,' but scholars differ on the banquet dialogue, its date, and the precise course of events.

Paragraph 3. Some generals left their former commands, and military authority was redistributed toward the center. Later writers called these changes 'Relinquishing Military Command over a Cup of Wine' and included conversations between sovereign and ministers in a banquet scene; the exact dialogue, timing, and historical sources remain disputed. The observable historical process was a change in offices and in methods of army control. There is no need to assume that every adjustment was settled in one evening. Once the new arrangements were established, the court still had to ensure that armies functioned under the new chain of command.

Paragraph 4. When commanders' positions changed, units still had to know which offices would issue their new orders. The court also had to arrange acceptable roles for those leaving their commands. Centralizing military authority thus involved more than reducing any individual's power; it also meant reconnecting the army's daily chain of command.

Xiang explanation — English

Although following brings gains, pursuing gain contrary to what is right is perilous; sincere conduct on the right path makes achievement clear.

The redistribution of command under the early Song can be compared with the risks of expanding power and the need to dispel doubts through legitimate institutional arrangements.

101 Line H17 Sui Shang Yang Builds Trust by Moving a Wooden Pole — Build Trust through Actions Others Can Verify▶

九五｜

101 case_id: XCASE-H17-L5 | event_id: E61 | grade: A | unit_id: XIANG-U-17-06 | publish_status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — translated paragraphs

Paragraph 1. As Shang Yang prepared to introduce new laws in Qin, he wanted residents to know that the government's promises of reward and punishment would be carried out. Before the regulations formally took effect, he selected a small task whose outcome people could see on the spot, so fulfillment of the promise would not require a long wait to verify.

Paragraph 2. The Records of the Grand Historian relate that, before promulgating the new laws, Shang Yang placed a wooden pole at a city gate and announced a reward for anyone who moved it. When someone did so, the reward was actually paid. The story uses a small, verifiable act to show how people might be persuaded to trust official promises.

Paragraph 3. According to the Records of the Grand Historian, Shang Yang set up a pole at the gate and offered a reward for moving it. At first no one believed the offer; later someone complied, and Shang Yang paid the announced sum. Residents saw that the order and payment matched, and the new laws were then published. This is a historian's account of establishing the credibility of commands. Carrying out one promised reward did not guarantee the fairness or leniency of every subsequent law. The effects of the reforms must also be assessed through their implementation in local communities.

Paragraph 4. When someone actually moved the pole, Shang Yang paid the amount he had announced, and onlookers could directly compare words with actions. This small-scale demonstration occurred before the new laws were implemented, allowing residents first to observe one reward order being fulfilled. The formal legislation still had to prove itself over a much wider area.

Xiang explanation — English

Trust placed in what is admirable is favorable because the position is central and correct.

102 Line H17 Sui The Jingnan Campaign Turns a Royal Power Struggle into Civil War — Overly Binding Relationships Can Become a Trap▶

上九｜

102 case_id: XCASE-H17-L6 | event_id: E37 | grade: B | unit_id: XIANG-U-17-07 | publish_status: editorial_review

Paragraph 1. After the Jianwen Emperor took the throne, the court sought to adjust the powers of imperial princes in different regions. Zhu Di, Prince of Yan, commanded forces in the north, and the reduction of princely fiefs affected whether he could retain his former military and political position. Such accounts must be checked separately against specific dates and actions.

Paragraph 4. The measures to reduce princely fiefs initially concerned the central government's adjustment of princes' authority, but after Zhu Di raised troops, large armies and local communities bore the consequences. When Nanjing was taken, the Jianwen regime lost control and the new monarch began organizing the court. Several years of actual warfare separated that outcome from the original dispute over the princes' fiefs.

103 Line H18 Gu Sima Guang Quotes the Xiang Commentary on Gu to Argue for Revising the New Policies — Correcting Earlier Policies Can Honor Their Original Intent▶

初九｜

103 case_id: XCASE-H18-L1 | event_id: E65 | grade: A | unit_id: XIANG-U-18-02 | publish_status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — translated paragraphs

Paragraph 1. After Emperor Shenzong of Song died, his successor Zhezong was still a child, and the court argued fiercely over whether Wang Anshi’s New Policies should continue. Sima Guang believed that certain measures harmed the people and the state. He submitted a memorial to the Grand Empress Dowager and Emperor Zhezong in an effort to change the direction of policy.

Paragraph 2. After Shenzong’s death, Sima Guang submitted the memorial entitled “Request to Remove Those New Policies That Harm the People and Injure the State” to the Grand Empress Dowager and Zhezong. Opposing the preservation of harmful measures simply because they were inherited from a father’s reign, he cited the Xiang Commentary on the first six and fourth six of Hexagram Gu in turn and argued that the benefits and harms of the New Policies must be distinguished. This was an argument made in a policy memorial; neither the merits and defects of the reforms nor the consequences of subsequently repealing them can be settled solely on the basis of his position.

Paragraph 3. In that memorial, Sima Guang cited the Xiang Commentary on the first six and fourth six of Gu in succession, opposing the retention of institutions merely because they had been introduced in the preceding reign. He wanted the court to distinguish among particular measures on the basis of their actual benefits and harms, and to abolish those he considered damaging. These are direct quotations traceable to the memorial and show how the Xiang Commentary entered a policy debate. The effects of the New Policies still require examination of other sources and of their local implementation.

Paragraph 4. The memorial preserves explicit quotations from the Xiang Commentary, enabling readers to trace how Sima Guang brought the expressions “repairing the father’s disorder” and “indulging the father’s disorder” into the controversy over changing the laws. Addressing the Grand Empress Dowager and Emperor Zhezong was a political attempt to alter court decisions. Quoting a classic, however, does not by itself prove that Sima Guang was correct in every criticism he made of the New Policies.

Xiang explanation — English

Paragraph 3. Liu Bang assembled the elders and publicly stated the simplified laws; his troops then had to act in accordance with those promises. Xiang Yu and other armed forces were still on the move, and conditions outside Guanzhong remained unsettled. The advance, promulgation of the rules, and continued contest with rival lords were successive, interconnected stages; the entry into Guanzhong should not be mistaken for the end of the struggle for the realm.

Paragraph 4. When the people of Guanzhong first heard these rules, they still faced soldiers bearing weapons. 136 Line H23 Bo The Tumu Crisis Reveals Operational Vulnerabilities — Do Not Treat an Approaching Danger as Distant▶

九四｜

Beijing’s defense had to begin while the emperor was still a prisoner.

Paragraph 4. The capture of the emperor immediately had consequences beyond an ordinary military retreat. Officials had to decide how the court would continue to exercise authority, and troops defending the city needed to know whose orders to follow. The capital’s emergency defense was organized with incomplete information from the front. Information carried from the Tumu battlefield to the capital tightly linked the military disaster to political decisions in Beijing.

In 1449 the Ming emperor Yingzong accompanied an expedition against the Oirats; the army suffered a serious defeat near Tumu on its return and the emperor was captured. Once implemented, however, disputes arose over interest, debt collection, and local officials compelling farmers to take loans. Paragraph 3. After the regulations took effect, local officials decided how loans were issued and collected. In some places, compulsory lending, interest charges, and repayment pressures prompted prolonged debate both inside and outside the court. The assistance the policy’s architects hoped to offer differed from what individual farmers actually experienced. From policy formulation to government lending and local recovery of principal and interest, each stage had its own implementers; the name of a law alone cannot tell us what happened in every locality.

Paragraph 4. If local officials pushed farmers to borrow merely to meet lending quotas, a measure intended to ease shortages of working capital could become a new burden. Borrowers also faced deadlines for repayment of principal and interest. These divergent experiences entered court debate, making it necessary to discuss policy objectives separately from the results of implementation.

Wang Anshi’s Green Sprouts Loans, their implementation, and the ensuing controversies invite scrutiny of successive policy adjustments. What Bao Zheng left was a formal objection to a personnel decision.

145 Line H25 Wu Wang Shang Yang Establishes Trust by Moving a Wooden Pole — Make Promises Consistent with Actions▶

初九｜

145 case_id: XCASE-H25-L1 | unit_id: XIANG-U-25-02 | original_event_id: E61 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

As Shang Yang prepared to introduce new laws in Qin, he wanted residents to know that the government's promises of reward and punishment would be carried out. Before the regulations formally took effect, he selected a small task whose outcome people could see on the spot, so fulfillment of the promise would not require a long wait to verify.

The Records of the Grand Historian relate that, before promulgating the new laws, Shang Yang placed a wooden pole at a city gate and announced a reward for anyone who moved it. When someone did so, the reward was actually paid. The story uses a small, verifiable act to show how people might be persuaded to trust official promises.

According to the Records of the Grand Historian, Shang Yang set up a pole at the gate and offered a reward for moving it. At first no one believed the offer; later someone complied, and Shang Yang paid the announced sum. Residents saw that the order and payment matched, and the new laws were then published. This is a historian's account of establishing the credibility of commands. Carrying out one promised reward did not guarantee the fairness or leniency of every subsequent law. The effects of the reforms must also be assessed through their implementation in local communities.

When someone actually moved the pole, Shang Yang paid the amount he had announced, and onlookers could directly compare words with actions. This small-scale demonstration occurred before the new laws were implemented, allowing residents first to observe one reward order being fulfilled. The formal legislation still had to prove itself over a much wider area.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Shang Yang’s publicly verified reward, as described in the Records of the Grand Historian, illustrates how a concrete and observable act can make official promises credible. This retrospectively parallels acting without false pretenses; it does not establish that all of Shang Yang’s policies lacked self-interest. The Xiang connects proceeding without falsity with the fulfillment of an aim.

Suitability review and revisions

146 Line H25 Wu Wang Emperor Wen of Han Remits the Land Tax — Policy Need Not Pursue Immediate Revenue Alone▶

九二｜

146 case_id: XCASE-H25-L2 | unit_id: XIANG-U-25-03 | original_event_id: E41 | grade: B | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

During Emperor Wen's reign, the court was concerned with agriculture and the burden on common people. Farmers obtained harvests by cultivating land, while the state collected revenue through the land tax and other means. Reducing one category of levy also required the court to consider the revenue the treasury would subsequently forgo.

The Basic Annals of Emperor Wen in the Records of the Grand Historian record that, in the thirteenth year of his reign, the emperor ordered the abolition of the land tax because of his concern for agriculture and people's burdens. The measure reduced a portion of state revenue taken from agricultural production, illustrating a ruler's choice between fiscal receipts and the livelihood of the population.

The Records of the Grand Historian state that the land tax was abolished by imperial edict in Emperor Wen's thirteenth year. The edict concerned one levy on land; other taxes and corvée obligations remained, so it cannot be described as the state ceasing to collect any resources from the people. After the policy was announced, local officials had to adjust collection in accordance with the edict before residents could experience the change. The event has a specific measure and date, but whether different farming households benefited equally requires separate study.

When local officials received the tax-remission edict, the revenues formerly collected from land had to be rearranged. Farming households consequently bore less of this particular levy, but whether they still owed other services or taxes must be examined separately. The scope of a policy must not be enlarged without limit merely because the word 'exempt' appears in it.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Emperor Wen’s remission of land tax, recorded in the Records of the Grand Historian, illustrates a choice between fiscal receipts and farmers’ burdens. The parallel concerns governing without treating immediate state revenue as the only objective. It does not dispense with fiscal planning, nor does the line encourage rewards without effort. The Xiang warns that “not ploughing yet harvesting” is not a guarantee of wealth.

Suitability review and revisions

Grade B — Partial suitability. The source retains the same historical event. The revised comparison illustrates one important aspect of the line but does not establish that the event encompasses the entire line text or all images of the Xiang Commentary. There is no evidence that the historical participant acted according to this line. Revisions are restricted to the comparison, interpretation limits, and necessary wording; no speeches, causation, or dates may be invented. One re-review retains Grade B, without repetitive further revisions.

Case-specific limitation: The lines “not ploughing yet harvesting; not clearing yet gaining cultivated land” do not praise idleness. Their point is to carry out one’s responsibility without taking private gain as the premise.

147 Line H25 Wu Wang Heavy Red Army Losses at the Xiang River — Losses in a Grand Campaign Fall on Individuals▶

九三｜

147 case_id: XCASE-H25-L3 | unit_id: XIANG-U-25-04 | original_event_id: E29 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

At the beginning of the Long March, the Central Red Army moved toward the Xiang River while facing blocking forces ahead and pursuit from behind. Crossing required different units to pass in sequence and demanded arrangements for supplies and noncombatants accompanying the march. The river itself was a physical obstacle the operation had to overcome.

During the Long March, blocking forces confronted the Central Red Army around the Xiang River, and the crossing caused major losses in personnel and organizational strength. Studies discuss the burden of the march, the route, and command decisions; they also caution that casualty or attrition figures based on different methods cannot simply be treated as equivalent.

The Xiang River fighting exacted severe casualties and organizational losses. Some of those who crossed continued the march, while the forces gradually reassessed earlier marching and command arrangements. Different sources use different starting and ending points and count different groups; all losses in the early Long March cannot be attributed to this single engagement. The battle involved actual river crossings and human costs, which should not be turned into an elegant abstraction.

The army had not only to cross the river but also to preserve passages for the units following behind; some formations paid a grave price to cover others. Continuing the march after the crossing did not erase the preceding deaths and injuries. Estimates using different methods should be retained together with their scope and sources.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The major losses at the Xiang River show how strategic decisions and fighting impose dangers on individuals who did not choose them. Casualty totals reported under different definitions must not be mixed. The Xiang image of one person obtaining an ox while another suffers should not be used to assign battle responsibility mechanically.

148 Line H25 Wu Wang Emperor Wen Respects the Rules at the Xiliu Camp — Preserve Rules That Have Proved Reliable▶

148 case_id: XCASE-H25-L4 | unit_id: XIANG-U-25-05 | original_event_id: E19 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Facing military pressure from the north, Emperor Wen of Han visited army camps to inspect their defenses. Zhou Yafu commanded the camp at Xiliu, where passage through the gate was governed by military rules. Even when the emperor’s carriage arrived, the guards had to verify an order rather than open the gate at will. Thus the visiting emperor first encountered procedures in force on the ground.

The Records of the Grand Historian recounts that when Emperor Wen inspected Zhou Yafu’s Xiliu camp, he could not enter directly as he had at other camps, but had to follow the camp’s notification procedures. After entering, his carriage also observed the rule against traveling quickly. The emperor consequently acknowledged Zhou Yafu’s ability to command troops.

After notice was given, the carriage entered Xiliu and proceeded slowly as the military orders required. Zhou Yafu received the emperor with military courtesies, and after leaving Emperor Wen praised the army’s discipline. The Records of the Grand Historian sets out the sequence of the gate, notification, speed of the carriage, and meeting, as well as the emperor’s assessment in comparison with other camps. The evidence shows how this particular inspection took place; it does not establish that he acted identically in every other circumstance.

The gate guards’ verification of arrivals, the carriage’s speed inside the camp, and Zhou Yafu’s reception of the emperor were details observed in succession during this visit. If only Emperor Wen’s final words of praise are retained, the different procedures he encountered at Xiliu before speaking those words become invisible.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

At Xiliu, Emperor Wen had to follow camp-entry procedures even as emperor, illustrating a disciplined institution whose rules did not change arbitrarily under outside pressure. The analogy concerns maintaining legitimate established principles, not obeying every rule regardless of justice.

149 Line H25 Wu Wang King Zhao of Chu Refuses a Sacrifice to the Yellow River — Do Not Apply Irrelevant Remedies▶

九五｜

149 case_id: XCASE-H25-L5 | unit_id: XIANG-U-25-06 | original_event_id: E25 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

King Zhao of Chu fell ill, and those around him searched for a cause and a remedy. A diviner attributed the illness to a river deity, prompting ministers to suggest making a sacrifice to the Yellow River. Following that proposal would have extended the ruler’s state sacrifices beyond the mountains and rivers customarily under Chu’s ritual responsibility.

According to the sixth year of Duke Ai in the Zuo Commentary, a diviner linked King Zhao’s illness to the river deity and ministers proposed a sacrifice. The king rejected it because the Yellow River lay outside the region for which Chu was responsible for performing sacrifices. His reply shows how he defined the scope of a ruler’s ritual duties.

The Zuo Commentary records that the king did not accept the proposed sacrifice. His reason was that the Yellow River did not belong to the places where Chu should perform its state rites; a ruler should observe the appropriate boundaries of his own rituals. The account preserves the divination, the ministers’ suggestion, and his reply but offers no medical evidence establishing the cause of the illness. It contains divination but no explicit citation of the Zhouyi; rejecting this sacrifice has no direct bearing on whether a person today should accept medical treatment.

The king gave his answer when ministers proposed the sacrifice in his presence. His reasoning relied not on a physician’s diagnosis but on Chu’s understanding of its ritual jurisdiction. The narrative never establishes whether the river deity had anything to do with the illness. What can be checked is that the proposal was made and the ruler explained his refusal.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

King Zhao of Chu rejected the proposed sacrifice because the Yellow River lay outside Chu’s ritual jurisdiction. The analogy is to checking whether a proposed remedy is actually relevant to the problem. Neither the divination nor the story provides medical treatment advice. The Xiang cautions against trying an unwarranted “medicine.”

Fu Jian of Former Qin controlled extensive territories in northern China and prepared a major invasion of Eastern Jin. His wide domain enabled him to mobilize armies, but forces drawn from different backgrounds still had to act in concert during a distant campaign. Eastern Jin, meanwhile, confronted severe pressure from the north in the Jiang–Huai region.

Fu Jian launched his great southern campaign against Eastern Jin but was routed by Jin counterattacks around the Fei River. Former Qin’s apparent superiority in numbers did not automatically provide stable organization or command. Divisions within the territories under its control became increasingly evident after the defeat.

In 383 the armies fought near the Fei River, where Former Qin’s forces collapsed under counterattack. Fu Jian failed to complete the invasion, and different groups previously held together by his regime reassessed their positions, followed by successive divisions. Ancient histories contain dramatic battlefield descriptions, and troop numbers cannot always be verified precisely. The essential sequence is large-scale mobilization, defeat at the Fei River, and diminishing Former Qin control.

Before the march south, Former Qin had to supply its expedition with grain and orders; once defeated, it had to preserve withdrawal routes for troops of differing origins. The collapse at the Fei River quickly affected the political structure of its empire. Forces that had previously accepted Fu Jian’s command began making different choices as the military situation changed.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Fu Jian’s defeat at the Fei River shows the danger of believing that the mere decision to advance can overcome structural and strategic constraints. Confidence did not erase difficulties of coordination. The analogy is limited: a poor result alone does not prove a decision had been irrational, and the Xiang was not cited by the actors.

151 Line H26 Da Xu Zhou Yafu Waits for the Right Moment during the Rebellion of the Seven States — Stop When Danger First Becomes Clear▶

初九｜

151 case_id: XCASE-H26-L1 | unit_id: XIANG-U-26-02 | original_event_id: E05 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

In 154 BCE, seven kingdoms raised forces against the Han, and the armies of Wu and Chu advanced, leaving the kingdom of Liang in urgent need of relief. The court sent Zhou Yafu to command its army. He had to weigh both Liang’s immediate peril and the supply situation of the principal rebel army. If the Han army reacted immediately to every enemy movement, it might be forced to fight under conditions chosen by its opponent.

After the rebellion began, Zhou Yafu did not constantly seek a direct, decisive engagement. He held his position and sent troops to cut the Wu–Chu army’s supply lines. He waited until the enemy encountered difficulties obtaining provisions and then exploited the moment of its retreat. Liang meanwhile endured pressure, making this deployment politically contentious.

Zhou Yafu maintained his own positions while dispatching other forces to interrupt the Wu–Chu supply routes. The danger facing Liang did not disappear, and Zhou was criticized politically for failing to come to its immediate rescue. Only after the enemy’s provisions were disrupted and its offensive became unsustainable did he strike during its withdrawal. Both the victory over the rebels and the risks borne by Liang belong to the outcome. This campaign illustrates how interference with supplies in the rear could alter conditions on the battlefield.

Zhou Yafu’s decision meant that Liang could not immediately receive comprehensive support, much to the displeasure of the Liang court. At the same time, the Han army still had to defend its own positions and prevent the enemy from readily redirecting its attack. Cutting supply lines was not passive observation: it was intended to make the offensive previously sustainable for the Wu–Chu forces progressively harder to maintain.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Zhou Yafu cut his opponents’ supply route and waited instead of immediately accepting a pitched battle. Such a pause can serve the larger mission rather than abandon it; it avoids engaging under the enemy’s preferred conditions. The Xiang image is one of stopping before danger becomes worse.

At Yiwu, Qi Jiguang stressed selection, discipline, and coordinated action. In campaigns against coastal raiders he employed formations and weapons designed to support one another. His military-training writings repeatedly stressed turning instruction into actions and standards that troops could actually carry out.

After being assigned to their units, the men practiced coordinating different weapons, positions, and movements. These arrangements were applied in campaigns against coastal raiders, and Qi also recorded training rules in his works. When the people of Guanzhong first heard these rules, they still faced soldiers bearing weapons. The subsequent contest among different forces for control of Guanzhong also kept this administrative experiment within an unstable political environment.

155 Line H26 Da Xu The Early Song Court Reorganizes Military Command — Reduce Risk by Addressing Its Source of Power▶

After Emperor Taizu founded the Song dynasty, the court faced the problem of senior commanders holding too much military power. The new state's military foundations came from existing forces, and abruptly severing relations with their commanders could also disrupt the army's operations. The center therefore gradually adjusted appointments and command authority.

After establishing his government, Emperor Taizu progressively reorganized senior commanders' positions and the means by which armies were controlled, reducing the risk that generals with their own troops could set up independent power bases. Later generations often describe this as 'Relinquishing Military Command over a Cup of Wine,' but scholars differ on the banquet dialogue, its date, and the precise course of events.

Some generals left their former commands, and military authority was redistributed toward the center. Later writers called these changes 'Relinquishing Military Command over a Cup of Wine' and included conversations between sovereign and ministers in a banquet scene; the exact dialogue, timing, and historical sources remain disputed. The observable historical process was a change in offices and in methods of army control. There is no need to assume that every adjustment was settled in one evening. Once the new arrangements were established, the court still had to ensure that armies functioned under the new chain of command.

When commanders' positions changed, units still had to know which offices would issue their new orders. The court also had to arrange acceptable roles for those leaving their commands. Centralizing military authority thus involved more than reducing any individual's power; it also meant reconnecting the army's daily chain of command.

The early Song court adjusted the command positions and authority of powerful generals to reduce the risk of independent military power. Later stories about a wine banquet are disputed in timing and details. The comparison concerns managing structural sources of danger, not justifying humiliating or harming anyone through animal imagery.

During the Sui and Tang periods, methods for selecting government officials gradually changed. Educated men could gain a chance of appointment through examinations, while the court continued to use recommendations and other routes. Families had unequal access to education, so the emergence of a new institution did not instantly put everyone on equal footing.

During the Sui and Tang dynasties, examination-based recruitment developed gradually, and degrees such as jinshi became one route into official service. This broadened opportunities for some scholars, but family standing, access to education, recommendations, and other means of entering office continued to matter.

Over time, the jinshi and other examination categories became part of the route to appointment. Candidates had to prepare and take the examinations, and those who passed still faced further procedures for assignment to posts. Historians define differently when the examination system began and when it reached maturity; Sui and Tang practices should not be conflated with all the rules of later periods. The path from access to examination to holding office developed gradually and remained shaped by family circumstances.

Candidates needed literacy and opportunities to study before taking examinations; successful candidates still depended on the distribution of official posts afterward. The emergence of the jinshi examination opened a route of advancement for some scholars, but examinations did not immediately become the court’s sole recruitment channel. Rules continued to change across dynasties, so Sui and Tang practices were not identical with the mature system of later ages.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Under Sui and Tang, examinations became one route for scholars to enter public service, though education, social standing, recommendations, and other channels remained important. This parallels the opening of a broad road. It does not claim that the system offered equal opportunity across gender, class, or resources.

161 Line H27 Yi Xiao He Supplies Liu Bang’s Campaign from Guanzhong — Recognizing Dependence Is Part of Responsibility▶

九五｜

161 case_id: XCASE-H27-L5 | unit_id: XIANG-U-27-06 | original_event_id: E27 | grade: B | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

During the Chu–Han conflict, Liu Bang’s armies at the front continually needed provisions, funds, and new soldiers. Guanzhong, which lay under his control, offered a base for transporting resources and administering the population. If local administration stalled, any short-term success gained on the battlefield would be difficult to sustain.

During the struggle between Chu and Han, Xiao He largely remained in Guanzhong, administering population registers, provisions, and the replenishment of troops so that Liu Bang’s forces at the front could receive continued support. Historical records such as the Book of Han describe this rear-area work as an important condition allowing the Han armies to keep fighting.

Xiao He stayed in Guanzhong to manage local administration and send personnel and grain to the front. After each expenditure of military resources, the rear still had to mobilize and transport supplies anew. In discussing the Han victory, records including the Book of Han also mention Xiao He’s administrative and logistical work. Before the First Sino-Japanese War, the Qing empire had acquired warships and established modern military industries. Equipment entering an army still required training, maintenance, supply and coordination across departments. When hostilities with Japan began in 1894, the accumulated material resources and institutional arrangements were subjected together to the pressures of a large-scale war.

During the war, Qing forces suffered successive defeats on land and at sea. The Treaty of Shimonoseki was ultimately signed, ceding Taiwan and the Penghu Islands, among other territories, to Japan. Warships and modern military industries built up beforehand had not ensured effective overall command, supply or institutional coordination.

After successive defeats on land and sea, the Qing government signed the Treaty of Shimonoseki with Japan in 1895, ceding Taiwan and Penghu. Military failure led to a treaty, while territorial changes altered the governing authority over residents. Earlier investments in modern armaments did not thereby become wholly worthless, but the failures of wartime command and coordination cannot be ignored either. The stages of equipment development, battlefield performance and territorial cession were interrelated.

Naval vessels and army units belonged to different chains of command and supply, requiring orders to be conveyed effectively across them in wartime. After the cession clauses were signed, residents of Taiwan and Penghu had to confront a change of rule. The fighting ended on the battlefield, but the treaty’s political and social consequences continued.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Defeat in the Sino-Japanese War demonstrated weaknesses in Qing coordination, training, logistics, and institutions despite modern warships and military industry. The collapsing ridgepole is a structural metaphor, not a claim that a single vessel or person caused the defeat.

167 Line H28 Da Guo Late-Qing Constitutional Preparations and a Crisis of Credibility — A Superficial Renewal May Not Last▶

九五｜

167 case_id: XCASE-H28-L5 | unit_id: XIANG-U-28-06 | original_event_id: E53 | grade: B | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

In 1906, the Qing court announced preparations for constitutional government to respond to calls for political reform. Supporters of reform hoped that political authority would gradually open up, while the imperial house still wished to preserve its leading role in government. They had different expectations about the preparatory timetable and what the new institutions would actually be empowered to do.

The Qing court announced preparations for constitutionalism, later set out annual preparatory tasks, and established new advisory and political-consultative institutions. Yet the reform timetable, retention of imperial authority, and the personnel composition of the 1911 cabinet disappointed supporters. Confidence among constitutional reformers in the court was damaged.

The court subsequently published preparatory measures and established institutions including provincial advisory councils and the National Assembly. As these bodies began operating, the retention of imperial power, the speed of reform, and the appointments to the cabinet in 1911 generated disappointment. Some who had originally hoped for constitutional government no longer believed the court was willing to surrender corresponding powers, while revolutionary activity and provincial political change intensified. Several years separated announcement, institutional creation, and the loss of confidence; the Qing collapse cannot be attributed solely to one cabinet appointment.

The establishment of the provincial advisory councils and the National Assembly enabled advocates of constitutionalism to operate within the new institutions; they continued to examine whether the imperial house would yield more important powers. When the 1911 cabinet appointments were announced, they could directly compare the current arrangements with earlier promises. Their disappointment did not arise overnight.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The Qing court’s constitutional preparations introduced new institutions, but delays, retained imperial authority, and the 1911 cabinet damaged confidence. The image of a withered willow briefly flowering distinguishes surface renewal from durable regeneration; the historical analogy should not reproduce the line’s gendered or age-based disparagement.

At the beginning of the Long March, the Central Red Army moved toward the Xiang River while facing blocking forces ahead and pursuit from behind. The river itself was a physical obstacle the operation had to overcome.

During the Long March, blocking forces confronted the Central Red Army around the Xiang River, and the crossing caused major losses in personnel and organizational strength. Studies discuss the burden of the march, the route, and command decisions; they also caution that casualty or attrition figures based on different methods cannot simply be treated as equivalent.

The Xiang River fighting exacted severe casualties and organizational losses. Continuing the march after the crossing did not erase the preceding deaths and injuries. Estimates using different methods should be retained together with their scope and sources.

Losses at the Xiang River invite reflection on the human sacrifices imposed by a dangerous campaign. “Not to be blamed” does not absolve commanders of responsibility: individual sacrifice must be distinguished from reviewing decisions that exposed the army to those losses.

169 Line H29 Kan The Tumu Crisis Reveals Weaknesses in Campaign Planning — Losing Direction Deepens the Danger▶

初九｜

169 case_id: XCASE-H29-L1 | unit_id: XIANG-U-29-02 | original_event_id: E23 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

In 1449, the Ming emperor Yingzong personally led troops north against the Oirats. A vast marching force required coordination of provisions, transport, and orders. Neither the advance northward nor the return journey could succeed on troop numbers alone. If deployments during the return were obstructed, losses at the front could directly affect the central government.

Emperor Yingzong led the army north against the Oirats, but during the return it suffered a devastating defeat near Tumu and the emperor was captured. The court faced a severe crisis. The episode involved decisions, movement, logistics, and command, and the defense of Beijing subsequently had to be reorganized.

The Ming army was struck heavily near Tumu and Yingzong was captured. On receiving the news, officials in Beijing had to reorganize military defense and affairs connected with the imperial succession to prevent a battlefield defeat from spreading into a wider catastrophe. Historical sources differ on troop numbers and the responsibility of some individuals, but the sequence is clear: departure on campaign, difficulties on the return, capture of the emperor, and emergency measures in the capital. Beijing’s defense had to begin while the emperor was still a prisoner.

The capture of the emperor immediately had consequences beyond an ordinary military retreat. Officials had to decide how the court would continue to exercise authority, and troops defending the city needed to know whose orders to follow. The capital’s emergency defense was organized with incomplete information from the front. Information carried from the Tumu battlefield to the capital tightly linked the military disaster to political decisions in Beijing.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The Tumu crisis exposed weaknesses in the Ming expedition’s planning: Emperor Yingzong marched against the Oirats, was captured after the army’s defeat, and left the court confronting a grave emergency. Decisions, supplies, movement, and command all mattered; the subsequent reorganization of Beijing’s defenses was also necessary. The predicament may illustrate how accumulated errors deepen danger, not merely an episode of bad luck. The Xiang commentary says that entering one abyss after another results in disaster from losing the path.

171 Line H29 Kan Fu Jian Is Defeated at the Fei River — Reassess When Neither Advance nor Retreat Is Easy▶

Fu Jian of Former Qin controlled extensive territories in northern China and prepared a major offensive against Eastern Jin. His far-reaching rule enabled him to assemble armies, but troops from different backgrounds also had to coordinate their actions throughout a distant campaign. Eastern Jin faced strong southward pressure in the Huai River region.

Fu Jian launched a large expedition against Eastern Jin, only to be counterattacked and routed by Jin forces near the Fei River. Former Qin’s apparent superiority in numbers did not automatically translate into reliable organizational or command superiority. Divisions within the regime became more evident after the defeat.

In 383, the armies fought near the Fei River, and Former Qin forces collapsed after the opposing counterattack. Fu Jian failed in his southern expedition, while the various powers that his regime had drawn together reassessed their positions and began to break away. Ancient narratives include dramatic battlefield descriptions, and troop totals cannot always be verified precisely. The clear sequence is massive mobilization, defeat at the Fei River, and the subsequent weakening of Former Qin control.

Before moving south, Former Qin needed to supply grain and maintain orders across its expeditionary forces; after defeat it had to preserve retreat routes for units from different backgrounds. The collapse at the Fei River quickly affected the regime’s structure. Forces previously willing to accept Fu Jian’s command began making different choices as the military situation changed.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Fu Jian mobilized Former Qin’s forces against Eastern Jin, but military superiority in appearance did not provide unity of command. The defeat at the Fei River and ensuing fragmentation can illuminate choices trapped by competing constraints. This is a retrospective analogy, not an assertion that battlefield movements necessarily followed the images of the hexagram. The Xiang describes going back and forth amid dangers and accomplishing nothing.

After Liao forces marched south, the Song court had to decide whether fighting on the frontier should expand further. Emperor Zhenzong reached Chanzhou, confronting decision-makers directly with conditions at the front and enabling envoys from both states to travel back and forth over ceasefire terms. Both Song and Liao possessed military forces; neither could dispense with subsequent practical arrangements simply by saying that the two sides were now reconciled.

After the Liao advance and Emperor Zhenzong’s arrival at Chanzhou, negotiations led to the Treaty of Chanyuan in 1005. Song undertook to provide annual payments to Liao, while each government retained its authority and an established order along the frontier. The arrangement carried a fiscal cost, but it also reduced large-scale warfare for a considerable period thereafter.

The negotiations culminated in the Treaty of Chanyuan: both states kept their own governments and Song undertook annual payments. After the agreement, the major campaign then under way ceased and the border had a framework both sides could invoke; the annual payments simultaneously became a recurring item of court expenditure. Warfare on a comparable scale was avoided for a long period, but diplomatic negotiations and frontier friction did not vanish. Military and fiscal consequences of the treaty both persisted.

The treaty settled the immediate fighting and also provided agreed terms that subsequent envoys could cite. Once the armies halted their advance, the court still had to prepare the annual payments on schedule; people in frontier communities meanwhile lived under the new arrangements. The direct benefits of the ceasefire and the continuing costs were not the same for every participant.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The Song-Liao Chanyuan Treaty of 1005 ended that phase of fighting through negotiation, at an ongoing fiscal cost to Song, while maintaining the two regimes and a workable border arrangement. The example concerns practical communication amid danger, not a literal claim that feasting resolved the war. The Xiang’s image of wine and vessels expresses an accommodation between firmness and flexibility.

174 Line H29 Kan Yuan Shikai’s Imperial Bid Provokes the National Protection Movement — A Wrong Course Can Create Prolonged Confinement▶

上九｜

174 case_id: XCASE-H29-L6 | unit_id: XIANG-U-29-07 | original_event_id: E12 | grade: B | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

After the establishment of the republic, Yuan Shikai held major positions in the central government, while relations with regional political forces remained complicated. In 1915 he pursued the restoration of monarchy, directly altering the republican designation of the state and the associated distribution of power. The enthusiasm of supporters could not ensure that the army, regional officials, or political parties would accept the proposed new regime.

In 1915 Yuan pressed ahead with replacing the republic by an imperial system, provoking political opposition and the National Protection War. Some forces that had formerly backed him ceased to cooperate; the monarchy was abandoned in 1916. Concentrating authority in one person did not automatically create a stable base of political support.

Opponents launched the National Protection movement, and political protest was progressively accompanied by military fighting. Some regional forces that had worked with Yuan were no longer willing to cooperate, testing the central government’s control of the provinces. Yuan abolished the monarchy in 1916, but the underlying struggle over power did not disappear that same day. The path from preparations for enthronement, through public opposition, to the abolition of the monarchy involved successive shifts in political allegiance and pressure on the battlefield.

As supporters proposed the institutional change, regional officials still had to choose between the existing republican order and the proposed monarchy. Responses from different provinces reached the center at different times, and Yuan’s orders were not necessarily carried out as originally expected. Once the National Protection War began, political resistance also translated directly into troop movements.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Yuan Shikai’s effort to restore monarchy in 1915 prompted opposition and the National Protection War, and he abandoned the imperial project in 1916. This narrowing of his political options can illuminate the image of entrapment. The “three years” in the Xiang are not offered as the duration of these events, nor as evidence of a particular punishment.

Nanjing became the seat of the provisional government, although the new regime’s effective control remained geographically limited.
