The provisional government established agencies and issued statements of policy, attempting to turn the revolution’s political objectives into everyday administration. Its finances and ability to exercise effective control throughout the country nevertheless remained limited.

Sun Yat-sen assumed the provisional presidency in Nanjing on January 1, 1912. The government established offices and published policy proclamations. Officials began working under new titles while still confronting the Qing court and military forces in other regions. During negotiations between north and south, the new government’s personnel and distribution of authority continued to change. The inauguration has a clear date, but making a new administration capable of enforcing orders across regions required separate financial and political support.

The Nanjing provisional government had to turn the personal and military relationships of the revolutionary period into offices, assigned duties, and official correspondence. Although provinces had declared support for a republic, they did not necessarily surrender control of tax revenues or military command at the same time. Following Sun Yat-sen’s inauguration, provisional agencies continued to conduct daily affairs under these constraints.

The Nanjing Provisional Government was organized following the 1911 Revolution; Sun Yat-sen assumed office on 1 January 1912, and administrative institutions and proclamations followed. After Liao forces marched south, the Song court had to decide whether fighting on the frontier should expand further. Both Song and Liao possessed military forces; neither could dispense with subsequent practical arrangements simply by saying that the two sides were now reconciled.

After the Liao advance and Emperor Zhenzong’s arrival at Chanzhou, negotiations led to the Treaty of Chanyuan in 1005. Song undertook to provide annual payments to Liao, while each government retained its authority and an established order along the frontier. The arrangement carried a fiscal cost, but it also reduced large-scale warfare for a considerable period thereafter.

The negotiations culminated in the Treaty of Chanyuan: both states kept their own governments and Song undertook annual payments. After the agreement, the major campaign then under way ceased and the border had a framework both sides could invoke; the annual payments simultaneously became a recurring item of court expenditure. Warfare on a comparable scale was avoided for a long period, but diplomatic negotiations and frontier friction did not vanish. Military and fiscal consequences of the treaty both persisted.

The treaty settled the immediate fighting and also provided agreed terms that subsequent envoys could cite. Once the armies halted their advance, the court still had to prepare the annual payments on schedule; people in frontier communities meanwhile lived under the new arrangements. The direct benefits of the ceasefire and the continuing costs were not the same for every participant.

The Chanyuan Treaty between Song and Liao brought that confrontation to an end through concrete reciprocal conditions, including Song’s annual payments. It can illustrate finding a measured response amid conflict, although whether the course was moderate requires judging the security and fiscal costs of the time. During Emperor Xuanzong's reign, the Tang court had experienced prosperity and held extensive territory, while the military strength of commanders in frontier garrisons also increased. An Lushan controlled frontier troops, and political tensions between center and provinces grew more difficult to manage as power became concentrated.

The Xuanzong reign saw prosperity and expansion, but problems involving frontier military power and central politics continued to accumulate. In 755, An Lushan raised a rebellion and shattered the court's control of the situation. The war had long-lasting effects on population, finances, and provincial authority.

In 755 An Lushan rebelled, disrupting the established Tang order, and Emperor Xuanzong left Chang'an. The fighting continued for years, affecting population movements, fiscal receipts, and local military-political power. The uprising has a date, but relations between frontier commands and the center had deteriorated over a much longer period. An account limited to palace anecdotes would fail to show why the lengthy war changed the ways in which Tang China was governed.

Provincial military governors held troops and local resources; the court's prosperity did not automatically assure its control over frontier commands. After An Lushan rebelled, armies advanced along their routes and the court made decisions about defense and flight. Prolonged warfare increased the extent to which local authorities handled finances and military affairs for themselves; the effects did not end in 755.

The An Lushan Rebellion erupted in 755 after mounting tensions between frontier commands and the Tang court. Distrust between the two camps over the future distribution of power deepened.

Li Shimin killed Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji in the coup at Xuanwu Gate, gained political and military advantage, and later became emperor. This was a succession dispute resolved through violence; later favorable judgments of the Zhenguan reign cannot erase the cost of that violence.

In 626, Li Shimin launched an armed operation at Xuanwu Gate, in which Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji were killed. He thereby gained military and political advantage and eventually ascended the throne, breaking the earlier succession arrangements. Policies during the later reign of Emperor Taizong have been judged in different ways, but that history came after the coup; it does not undo the deaths on the day. Because chronicles were often compiled after the victor had established a new order, their narrative perspective also deserves attention.

Xuanwu Gate was an important passage into the palace. By choosing to use force there, Li Shimin brought military action directly to bear on the court’s succession arrangements. Once Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji were killed, the former crown prince could no longer succeed. The later actions of Emperor Taizong must be distinguished from the loss of life and transfer of power on the day of the coup.

The Xuanwu Gate coup altered the Tang succession through the killing of Li Jiancheng and Li Yuanji and helped bring Li Shimin to the throne. 182 Line H31 Xian Zhou Yafu Waits for an Opening during the Seven States Rebellion — Do Not Follow Every Impulse to Act▶

182 case_id: XCASE-H31-L2 | unit_id: XIANG-U-31-03 | original_event_id: E05 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

In 154 BCE, seven kingdoms raised forces against the Han, and the armies of Wu and Chu advanced, leaving the kingdom of Liang in urgent need of relief. The court sent Zhou Yafu to command its army. He had to weigh both Liang’s immediate peril and the supply situation of the principal rebel army. If the Han army reacted immediately to every enemy movement, it might be forced to fight under conditions chosen by its opponent.

After the rebellion began, Zhou Yafu did not constantly seek a direct, decisive engagement. He held his position and sent troops to cut the Wu–Chu army’s supply lines. He waited until the enemy encountered difficulties obtaining provisions and then exploited the moment of its retreat. Liang meanwhile endured pressure, making this deployment politically contentious.

Zhou Yafu maintained his own positions while dispatching other forces to interrupt the Wu–Chu supply routes. The danger facing Liang did not disappear, and Zhou was criticized politically for failing to come to its immediate rescue. Only after the enemy’s provisions were disrupted and its offensive became unsustainable did he strike during its withdrawal. Both the victory over the rebels and the risks borne by Liang belong to the outcome. This campaign illustrates how interference with supplies in the rear could alter conditions on the battlefield.

Zhou Yafu’s decision meant that Liang could not immediately receive comprehensive support, much to the displeasure of the Liang court. At the same time, the Han army still had to defend its own positions and prevent the enemy from readily redirecting its attack. Cutting supply lines was not passive observation: it was intended to make the offensive previously sustainable for the Wu–Chu forces progressively harder to maintain.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Zhou Yafu held his position during the Seven States Rebellion rather than rushing into direct battle, cut enemy supply routes, and chose his opportunity. Political controversy followed because Liang remained under pressure. The case illuminates disciplined resistance to immediate demands, but the soundness of waiting depends on actual military information. The Xiang links remaining in place with avoiding harm.

184 Line H31 Xian The Chongqing Negotiations Produce the Double Tenth Agreement — Frequent Contact Does Not Guarantee Trust▶

After victory in the War of Resistance against Japan in 1945, both the Nationalist government and the Chinese Communist Party faced questions of military reorganization, the takeover of local administrations, and the form of the national government. To avoid a wider internal war, they needed to write down principles both sides could accept while also addressing which forces actually controlled troops on the ground.

Following the war, representatives of the Nationalist government and the Communist Party negotiated in Chongqing and produced the Summary of Talks between the Government and Representatives of the Chinese Communist Party, commonly known as the Double Tenth Agreement. They articulated principles for a peaceful reconstruction of the country, but such central issues as the armies and control of local governments were not fully resolved.

Representatives held talks in Chongqing and publicized the Summary of Talks, or Double Tenth Agreement. The document set out aims concerning peaceful nation-building, but the fundamental questions of military forces and local authority remained unsettled. After publication, disputes over effective control and military clashes continued to develop. Talks, an agreed text, and the implementation of that text are three related stages that do not take place simultaneously. Issuing the agreement must not be described as if peace had already been secured.

What could be written at the negotiating table did not necessarily correspond to territories already controlled by the respective armies. After representatives published the agreement, their organizations still had to communicate the commitments internally and decide whether to implement them. The difficulty of sustaining peace after the war must also be understood through the sequence of, and gaps between, these practical actions.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

After the war against Japan, the Chongqing negotiations led to the Double Tenth Agreement, yet military integration and local political authority remained unresolved. Repeated meetings did not guarantee substantial mutual trust, although the negotiations themselves represented real efforts. The Xiang contrasts continual coming and going with a wider, more lasting influence.

The Qing court announced preparations for constitutionalism, later set out annual preparatory tasks, and established new advisory and political-consultative institutions. Yet the reform timetable, retention of imperial authority, and the personnel composition of the 1911 cabinet disappointed supporters. Confidence among constitutional reformers in the court was damaged.

The court subsequently published preparatory measures and established institutions including provincial advisory councils and the National Assembly. As these bodies began operating, the retention of imperial power, the speed of reform, and the appointments to the cabinet in 1911 generated disappointment. Some who had originally hoped for constitutional government no longer believed the court was willing to surrender corresponding powers, while revolutionary activity and provincial political change intensified. Several years separated announcement, institutional creation, and the loss of confidence; the Qing collapse cannot be attributed solely to one cabinet appointment.

The establishment of the provincial advisory councils and the National Assembly enabled advocates of constitutionalism to operate within the new institutions; they continued to examine whether the imperial house would yield more important powers. When the 1911 cabinet appointments were announced, they could directly compare the current arrangements with earlier promises. Their disappointment did not arise overnight.

The late-Qing constitutional program made institutional changes but fell short of public expectations, with limited impact on the broader crisis of trust. This analogy describes a restricted reach; it does not dismiss every reform as ineffective. The Xiang presents an influence that stops short of its highest purpose.

186 Line H31 Xian The Chongqing Negotiations Produce the Double Tenth Agreement — Verbal Commitments Need Working Mechanisms▶

186 case_id: XCASE-H31-L6 | unit_id: XIANG-U-31-07 | original_event_id: E58 | grade: B | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

After victory in the War of Resistance against Japan in 1945, both the Nationalist government and the Chinese Communist Party faced questions of military reorganization, the takeover of local administrations, and the form of the national government. To avoid a wider internal war, they needed to write down principles both sides could accept while also addressing which forces actually controlled troops on the ground.

Following the war, representatives of the Nationalist government and the Communist Party negotiated in Chongqing and produced the Summary of Talks between the Government and Representatives of the Chinese Communist Party, commonly known as the Double Tenth Agreement. They articulated principles for a peaceful reconstruction of the country, but such central issues as the armies and control of local governments were not fully resolved.

Representatives held talks in Chongqing and publicized the Summary of Talks, or Double Tenth Agreement. The document set out aims concerning peaceful nation-building, but the fundamental questions of military forces and local authority remained unsettled. After publication, disputes over effective control and military clashes continued to develop. Talks, an agreed text, and the implementation of that text are three related stages that do not take place simultaneously. Issuing the agreement must not be described as if peace had already been secured.

What could be written at the negotiating table did not necessarily correspond to territories already controlled by the respective armies. After representatives published the agreement, their organizations still had to communicate the commitments internally and decide whether to implement them. The difficulty of sustaining peace after the war must also be understood through the sequence of, and gaps between, these practical actions.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The 1945 Double Tenth Agreement articulated principles for peaceful political reconstruction but lacked agreed means to settle major military and governmental issues. Subsequent conflict shows that verbal or written agreement needs implementation conditions. The Xiang’s image of cheeks, tongue, and mouth concerns speech, not an insult to individual negotiators.

187 Line H32 Heng Late-Qing Constitutional Preparations and the Crisis of Credibility — Expecting Immediate Completion Breeds Frustration▶

初九｜

187 case_id: XCASE-H32-L1 | unit_id: XIANG-U-32-02 | original_event_id: E53 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

In 1906, the Qing court announced preparations for constitutional government to respond to calls for political reform. Supporters of reform hoped that political authority would gradually open up, while the imperial house still wished to preserve its leading role in government. They had different expectations about the preparatory timetable and what the new institutions would actually be empowered to do.

The Qing court announced preparations for constitutionalism, later set out annual preparatory tasks, and established new advisory and political-consultative institutions. Yet the reform timetable, retention of imperial authority, and the personnel composition of the 1911 cabinet disappointed supporters. Confidence among constitutional reformers in the court was damaged.

The court subsequently published preparatory measures and established institutions including provincial advisory councils and the National Assembly. As these bodies began operating, the retention of imperial power, the speed of reform, and the appointments to the cabinet in 1911 generated disappointment. Some who had originally hoped for constitutional government no longer believed the court was willing to surrender corresponding powers, while revolutionary activity and provincial political change intensified. Several years separated announcement, institutional creation, and the loss of confidence; the Qing collapse cannot be attributed solely to one cabinet appointment.

The establishment of the provincial advisory councils and the National Assembly enabled advocates of constitutionalism to operate within the new institutions; they continued to examine whether the imperial house would yield more important powers. When the 1911 cabinet appointments were announced, they could directly compare the current arrangements with earlier promises. Their disappointment did not arise overnight.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The mismatch between urgent hopes and the Qing court’s stepwise constitutional preparations illustrates the danger of demanding complete transformation at the outset. This does not excuse deliberate delay or deny the need for reform. The Xiang says that digging too deeply at the beginning produces misfortune.

188 Line H32 Heng On Protracted War Sets Out a Strategy of Staged Resistance — Long-Term Strategy Requires Steady Judgment▶

九二｜

188 case_id: XCASE-H32-L2 | unit_id: XIANG-U-32-03 | original_event_id: E32 | grade: B | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

The Sino-Japanese War was still under way in 1938. Victories and defeats at different fronts, together with civilian mobilization, produced divergent judgments about the war’s prospects. Mao Zedong wrote On Protracted War at that time to address whether resistance could continue, how circumstances might change, and how different stages might be organized.

In On Protracted War (1938), Mao Zedong analyzed conditions in the Sino-Japanese War and proposed a conception of prolonged resistance developing through stages. This was a strategic argument about the conflict as it stood at the time, considering time, changes in relative power, and organizational mobilization together.

The text examined the strengths of the opposing sides and the importance of time, proposing a staged approach to the war. When published, the subsequent course of the conflict had not yet unfolded. It was a contemporary strategic argument, and later developments depended on various fronts, political forces, and international circumstances. The eventual victory cannot be used retrospectively to claim that the work had already answered every specific military problem. Starting from the questions of 1938 clarifies which conditions the author chose to examine.

After publication, readers and soldiers still confronted changing front lines. The staged framework supplied a way of thinking about time, while individual forces still had to solve their own supply, command, and battlefield-intelligence problems. The work’s strategic assessments should not be collapsed together with concrete military outcomes occurring many years later as though they formed one decision.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

On Protracted War (1938) analyzed how relative power and the course of the Sino-Japanese War might change across successive phases. It may illustrate sustaining appropriate strategic judgment over time, while leaving room for practical revision as circumstances change. The Xiang commends the ability to endure in the middle.

189 Line H32 Heng Yuan Shikai’s Imperial Bid Provokes the National Protection Movement — Changing Principles Erodes Trust▶

九三｜

189 case_id: XCASE-H32-L3 | unit_id: XIANG-U-32-04 | original_event_id: E12 | grade: B | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

After the establishment of the republic, Yuan Shikai held major positions in the central government, while relations with regional political forces remained complicated. In 1915 he pursued the restoration of monarchy, directly altering the republican designation of the state and the associated distribution of power. The enthusiasm of supporters could not ensure that the army, regional officials, or political parties would accept the proposed new regime.

In 1915 Yuan pressed ahead with replacing the republic by an imperial system, provoking political opposition and the National Protection War. Some forces that had formerly backed him ceased to cooperate; the monarchy was abandoned in 1916. Concentrating authority in one person did not automatically create a stable base of political support.

Opponents launched the National Protection movement, and political protest was progressively accompanied by military fighting. Some regional forces that had worked with Yuan were no longer willing to cooperate, testing the central government’s control of the provinces. Yuan abolished the monarchy in 1916, but the underlying struggle over power did not disappear that same day. The path from preparations for enthronement, through public opposition, to the abolition of the monarchy involved successive shifts in political allegiance and pressure on the battlefield.

As supporters proposed the institutional change, regional officials still had to choose between the existing republican order and the proposed monarchy. Responses from different provinces reached the center at different times, and Yuan’s orders were not necessarily carried out as originally expected. Once the National Protection War began, political resistance also translated directly into troop movements.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Yuan Shikai moved from republican presidency toward monarchy, undermining confidence in his political commitments and provoking armed opposition. This example illustrates how repeated changes of basic course can erode legitimacy, rather than claiming that a single historical act precisely embodies the Xiang. The Xiang warns that virtue without constancy finds no place.

190 Line H32 Heng The Self-Strengthening Movement Builds Modern Military Industries — Sustained Effort Must Have the Right Focus▶

九四｜

190 case_id: XCASE-H32-L4 | unit_id: XIANG-U-32-05 | original_event_id: E09 | grade: B | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

After the wars of the mid-nineteenth century, the Qing court and provincial officials confronted gaps in manufacturing, navigation, and military training. They planned arsenals, naval administration facilities, and schools. Acquiring equipment and training operators required funding and continuing personnel arrangements. Projects in different localities were not all completed by one authority at the same time.

During the Self-Strengthening Movement, Qing authorities and provincial officials established arsenals, naval institutions, and modern schools, gradually acquiring manufacturing, navigation, and military skills. These projects left equipment and trained personnel behind, but problems of finance, administration, and coordination across regions were not resolved at the same time.

Some factories began production, students received technical education, and naval institutions and fleets gradually accumulated skilled personnel. Once equipment was installed, maintenance, salaries, command arrangements, and interprovincial deployment still had to be coordinated separately. By the end of the nineteenth century the Qing state possessed a range of modern facilities but also faced financial and administrative deficiencies. Subsequent military defeats neither erased the people and equipment that had been developed nor rendered organizational problems unimportant.

Graduates of the schools still had to be assigned to working institutions, and machinery produced by factories had to reach military units. Between establishing a facility and putting it to effective use in war came purchasing, learning, and maintenance. The greater the differences among regional institutions, the harder it became to make resources work together when needed.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The Self-Strengthening Movement sustained investment in arsenals, shipbuilding, and modern training, but financial and coordination limits remained. Long duration alone does not prove that a policy’s focus is right; neither does criticism erase genuine technological and educational gains. The Xiang asks what can be obtained by remaining long in the wrong position.

191 Line H32 Heng Zhou Yafu Waits for an Opening during the Seven States Rebellion — Persistence Also Requires Responsible Judgment▶

九五｜

191 case_id: XCASE-H32-L5 | unit_id: XIANG-U-32-06 | original_event_id: E05 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

In 154 BCE, seven kingdoms raised forces against the Han, and the armies of Wu and Chu advanced, leaving the kingdom of Liang in urgent need of relief. The court sent Zhou Yafu to command its army. He had to weigh both Liang’s immediate peril and the supply situation of the principal rebel army. If the Han army reacted immediately to every enemy movement, it might be forced to fight under conditions chosen by its opponent.

After the rebellion began, Zhou Yafu did not constantly seek a direct, decisive engagement. He held his position and sent troops to cut the Wu–Chu army’s supply lines. He waited until the enemy encountered difficulties obtaining provisions and then exploited the moment of its retreat. Liang meanwhile endured pressure, making this deployment politically contentious.

Zhou Yafu maintained his own positions while dispatching other forces to interrupt the Wu–Chu supply routes. The danger facing Liang did not disappear, and Zhou was criticized politically for failing to come to its immediate rescue. Only after the enemy’s provisions were disrupted and its offensive became unsustainable did he strike during its withdrawal. Both the victory over the rebels and the risks borne by Liang belong to the outcome. This campaign illustrates how interference with supplies in the rear could alter conditions on the battlefield.

Zhou Yafu’s decision meant that Liang could not immediately receive comprehensive support, much to the displeasure of the Liang court. At the same time, the Han army still had to defend its own positions and prevent the enemy from readily redirecting its attack. Cutting supply lines was not passive observation: it was intended to make the offensive previously sustainable for the Wu–Chu forces progressively harder to maintain.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Zhou Yafu’s conduct during the Seven States Rebellion offers an example of deciding independently when to hold position and when to act, even under pressure for immediate relief. This is used to consider the limits of obedience and personal judgment, not to impose the ancient text’s division of male and female duties upon present-day responsibilities.

Suitability review and revisions

192 Line H32 Heng Qing Decision-Making Breaks Down during the Boxer Crisis — Restless Reversals Undermine Results▶

In 1900, Boxer activity, foreign intervention, and decision-making within the Qing court became entangled, while the diplomatic and military situation in Beijing deteriorated rapidly. The court’s approach to foreign troops and regional officials’ judgments about the security of their own jurisdictions had already begun to diverge.

After the Boxer movement and foreign military intervention intensified, the Qing court issued an edict declaring war on foreign powers, further widening the crisis. Allied troops entered Beijing, the court fled, and the Boxer Protocol was signed the following year. Some regional officials pursued the Mutual Protection of Southeast China, also showing that central and regional authorities did not share the same judgment.

The Qing government issued its declaration of war; hostilities spread, allied forces entered Beijing, and the court fled. Some officials in the southeast pursued mutual-protection arrangements, revealing that different regions did not respond uniformly. The Boxer Protocol was signed the next year, imposing serious consequences on the court and population. Any discussion of mistakes made by the central government must also explicitly acknowledge the armed incursion by foreign powers. The transition from local movements to international war resulted from more than one person’s decision.

After the war edict, not all officials across the empire responded in the same way: the southeastern mutual-protection arrangements highlight the difference between central and regional choices. The allied occupation of Beijing and treaty indemnities transformed a crisis in political judgment into military and fiscal consequences. Different actors made decisions and bore costs at each stage.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The Qing court’s reversals and escalation during the Boxer crisis illustrate the costs of unstable high-level decisions. The external use of force and the different views within China must also be considered, rather than attributing the entire crisis to restlessness alone. The Xiang says agitation at the top produces no great achievement.

193 Line H33 Dun The Tumu Crisis — Delaying Withdrawal Increases the Danger▶

初九｜

193 case_id: XCASE-H33-L1 | unit_id: XIANG-U-33-02 | original_event_id: E23 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

In 1449, the Ming emperor Yingzong personally led troops north against the Oirats. A vast marching force required coordination of provisions, transport, and orders. Neither the advance northward nor the return journey could succeed on troop numbers alone. If deployments during the return were obstructed, losses at the front could directly affect the central government.

Emperor Yingzong led the army north against the Oirats, but during the return it suffered a devastating defeat near Tumu and the emperor was captured. The court faced a severe crisis. The episode involved decisions, movement, logistics, and command, and the defense of Beijing subsequently had to be reorganized.

The Ming army was struck heavily near Tumu and Yingzong was captured. On receiving the news, officials in Beijing had to reorganize military defense and affairs connected with the imperial succession to prevent a battlefield defeat from spreading into a wider catastrophe. Historical sources differ on troop numbers and the responsibility of some individuals, but the sequence is clear: departure on campaign, difficulties on the return, capture of the emperor, and emergency measures in the capital. Beijing’s defense had to begin while the emperor was still a prisoner.

The capture of the emperor immediately had consequences beyond an ordinary military retreat. Officials had to decide how the court would continue to exercise authority, and troops defending the city needed to know whose orders to follow. The capital’s emergency defense was organized with incomplete information from the front. Information carried from the Tumu battlefield to the capital tightly linked the military disaster to political decisions in Beijing.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The Tumu disaster exposed the fragility of the Ming expedition: the emperor was captured after the army suffered grave losses, and Beijing’s defense had to be reorganized. Decisions about movement, supplies, and command all mattered. The difficulty of withdrawing after conditions had already deteriorated illustrates the danger of remaining at the rear too long; it does not prove that merely fleeing earlier would have prevented every loss. The Xiang says: “Peril at the tail of retreat; if one does not go, what disaster is there?”

Suitability review and revisions

195 Line H33 Dun Liu Bei Retreats after Changban — Withdrawal Carries Responsibilities toward Others▶

九三｜

195 case_id: XCASE-H33-L3 | unit_id: XIANG-U-33-04 | original_event_id: E33 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

When Cao Cao advanced into Jingzhou, Liu Bei could no longer maintain his previous position there and moved south with his troops and the people accompanying them. Not everyone in the column was a soldier able to march quickly. The distances between their pursuers and possible supporters along the route were continually changing.

As Cao Cao advanced into Jingzhou, Liu Bei retreated south. He was pursued and routed at Changban, then joined forces with Guan Yu, Liu Qi, and others, and sought cooperation with Sun Quan. The withdrawal allowed some of his strength to survive, but it was neither smooth nor free of serious losses.

After Cao Cao’s forces pursued and attacked him at Changban, Liu Bei’s army suffered heavily. He later joined Guan Yu, Liu Qi, and other units, gradually rebuilt usable military strength, and sought an alliance with Sun Quan. The subsequent alliance did not turn the rout at Changban into a successful retreat calculated from the beginning. The process included departure from Jingzhou, pursuit, the regrouping of some troops, and the search for an external ally, as well as genuine dangers faced by those accompanying the army.

Because civilians followed the army, Liu Bei’s speed of withdrawal differed from that of troops marching alone. Once the pursuit at Changban had scattered his forces, separate units had to find one another again before they could negotiate with outside allies. Both the people who survived and the losses suffered on the spot were part of the withdrawal.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

When Cao Cao advanced into Jingzhou, Liu Bei withdrew southward and was defeated during the pursuit at Changban before regrouping with other forces. Movement involved soldiers and accompanying civilians; planning could not consider troop speed alone. This illustrates how personal and organizational obligations constrain retreat. The archaic wording about servants and concubines must not be turned into a modern rule for controlling other persons. The Xiang warns of burdens and exhaustion in a constrained retreat.

196 Line H33 Dun Zhuge Liang Withdraws after Jieting — Stepping Back Requires Judgment▶

196 case_id: XCASE-H33-L4 | unit_id: XIANG-U-33-05 | original_event_id: E39 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

When Zhuge Liang's first Northern Expedition reached Longyou, Jieting was an important location influencing subsequent operations. Ma Su was appointed to manage the local deployment; the main army's ability to maintain conditions for advancing was directly connected to the defense of Jieting.

During the first Northern Expedition, Ma Su lost Jieting. Zhuge Liang withdrew and submitted a memorial requesting his own demotion, acknowledging his poor judgment in appointments. In this self-demotion memorial, the commander tied the defeat to his responsibility for selecting personnel rather than blaming only subordinates at the front.

After Ma Su lost Jieting, Zhuge Liang withdrew his army instead of pressing ahead along the previous route. He memorialized the court asking to be demoted and admitted responsibility for his appointments. This was a public accounting to the court of the commander's judgment after military defeat; it must not be taken to eliminate other causes on the battlefield. The sequence of appointment, fighting at Jieting, withdrawal, and the self-demotion memorial is clear. The fictional Empty Fort Strategy is not part of this historically supported episode.

The loss at Jieting deprived later Shu deployments of support. Zhuge Liang's withdrawal did not restore the resources already expended. Assuming responsibility through a memorial was a political accounting to the court; the troops still had to leave the theater and rearrange their defenses in practice. Battlefield action and subsequent responsibility followed one another in this affair.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

After Ma Su’s defeat at Jieting, Zhuge Liang withdrew his forces and requested a reduction in rank, acknowledging responsibility for the appointment. The decision shows that continued attack is not always wise, but it does not authorize sorting real historical actors into “gentlemen” and “petty men” based only on whether they advance or retreat. The Xiang contrasts a worthy withdrawal with its opposite.

197 Line H33 Dun The Korean Armistice Agreement — An Armistice Can Serve Long-Term Goals▶

九五｜

197 case_id: XCASE-H33-L5 | unit_id: XIANG-U-33-06 | original_event_id: E52 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

After prolonged fighting in the Korean War, representatives debated the timing and location of a halt to hostilities as well as the handling of prisoners of war. Chinese People’s Volunteers had joined the conflict, so a ceasefire had to be recorded in terms accepted by the military parties before troops along the front could adjust their conduct.

In 1953 representatives of the Korean People’s Army and Chinese People’s Volunteers, on one side, and the United Nations Command, on the other, concluded a military armistice. It established arrangements for ceasing hostilities and drawing a military demarcation line. The extended fighting paused, but the agreement was not a formal peace treaty.

The armistice signed in 1953 specified a cessation of military operations and a demarcation arrangement, bringing large-scale combat to a halt. It remained a military agreement rather than a definitive peace settlement; political disputes on the peninsula persisted. The passage from protracted fighting through difficult negotiations to implementation at the front required coordinated action by several parties.

Once the armistice terms reached forward units, both sides had to determine exactly when and where firing should cease. A written agreement alone could not end fighting without such implementation. Establishing a military demarcation line did not settle every territorial or sovereignty dispute. The armistice thus had a distinct practical achievement and equally distinct limits.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The Korean Armistice Agreement of 1953 created arrangements for stopping hostilities after long negotiations. The result may illustrate an orderly termination of military action in pursuit of a longer-term purpose. It did not settle the remaining political disputes and was not a peace treaty. The Xiang associates a praiseworthy withdrawal with rectifying one’s aims.

Suitability review and revisions

199 Line H34 Da Zhuang Fu Jian’s Defeat at the Fei River — Having Strength Does Not Mean Attack Immediately▶

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

Fu Jian of Former Qin controlled extensive territories in northern China and prepared a major offensive against Eastern Jin. His far-reaching rule enabled him to assemble armies, but troops from different backgrounds also had to coordinate their actions throughout a distant campaign. Eastern Jin faced strong southward pressure in the Huai River region.

Fu Jian launched a large expedition against Eastern Jin, only to be counterattacked and routed by Jin forces near the Fei River. Former Qin’s apparent superiority in numbers did not automatically translate into reliable organizational or command superiority. Divisions within the regime became more evident after the defeat.

In 383, the armies fought near the Fei River, and Former Qin forces collapsed after the opposing counterattack. Before moving south, Former Qin needed to supply grain and maintain orders across its expeditionary forces; after defeat it had to preserve retreat routes for units from different backgrounds. The collapse at the Fei River quickly affected the regime’s structure. Forces previously willing to accept Fu Jian’s command began making different choices as the military situation changed.

Fu Jian assembled extensive Former Qin forces against Eastern Jin, yet was defeated at the Fei River and saw his realm weaken afterward. 200 Line H34 Da Zhuang Zhou Yafu’s Campaign against the Seven States — Use Strength with Restraint▶

九二｜

200 case_id: XCASE-H34-L2 | unit_id: XIANG-U-34-03 | original_event_id: E05 | grade: A | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

In 154 BCE, seven kingdoms raised forces against the Han, and the armies of Wu and Chu advanced, leaving the kingdom of Liang in urgent need of relief. The court sent Zhou Yafu to command its army. He had to weigh both Liang’s immediate peril and the supply situation of the principal rebel army. If the Han army reacted immediately to every enemy movement, it might be forced to fight under conditions chosen by its opponent.

After the rebellion began, Zhou Yafu did not constantly seek a direct, decisive engagement. He held his position and sent troops to cut the Wu–Chu army’s supply lines. He waited until the enemy encountered difficulties obtaining provisions and then exploited the moment of its retreat. Liang meanwhile endured pressure, making this deployment politically contentious.

Zhou Yafu maintained his own positions while dispatching other forces to interrupt the Wu–Chu supply routes. The danger facing Liang did not disappear, and Zhou was criticized politically for failing to come to its immediate rescue. Only after the enemy’s provisions were disrupted and its offensive became unsustainable did he strike during its withdrawal. Both the victory over the rebels and the risks borne by Liang belong to the outcome. This campaign illustrates how interference with supplies in the rear could alter conditions on the battlefield.

Zhou Yafu’s decision meant that Liang could not immediately receive comprehensive support, much to the displeasure of the Liang court. At the same time, the Han army still had to defend its own positions and prevent the enemy from readily redirecting its attack. Cutting supply lines was not passive observation: it was intended to make the offensive previously sustainable for the Wu–Chu forces progressively harder to maintain.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

During the Seven States Rebellion, Zhou Yafu held his positions and attacked enemy supply routes instead of seeking only a frontal clash, despite pressure surrounding Liang’s defense. His conduct illustrates the usefulness of exercising force from a suitable position and with restraint. The Xiang connects the good fortune of the second line with maintaining the center.

Emperor Yingzong led the army north against the Oirats, but during the return it suffered a devastating defeat near Tumu and the emperor was captured. The court faced a severe crisis. The episode involved decisions, movement, logistics, and command, and the defense of Beijing subsequently had to be reorganized.

The Ming army was struck heavily near Tumu and Yingzong was captured. Beijing’s defense had to begin while the emperor was still a prisoner.

The capture of the emperor immediately had consequences beyond an ordinary military retreat. Officials had to decide how the court would continue to exercise authority, and troops defending the city needed to know whose orders to follow. The capital’s emergency defense was organized with incomplete information from the front. Information carried from the Tumu battlefield to the capital tightly linked the military disaster to political decisions in Beijing.

At Tumu, the Ming emperor’s personal status and the army’s apparent momentum did not protect the expedition from failures of planning and command. The example cautions against treating rank or display of strength as a substitute for preparation; it does not shift blame onto ordinary soldiers. The Northern Expeditionary Army did not take Wuchang in a single assault. It suffered setbacks in storming the city, conducted a siege, and sustained operations until it captured Wuchang in October 1926. The campaign enlarged the Northern Expedition's political and military influence, but also entailed casualties among soldiers and civilians and the hardships of a besieged city.

The siege imposed losses on defenders, attackers, and the city's inhabitants; urban life was also constrained by war. The fall of Wuchang expanded the Northern Expedition's political and military influence, but the failed earlier assaults must not be removed from the story. The city was captured after multiple deployments and continued fighting, and new political disputes subsequently arose within the Northern Expedition camp.

Defenders could use the city fortifications to delay an attack, while besiegers had to sustain their encirclement and supplies. Only when Wuchang changed hands in October did this siege have a clear military outcome. The suffering of city residents throughout the encirclement should not disappear from a narrative of victory.

The Northern Expedition’s capture of Wuchang in October 1926 followed setbacks, siege operations, and sustained combat, rather than an effortless assault. The result illustrates a breakthrough once obstacles were overcome through real capabilities, while casualties and the costs of surrounding the city remain part of the account. The Xiang describes a breached barrier that no longer obstructs forward movement.

203 Line H34 Da Zhuang Song Taizu Reorganizes Military Command — Relinquishing Power Can Reduce Risk▶

203 case_id: XCASE-H34-L5 | unit_id: XIANG-U-34-06 | original_event_id: E16 | grade: B | evidence: retrospective analogy | status: editorial_review

Historical narrative — full four-paragraph English translation

After Emperor Taizu founded the Song dynasty, the court faced the problem of senior commanders holding too much military power. The new state's military foundations came from existing forces, and abruptly severing relations with their commanders could also disrupt the army's operations. The center therefore gradually adjusted appointments and command authority.

After establishing his government, Emperor Taizu progressively reorganized senior commanders' positions and the means by which armies were controlled, reducing the risk that generals with their own troops could set up independent power bases. Later generations often describe this as 'Relinquishing Military Command over a Cup of Wine,' but scholars differ on the banquet dialogue, its date, and the precise course of events.

Some generals left their former commands, and military authority was redistributed toward the center. Later writers called these changes 'Relinquishing Military Command over a Cup of Wine' and included conversations between sovereign and ministers in a banquet scene; the exact dialogue, timing, and historical sources remain disputed. The observable historical process was a change in offices and in methods of army control. There is no need to assume that every adjustment was settled in one evening. Once the new arrangements were established, the court still had to ensure that armies functioned under the new chain of command.

When commanders' positions changed, units still had to know which offices would issue their new orders. The court also had to arrange acceptable roles for those leaving their commands. Centralizing military authority thus involved more than reducing any individual's power; it also meant reconnecting the army's daily chain of command.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

After founding the Song dynasty, Taizu reorganized senior military appointments and their control of troops to reduce the risk of independent armed power. The episode may illustrate the value of relinquishing part of one’s authority, but sources differ about the celebrated banquet dialogue, and not all officers can be assumed to have consented freely. The Xiang speaks of losing a ram because the position is inappropriate.

When Sun Quan governed Jiangdong, Lü Meng was already serving as a military officer, but battlefield experience could not replace knowledge of earlier political and military events. Lü Meng cited the pressure of military duties; Sun Quan nevertheless urged him to study historical accounts while continuing his work. The advice was meant to broaden a commander’s resources for judgment, not to make him resign his commission and specialize in classical scholarship.

According to the Jiangbiao Zhuan, quoted by Pei Songzhi in his annotations to the Records of the Three Kingdoms, Sun Quan encouraged Lü Meng to read in order to understand history and practical experience, not to become a scholar devoted exclusively to the classics. After Lü Meng followed this advice, his knowledge grew, and Lu Su’s assessment of him also changed.

Lü Meng began to read and later discussed affairs of state with Lu Su. Lu Su discovered that he could now address questions formerly unfamiliar to him and revised his opinion. What the historical account permits us to identify is encouragement to learn, acceptance of advice, and a change in a colleague’s judgment. Their meeting did not guarantee the outcome of every campaign Lü Meng would later undertake.

Sun Quan did not transfer Lü Meng’s military post to someone else: he wanted him to gain useful experience through reading while continuing his existing responsibilities. Lu Su’s later reaction came in conversation, not as the result of a single formal examination. Historical judgments concerning a figure’s growth coexist with the concrete military responsibilities that the person continued to shoulder.

206 Line H35 Jin The Sui–Tang Civil-Service Examinations — Progress Needs Workable Institutional Channels▶

During the Sui and Tang periods, governments gradually altered the way officials were selected. Literate candidates could gain opportunities for service through examinations, while recommendation and other recruitment routes continued. Families did not possess equal educational resources, and the creation of an examination route did not immediately place every applicant on equal footing.

Selection of officials through examinations developed progressively in the Sui and Tang periods. The jinshi examination and related categories became one possible route into office. They opened opportunities for some educated men, but family standing, access to education, recommendations, and other appointment routes remained important.

As the jinshi and other examinations developed, candidates had to prepare and sit for tests, and success did not itself dispense with further arrangements for appointment. Scholars disagree about precisely when the examination system began and when it became mature. Sui–Tang practices must not be conflated with all later examination rules. The route from taking an examination to securing office emerged gradually and was still affected by family background.

Before attempting an examination, an applicant needed literacy and access to learning; after passing, distribution of offices remained a separate issue. The jinshi examination supplied some scholars with a route upward, but did not immediately become the court’s only recruitment method. Later dynasties continued to revise examination rules, so Sui–Tang practice was not identical to the fully developed later system.

The gradually emerging civil-service examinations of the Sui and Tang offered some educated men a route toward office under institutional rules. Access to schooling and other channels of appointment remained unequal, so this cannot be described as a completely fair modern examination system. The Xiang associates receiving a substantial blessing with centered and upright conduct.

207 Line H35 Jin The 1949 Political Consultative Conference — Shared Endorsement Supports Political Action▶

In 1949, as a new central government was being formed, the participants needed to discuss governmental institutions, personnel, and principles of administration. With the military situation and control of local areas changing, a shared institutional document could tell participants which arrangements would serve as the basis for establishing the government.

The First Plenary Session of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference adopted the Common Program and addressed the organizational arrangements of the central government. The document set basic directions for state-building and political institutions, translating cooperation among participants into an institutional text for the establishment of the new government.

The document set directions for institutions and policies during the early years of the new state; government agencies still had to be established and put those directions into practice. Participation was confined to a particular political range: the conference was not a procedure in which all residents voted directly. Additional administrative and political work was needed between a conference resolution and the operation of local institutions according to its provisions.

Only after the Common Program was adopted did the new central institutions have a shared text on which to base the assignment of responsibilities. When delegates dispersed, the administrative work was just beginning: appointments, the issuance of orders, and the takeover of local administrations all had to be carried out by institutions. There was a time lag between adopting a document and having it followed in practice in every part of the country.

At the first plenary session of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference in 1949, participants adopted the Common Program and arranged central institutions. This illustrates political progress supported by agreement among those involved, not proof that every individual in the population consented. 208 Line H35 Jin Yuan Shikai’s Attempt to Restore Monarchy — Office without Legitimacy Creates Risk▶

After the establishment of the republic, Yuan Shikai held major positions in the central government, while relations with regional political forces remained complicated. In 1915 he pursued the restoration of monarchy, directly altering the republican designation of the state and the associated distribution of power. The enthusiasm of supporters could not ensure that the army, regional officials, or political parties would accept the proposed new regime.

In 1915 Yuan pressed ahead with replacing the republic by an imperial system, provoking political opposition and the National Protection War. Some forces that had formerly backed him ceased to cooperate; the monarchy was abandoned in 1916. Opponents launched the National Protection movement, and political protest was progressively accompanied by military fighting. Responses from different provinces reached the center at different times, and Yuan’s orders were not necessarily carried out as originally expected. Once the National Protection War began, political resistance also translated directly into troop movements.

The Xiang says not to worry excessively over loss and gain when benefit may follow.

After the victors founded a new regime, their accounts of the reasons for the uprising and of the war could also influence the records available to later generations. The measures to reduce princely fiefs initially concerned the central government's adjustment of princes' authority, but after Zhu Di raised troops, large armies and local communities bore the consequences. When Nanjing was taken, the Jianwen regime lost control and the new monarch began organizing the court. Several years of actual warfare separated that outcome from the original dispute over the princes' fiefs.

The Jingnan civil war emerged from conflicts over princely authority and culminated in Zhu Di’s accession after Nanjing fell in 1402. An internal succession dispute in Jin led Chong’er to leave his home state and travel among other rulers for years. Unable to rely directly on Jin’s administration, he and his followers needed each host to supply reception and basic resources before they could discuss political support.

After leaving Jin, Chong’er moved among several states and received varying degrees of hospitality and assistance. Ultimately, support from Qin enabled his return and accession in Jin. His experience illustrates the dependence of a political exile on hosts, followers, and outside resources.

Chong’er was treated differently in the places he visited and sometimes suffered neglect. Later assistance from Qin made his return possible, and he became Duke Wen of Jin. His accession followed a long period of exile; it was not assured on the day he departed. The choices of hosts, continued loyalty of his followers, and internal changes in Jin all influenced his return.

At every stop, the host determined the kind of welcome Chong’er would receive, while his followers had to decide whether to stay with him. No single refuge automatically guaranteed a successful return. Only when Qin provided support and conditions in Jin were favorable could he reenter his home state’s politics.

237 Line H40 Jie Yuan Shikai’s Monarchical Plan Provokes Opposition — Misalignment between Office and Conduct Breeds Opposition▶

九三｜

237 case_id: XCASE-H40-L3 | unit_id: XIANG-U-40-04 | original_event_id: E12 | grade: A | status: editorial_review

Historical event — full four-paragraph English translation

After the establishment of the republic, Yuan Shikai held major positions in the central government, while relations with regional political forces remained complicated. In 1915 he pursued the restoration of monarchy, directly altering the republican designation of the state and the associated distribution of power. The enthusiasm of supporters could not ensure that the army, regional officials, or political parties would accept the proposed new regime.

In 1915 Yuan pressed ahead with replacing the republic by an imperial system, provoking political opposition and the National Protection War. Some forces that had formerly backed him ceased to cooperate; the monarchy was abandoned in 1916. Concentrating authority in one person did not automatically create a stable base of political support.

Opponents launched the National Protection movement, and political protest was progressively accompanied by military fighting. Some regional forces that had worked with Yuan were no longer willing to cooperate, testing the central government’s control of the provinces. Yuan abolished the monarchy in 1916, but the underlying struggle over power did not disappear that same day. The path from preparations for enthronement, through public opposition, to the abolition of the monarchy involved successive shifts in political allegiance and pressure on the battlefield.

As supporters proposed the institutional change, regional officials still had to choose between the existing republican order and the proposed monarchy. Responses from different provinces reached the center at different times, and Yuan’s orders were not necessarily carried out as originally expected. Once the National Protection War began, political resistance also translated directly into troop movements.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Yuan Shikai’s 1915 imperial project provoked opposition and was cancelled in 1916. The episode warns that a mismatch between official position and conduct can provoke resistance. The Xiang’s image of bringing on conflict oneself does not eliminate the responsibilities of other participants.

Editorial review and revision limitations

Grade A: editorial suitability classification retained; it is not independent proof that historical actors used the Xiang text.

238 Line H40 Jie The Early Song Reorganizes Military Command — Remove Improper Attachments of Power▶

九四｜

238 case_id: XCASE-H40-L4 | unit_id: XIANG-U-40-05 | original_event_id: E16 | grade: A | status: editorial_review

Historical event — full four-paragraph English translation

After Emperor Taizu founded the Song dynasty, the court faced the problem of senior commanders holding too much military power. The new state's military foundations came from existing forces, and abruptly severing relations with their commanders could also disrupt the army's operations. The center therefore gradually adjusted appointments and command authority.

After establishing his government, Emperor Taizu progressively reorganized senior commanders' positions and the means by which armies were controlled, reducing the risk that generals with their own troops could set up independent power bases. Later generations often describe this as 'Relinquishing Military Command over a Cup of Wine,' but scholars differ on the banquet dialogue, its date, and the precise course of events.

Some generals left their former commands, and military authority was redistributed toward the center. Later writers called these changes 'Relinquishing Military Command over a Cup of Wine' and included conversations between sovereign and ministers in a banquet scene; the exact dialogue, timing, and historical sources remain disputed. The observable historical process was a change in offices and in methods of army control. There is no need to assume that every adjustment was settled in one evening. Once the new arrangements were established, the court still had to ensure that armies functioned under the new chain of command.

When commanders' positions changed, units still had to know which offices would issue their new orders. The court also had to arrange acceptable roles for those leaving their commands. Centralizing military authority thus involved more than reducing any individual's power; it also meant reconnecting the army's daily chain of command.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

After the Song dynasty was founded, Taizu gradually revised appointments and centralized military command to reduce the danger of independent forces. The case illustrates removing an inappropriate attachment of power. Details of the celebrated banquet and purported dialogue remain historically disputed.

Editorial review and revision limitations

Grade A: editorial suitability classification retained; it is not independent proof that historical actors used the Xiang text.

Translation verification: narrative paragraph structure aligned; complete independent sentence-level semantic approval pending.

239 Line H40 Jie Bao Zheng Opposes Zhang Yaozuo’s Advancement — Correcting Improper Appointments Reduces Abuse▶

九五｜

239 case_id: XCASE-H40-L5 | unit_id: XIANG-U-40-06 | original_event_id: E21 | grade: A | status: editorial_review

Historical event — full four-paragraph English translation

During the Northern Song reign of Emperor Renzong, Zhang Yaozuo gained promotion through family ties to the palace, drawing the attention of court officials. For remonstrance officials responsible for advising the throne, this was more than an individual change of office: it raised the question of whether appointments would be influenced by the relatives of imperial consorts.

Zhang Yaozuo’s rise through palace connections drew objections from Bao Zheng and other remonstrance officials. They presented memorials and argued with the court, asking the emperor to reconsider the appointment. The central issue is how officials attempted to place checks on the power to make personnel decisions.

Bao Zheng and others submitted memorials stating their objections and asking the emperor to reconsider Zhang Yaozuo’s appointments. The court disputed the respective roles of appointment authority and the right to remonstrate, and opinions were conveyed through formal documents and court audiences. This episode belonged to the procedure of appointing officials; it must not be recast as the fictional Judge Bao conducting a criminal trial of Zhang Yaozuo. The issues were who should hold office, on what grounds, and how the emperor should answer officials’ objections.

Remonstrance officials could not directly appoint or dismiss officials in the emperor’s place. They could submit opinions and continue making their case at court. Zhang Yaozuo’s appointments also have to be distinguished by post and date, rather than collapsing every dispute into a simple accusation that a palace relative was criminally guilty. What Bao Zheng left was a formal objection to a personnel decision.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Bao Zheng and other remonstrance officials objected to Zhang Yaozuo’s advancement through palace connections. Their petitions illustrate oversight of appointments and attempts to reduce improper advantage. Political opponents should not all be indiscriminately labeled “petty people.”

Editorial review and revision limitations

Grade A: editorial suitability classification retained; it is not independent proof that historical actors used the Xiang text.

Translation verification: narrative paragraph structure aligned; complete independent sentence-level semantic approval pending.

240 Line H40 Jie Qi Jiguang Recruits and Trains in Yiwu — Address the Actual Threat through Coordinated Training▶

上九｜

240 case_id: XCASE-H40-L6 | unit_id: XIANG-U-40-07 | original_event_id: E26 | grade: B | status: editorial_review

Historical event — full four-paragraph English translation

The southeastern coast of Ming China suffered raids by wokou forces, and local troops faced difficulties in recruiting men, training them, and fighting effectively. Qi Jiguang went to Yiwu to recruit soldiers who could maintain discipline and were willing to train. Individual courage alone could not ensure that the members of a unit would move in rhythm on the battlefield.

At Yiwu, Qi Jiguang stressed selection, discipline, and coordinated action. In campaigns against coastal raiders he employed formations and weapons designed to support one another. His military-training writings repeatedly stressed turning instruction into actions and standards that troops could actually carry out.

After being assigned to their units, the men practiced coordinating different weapons, positions, and movements. These arrangements were applied in campaigns against coastal raiders, and Qi also recorded training rules in his works. From recruitment and unit formation to drill, it took time for men to learn how to cover and support one another. Battlefield results also depended on terrain, supply, and the enemy; they cannot all be credited to a single formation with a memorable name.

If recruits never trained together in peacetime and first tried to cooperate only when they encountered an enemy, differences in weapon length and unit positions could interfere with one another. Qi required soldiers to drill repeatedly under a common set of rules so that battlefield commands had a practical foundation. The troops subsequently still had to adapt to changing opponents and conditions in different theaters.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Qi Jiguang’s Yiwu recruitment and coordinated training addressed practical threats along the Ming southeastern coast. The Xiang’s image of shooting a hawk may illustrate removing a specific danger. It must not be interpreted as endorsing assassination or unrestrained violence.

Editorial review and revision limitations

Grade B, partially suitable. The source case supports a limited retrospective analogy, not an exact one-to-one correspondence between the historical event and every image of the line. It is not evidence that historical participants used this classical text to make their choices. The original review calls for a single limited revision and recheck rather than rewriting the historical record.

241 Line H41 Sun Xiao He Supports the Chu–Han War from Guanzhong — Support a Shared Need▶

初九｜

241 case_id=XCASE-H41-L1 | hexagram_no=41 | line_no=1 | global_line_no=241 | event_id_original=E27 | final_grade=A | publication_status=editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English translation

Once the task is finished, go promptly: the intention remains shared.

Existing interpretation — English translation

Finish one’s own work and then go promptly to help, without blame; consider how much to reduce from oneself. The Xiang explains: the intentions remain aligned.

Historical event — four English narrative paragraphs

During the Chu–Han conflict, Liu Bang’s armies at the front continually needed provisions, funds, and new soldiers. Guanzhong, which lay under his control, offered a base for transporting resources and administering the population. If local administration stalled, any short-term success gained on the battlefield would be difficult to sustain.

During the struggle between Chu and Han, Xiao He largely remained in Guanzhong, administering population registers, provisions, and the replenishment of troops so that Liu Bang’s forces at the front could receive continued support. Historical records such as the Book of Han describe this rear-area work as an important condition allowing the Han armies to keep fighting.

Xiao He stayed in Guanzhong to manage local administration and send personnel and grain to the front. After each expenditure of military resources, the rear still had to mobilize and transport supplies anew. In discussing the Han victory, records including the Book of Han also mention Xiao He’s administrative and logistical work. These responsibilities do not appear in images of pitched battles, but they were carried out between one engagement and the next. Assessments of military merit could therefore extend beyond frontline commanders.

Replenishing soldiers was not simply a matter of writing a figure into a register. It required organizing men locally, securing provisions, and delivering them to the front. Xiao He’s administrative duties were directly connected to each new battlefield demand placed upon Liu Bang, leaving the Han with men and materiel to fight again after repeated engagements.

V4.3.1 amended line-specific comparison — English translation

During the Chu–Han war Xiao He stayed in Guanzhong to administer population registers, provisions, and troop replenishment, sustaining Liu Bang’s forces. The Book of Han and other histories recognize this rear-area contribution. The front repeatedly needed food and soldiers. Xiao He’s support may be compared to answering the common mission after completing one’s own work. Support requires reasonable division of labor and must not become unlimited sacrifice by one party. The Xiang says, “Once the task is finished, go promptly; the intention remains shared.” The focus is willingness to support a shared need.

Editorial decision / evidence limitations

242 Line H41 Sun Emperor Wen of Han Abolishes Land Rent — Maintain Principles While Reducing Burdens▶

九二｜

242 case_id=XCASE-H41-L2 | hexagram_no=41 | line_no=2 | global_line_no=242 | event_id_original=E41 | final_grade=A | publication_status=editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English translation

Constancy benefits the second nine: it takes the center as its aim.

Existing interpretation — English translation

It is favorable to remain steadfast; an expedition would be inauspicious. Do not diminish yourself, but benefit others. The Xiang explains: taking the center as one’s aim.

Historical event — four English narrative paragraphs

During Emperor Wen of Han’s reign, the court paid attention to agriculture and the burdens borne by the people. Farmers cultivated land and harvested crops, while the state collected revenue through land rent and other levies. In deciding to remove one category of collection, the court also had to consider the revenue the treasury would subsequently forgo.

The Basic Annals of Emperor Wen in the Records of the Grand Historian records that, in the thirteenth year of his reign, the emperor ordered the abolition of land rent out of concern for agriculture and the burdens of the people. The measure reduced one portion of state revenue derived from agricultural production, illustrating a ruler’s choice between fiscal receipts and public livelihood.

The Records of the Grand Historian records the order to abolish land rent in Emperor Wen’s thirteenth year. It concerned a particular revenue item levied on land; other taxes and labor obligations still existed in various localities. It would therefore be wrong to say that the state ceased collecting any resources from its people. Once the policy was announced, local officials had to adjust collection in accordance with the order before residents could experience the change. The measure and year are identifiable, but whether all farming households benefited equally requires further study.

Upon receiving the exemption order, local officials had to rearrange revenues previously expected from the land. Farm households consequently faced a lighter burden under that specific tax item. Whether they still owed other labor services or taxes must be examined separately. The scope of the policy should not be exaggerated simply because it used the word “exemption.”

V4.3.1 amended line-specific comparison — English translation

The Records of the Grand Historian states that Emperor Wen abolished land rent in his thirteenth year to ease farmers’ burdens. This reduced one source of state revenue and shows a choice between public finance and livelihood. The policy can be compared to reducing burdens without losing a stable direction of governance; its appropriateness still depends on fiscal and social conditions. The Xiang says, “Constancy benefits the second nine; the center is its aim.” The focus is stable principles when easing burdens.

Editorial decision / evidence limitations

Original case retained; no revision required. Final grade A.

243 Line H41 Sun Guan Zhong’s Setbacks and Bao Shu’s Recommendation — Understand Partners’ Circumstances▶

九三｜

243 case_id=XCASE-H41-L3 | hexagram_no=41 | line_no=3 | global_line_no=243 | event_id_original=replacement_pending | final_grade=B | publication_status=editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English translation

When one person goes alone, three give rise to doubt.

Existing interpretation — English translation

Three people traveling together lose one; one traveling alone gains a friend. The Xiang explains: three produce suspicion.

Historical event — four English narrative paragraphs

The “Biographies of Guan Zhong and Yan Ying” in the Records of the Grand Historian states that Guan Zhong befriended Bao Shuya when they were young and that they once conducted business together.

Guan Zhong later recalled that he had entered office three times and been dismissed three times, and had gone into battle three times and retreated three times. Bao Shu did not infer from those outcomes alone that Guan Zhong lacked ability or courage; he understood Guan Zhong’s circumstances.

After the faction of Prince Jiu, whom Guan Zhong served, was defeated, Guan Zhong was imprisoned. Bao Shu then recommended him after Prince Xiaobai became Duke Huan of Qi, enabling Guan Zhong to take up government responsibilities.

The account distinguishes repeated setbacks and the possibility of others’ suspicion from a trusted friend’s refusal to judge hastily. It is not a literal instance of “three companions causing doubt”; nor may Guan Zhong’s “three appointments” and “three battles” be equated with the three persons mentioned in the line text.

V4.3.1 amended line-specific comparison — English translation

Replace the broad slogan “three people together necessarily cause doubt” with a narrower interpretation: where several parties participate, judgments may differ, and the essential question is whether they understand one another’s circumstances. Guan Zhong’s three setbacks in office must not be mistaken for three persons traveling together.

Editorial decision / evidence limitations

Event replaced: Guan Zhong’s repeated dismissals and Bao Shu’s recognition and recommendation (Records of the Grand Historian). Final grade B; original Sun–Liu alliance case is archival.

Historical event — four English narrative paragraphs

When Zhuge Liang's first Northern Expedition reached Longyou, Jieting was an important location influencing subsequent operations. Ma Su was appointed to manage the local deployment; the main army's ability to maintain conditions for advancing was directly connected to the defense of Jieting.

During the first Northern Expedition, Ma Su lost Jieting. Zhuge Liang withdrew and submitted a memorial requesting his own demotion, acknowledging his poor judgment in appointments. In this self-demotion memorial, the commander tied the defeat to his responsibility for selecting personnel rather than blaming only subordinates at the front.

After Ma Su lost Jieting, Zhuge Liang withdrew his army instead of pressing ahead along the previous route. He memorialized the court asking to be demoted and admitted responsibility for his appointments. This was a public accounting to the court of the commander's judgment after military defeat; it must not be taken to eliminate other causes on the battlefield. The sequence of appointment, fighting at Jieting, withdrawal, and the self-demotion memorial is clear. The fictional Empty Fort Strategy is not part of this historically supported episode.

The loss at Jieting deprived later Shu deployments of support. Zhuge Liang's withdrawal did not restore the resources already expended. Assuming responsibility through a memorial was a political accounting to the court; the troops still had to leave the theater and rearrange their defenses in practice. Battlefield action and subsequent responsibility followed one another in this affair.
