Historical event — four English narrative paragraphs

A succession dispute broke out in Jin, and Chong’er left his home state and spent many years moving among other rulers’ territories. Without Jin’s administration to rely on, he and his companions first had to obtain hospitality and the means of subsistence at each stop before they could discuss political support.

After leaving Jin, Chong’er passed through several states and received varying degrees of hospitality and assistance. He eventually returned to Jin and took the throne with Qin’s support. His experience shows how an exiled political figure depended on hosts, attendants, and outside resources.

Chong’er received unequal assistance in different states and at times met with neglect. Later Qin supported his return, allowing him to become Duke Wen of Jin. His accession resulted from a long exile; it was not guaranteed on the day he left home. The choices of hosts, his followers’ willingness to remain with him, and changes within Jin all affected whether he could return.

At each state, the host determined how an exile would be received, while Chong’er’s companions had to decide whether to continue with him. No single stop automatically meant a successful return. Only when Qin provided assistance and conditions in Jin were favorable did he gain an opportunity to reenter his state’s political affairs.

V4.3.1 amended line-specific comparison — English translation

Identifiable choices, constraints, and consequences allow only a limited comparison with the Xiang, “Great good fortune for the fifth six; aid comes from above.” The event does not cover all the line’s images. 246 case_id=XCASE-H41-L6 | hexagram_no=41 | line_no=6 | global_line_no=246 | event_id_original=E48 | final_grade=A | publication_status=editorial_review

Historical event — four English narrative paragraphs

When Qin governed the Shu region, agriculture on the Chengdu Plain needed a dependable water supply and had to contend with changes in the Min River’s flow and channels. The tradition of Li Bing’s water-control work is associated with the early Dujiangyan works; local officials needed to lead river water onto land that could be irrigated.

The establishment of Dujiangyan is linked to Qin governance in Shu and the tradition of Li Bing’s hydraulic engineering. Diversion and distribution works improved water availability on the Chengdu Plain, and the system continued to depend on maintenance by later generations. Public resources cannot simply be left unattended after the initial construction.

Diversion and water distribution improved irrigation, but subsequent generations continued to repair and adjust the works. Channels carried sediment, while irrigation allocations had to be managed; the structures could not operate indefinitely without supervision. The Dujiangyan visible today reflects reconstruction over a long period and cannot all be attributed to one person working on one occasion. From initial building to irrigation and maintenance, this public work extended across many generations and remained connected to local agriculture.

The Min River supplied water for irrigation but also continually changed its course and sediment deposits. To keep the system working, local communities needed regular maintenance and arrangements for water withdrawals, so fields would benefit beyond the first years of construction. Craftsmen and administrators from different periods together sustained the works that remain visible today.

V4.3.1 amended line-specific comparison — English translation

Dujiangyan arose in connection with Qin administration in Shu and Li Bing’s hydraulic-engineering tradition. Its diversion and irrigation works improved water supplies on the Chengdu Plain but required maintenance in later generations. Qin-era agriculture faced changing flows of the Min River. The works can be compared to increasing common resources, not merely redistributing them; construction and maintenance were not cost-free. The Xiang says, “Increase it without diminishing; the great aspiration is achieved.” The focus is infrastructure that benefits the community.

Historical event — four English narrative paragraphs

Cao Cao's southward advance rapidly changed the situation in Jingzhou, and Liu Bei and Sun Quan each faced a threat from the northern forces. Lu Su, Zhuge Liang, and others took part in talks that brought about cooperation between Sun Quan and Liu Bei. Before the coalition formed, envoys had to establish whether both parties would jointly resist Cao's army. Afterward, the two sides had to coordinate while retaining their separate forces. 249 Line H42 Yi Major Red Army Losses at the Xiang River — Seek Improvement after Loss▶

At the beginning of the Long March, the Central Red Army moved toward the Xiang River, with blocking forces ahead and pursuers behind. Crossing required units to pass in sequence while dealing with supplies and accompanying personnel. The river itself was a physical obstacle the operation had to overcome.

During the Long March, the Central Red Army encountered blocking forces in the Xiang River region and suffered major personnel and organizational losses while crossing. Research discusses the burdens of the march, route selection, and command problems, while warning that troop-loss figures calculated using different definitions cannot simply be conflated.

The Xiang River fighting inflicted severe casualties and organizational losses. Some who crossed continued marching, and the force gradually reassessed its early marching and command practices. Sources differ in their starting and ending dates and in whom they count as losses; all losses during the early Long March cannot be attributed to this single battle. There were real crossing points and human costs, which need not be recast as elegant abstractions about sacrifice.

The army needed not only to cross the Xiang River but also to leave passages for units following behind. Some formations paid a heavy price while covering others. Sun Yat-sen assumed the provisional presidency in Nanjing on January 1, 1912. The government established offices and published policy proclamations. During negotiations between north and south, the new government’s personnel and distribution of authority continued to change. The inauguration has a clear date, but making a new administration capable of enforcing orders across regions required separate financial and political support.

The Nanjing provisional government had to turn the personal and military relationships of the revolutionary period into offices, assigned duties, and official correspondence. During Emperor Wen of Han’s reign, the court paid attention to agriculture and the burdens borne by the people. Farmers cultivated land and harvested crops, while the state collected revenue through land rent and other levies. In deciding to remove one category of collection, the court also had to consider the revenue the treasury would subsequently forgo.

The Basic Annals of Emperor Wen in the Records of the Grand Historian records that, in the thirteenth year of his reign, the emperor ordered the abolition of land rent out of concern for agriculture and the burdens of the people. The measure reduced one portion of state revenue derived from agricultural production, illustrating a ruler’s choice between fiscal receipts and public livelihood.

The Records of the Grand Historian records the order to abolish land rent in Emperor Wen’s thirteenth year. It concerned a particular revenue item levied on land; other taxes and labor obligations still existed in various localities. It would therefore be wrong to say that the state ceased collecting any resources from its people. Once the policy was announced, local officials had to adjust collection in accordance with the order before residents could experience the change. The measure and year are identifiable, but whether all farming households benefited equally requires further study.

Upon receiving the exemption order, local officials had to rearrange revenues previously expected from the land. Farm households consequently faced a lighter burden under that specific tax item. Whether they still owed other labor services or taxes must be examined separately. The scope of the policy should not be exaggerated simply because it used the word “exemption.”

After a republic was established in name in the early Republic of China, the distribution of power among the president, cabinet, parliament, and political parties remained disputed. The gate guards’ verification of arrivals, the carriage’s speed inside the camp, and Zhou Yafu’s reception of the emperor were details observed in succession during this visit. Zhang Yaozuo’s rise through palace connections drew objections from Bao Zheng and other remonstrance officials. Remonstrance officials could not directly appoint or dismiss officials in the emperor’s place. They could submit opinions and continue making their case at court. After establishing his government, Emperor Taizu progressively reorganized senior commanders' positions and the means by which armies were controlled, reducing the risk that generals with their own troops could set up independent power bases. Once the new arrangements were established, the court still had to ensure that armies functioned under the new chain of command.

When commanders' positions changed, units still had to know which offices would issue their new orders. The court also had to arrange acceptable roles for those leaving their commands. After the Qin dynasty collapsed, Liu Bang entered Guanzhong before Xiang Yu, arousing suspicion among Xiang Yu’s followers. The two leaders had previously belonged to forces opposing Qin, but now competed over who would command territory and armies. Liu Bang went to Xiang Yu’s camp at Hongmen for a banquet that was also a hazardous political negotiation.

According to the Records of the Grand Historian, Liu Bang and Xiang Yu came into conflict after the Qin collapse. Liu Bang attended negotiations at Hongmen, where tensions mounted during the banquet, and later departed. The account shows how information, intermediaries, and judgment in the moment could shape a political meeting between parties of unequal power.

The Records of the Grand Historian describes people at the banquet urging action against Liu Bang, while others carried messages between the two sides. Liu Bang found a way to leave, arranging for his companions to respond afterward, and ultimately escaped Xiang Yu’s camp. The meeting avoided his immediate death at the banquet, but the contest for power following Qin’s fall went on. Dialogues in historical biographies were shaped by their historians and should not be treated as word-for-word transcripts from that evening. Attendance, negotiation, and departure are the main stages of the narrative.

Suspicion between the two groups had formed before the banquet, and Liu Bang could not fully control others’ actions once he entered Xiang Yu’s camp. Messengers and intermediaries influenced the proceedings, and someone still had to respond after he left. His escape dealt only with the immediate danger; it did not end the subsequent struggle between the two sides.

Attendance, negotiation, and departure at the Feast of Hongmen show constrained choices about advancing or withdrawing; events could not proceed entirely according to one party’s wishes. The history lacks actions exactly matching the images of “buttocks without skin” and “halting progress,” so it is only a limited analogy for cautious advance.

Historical texts describe the palace’s splendor and labor costs, and Emperor Wen’s displeasure after seeing it. His reaction came after construction and could not undo labor already requisitioned. Historical event — four English narrative paragraphs

The establishment of Dujiangyan is linked to Qin governance in Shu and the tradition of Li Bing’s hydraulic engineering. Diversion and distribution works improved water availability on the Chengdu Plain, and the system continued to depend on maintenance by later generations. Public resources cannot simply be left unattended after the initial construction.

Diversion and water distribution improved irrigation, but subsequent generations continued to repair and adjust the works. Channels carried sediment, while irrigation allocations had to be managed; the structures could not operate indefinitely without supervision. The Dujiangyan visible today reflects reconstruction over a long period and cannot all be attributed to one person working on one occasion. From initial building to irrigation and maintenance, this public work extended across many generations and remained connected to local agriculture.

The Min River supplied water for irrigation but also continually changed its course and sediment deposits. To keep the system working, local communities needed regular maintenance and arrangements for water withdrawals, so fields would benefit beyond the first years of construction. Craftsmen and administrators from different periods together sustained the works that remain visible today.

To keep the system working, local communities needed regular maintenance and arrangements for water withdrawals, so fields would benefit beyond the first years of construction. Craftsmen and administrators from different periods together sustained the works that remain visible today.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Dujiangyan’s diversion and irrigation systems improved water supply and required maintenance across generations. Their continued public benefit can illustrate the ideal of a resource successfully made available to many. This does not mean every era was free of disputes over management or unequal distribution. The Xiang describes supreme good fortune at the top as great accomplishment; the focus is keeping shared resources useful over time.

Editorial decision and evidence limitations

Final grade A. The original case is retained; no change to the historical event was required.

Binding with yellow oxhide means that one cannot yet undertake action.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

In 1906, the Qing court announced preparations for constitutional government in response to demands for reform. Advocates hoped for gradual political opening, while the imperial family sought to retain control. They differed on timing and the powers of new bodies.

The court announced preparatory measures and created consultative institutions. Delays, retained imperial authority, and the composition of the 1911 cabinet disappointed constitutional advocates and damaged their trust.

The new assemblies gave constitutional advocates places to participate, but they continued assessing whether the throne would surrender substantial power. The 1911 cabinet appointments made earlier promises and current practice directly comparable. Distrust did not emerge overnight.

290 Line H49 Ge The 1911 Revolution Ends Qing Rule — Change Requires a Viable Moment▶

九二｜

290 case_id=XCASE-H49-L2 | hexagram_no=49 | line_no=2 | global_line_no=290 | original_event_id=E49 | final_grade=A | publication_status=editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English rendering

Reforming on the appointed day means that action can bring a favorable result.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

After the Wuchang Uprising of 1911, several provinces announced their separation from the Qing court. Rebels, local troops, and political figures did not all seek identical outcomes, but the existing Qing network of authority was already under pressure. Fighting and negotiations between north and south proceeded concurrently, raising questions about the future of the monarchy and representation of central power.

After Wuchang, multiple provinces broke with the Qing court, while military conflict and north–south negotiations shaped the political settlement. In 1912 the Qing emperor abdicated, and a republic replaced the monarchical system. Many actors contributed to the change; neither one leader nor one uprising completed it alone.

The emperor’s abdication in 1912 marked an identifiable institutional turning point. Questions about the incorporation of troops, provinces, and finances into the new administration still required negotiation. From the initial uprising to the provinces’ responses and the north–south settlement, no single city or individual accomplished the entire transformation. Winning a military revolution and sustaining republican institutions were separate tasks.

Following abdication, officials and soldiers formerly loyal to Qing had to decide how to function in the new arrangements. Negotiations resolved the question of the imperial title but could not instantly establish fiscal and military rules for every province. The republican government still had to negotiate with local authorities after the change of regime.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The Wuchang Uprising, provincial separations, north–south negotiations, and the Qing emperor’s abdication show that political change depended on interacting forces and a workable moment. The “appointed day” in the line is not a date that can be mapped predictively onto the Gregorian calendar.

Suitability review and evidence limitations

Final suitability grade A. The historical event is retained; the comparison remains a retrospective editorial interpretation, not evidence that the historical actors invoked the Xiang text.

291 Line H49 Ge Shang Yang Reforms Qin Institutions — Major Reform Requires Deliberation▶

291 case_id=XCASE-H49-L3 | hexagram_no=49 | line_no=3 | global_line_no=291 | original_event_id=E18 | final_grade=B | publication_status=editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English rendering

When words of reform have been discussed three times, where else need one go?

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

During the reign of Duke Xiao, Qin faced competition among the states and needed to manage land, population, and soldiers more effectively. Once appointed, Shang Yang proposed a series of new laws affecting household registration, taxation and labor service, rewards for military merit, and local administration. As rules moved from the court into villages and armies, established interests and everyday arrangements were disrupted.

Duke Xiao employed Shang Yang to change systems of registration, levies, military rewards, and administration, strengthening Qin’s capacity to mobilize resources. The reforms challenged entrenched interests and employed severe punishments. They contributed to state power but also imposed social burdens and political coercion.

Local officials registered residents and collected levies under the new laws, while rewards for military merit changed soldiers’ paths to advancement. Qin’s mobilization capacity grew, but harsh penalties and methods of enforcement also imposed costs. After Duke Xiao died, Shang Yang lost his political patron and was executed, although some institutions endured. The state’s trajectory and the reformer’s personal fate did not follow the same course.

Once the new laws were promulgated, existing kinship ties, farming practices, and obligations to serve were subject to new rules. Qin’s greater ability to mobilize in interstate competition was a state-level outcome; the punishments and requisitions experienced by individual residents require separate examination in the context of daily implementation.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The policy debate and implementation surrounding Shang Yang’s reforms suggest the need to explain major changes and test their conditions. The line’s “three times” does not authorize inventing three recorded formal votes. Reform brought both state capacity and coercive costs.

Suitability review and evidence limitations

The great person changes like a tiger; the pattern becomes brilliant.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

After the 1911 Revolution, the southern provinces needed an authority that could represent the republic externally and administer government business internally. Establishing a government required more than announcing political objectives: officials had to handle departmental responsibilities, finances, and military orders. Nanjing became the seat of the provisional government, although the new regime’s effective control remained geographically limited.

The provisional government established agencies and issued statements of policy, attempting to turn the revolution’s political objectives into everyday administration. Its finances and ability to exercise effective control throughout the country nevertheless remained limited.

Sun Yat-sen assumed the provisional presidency in Nanjing on January 1, 1912. The government established offices and published policy proclamations. Officials began working under new titles while still confronting the Qing court and military forces in other regions. During negotiations between north and south, the new government’s personnel and distribution of authority continued to change. The inauguration has a clear date, but making a new administration capable of enforcing orders across regions required separate financial and political support.

The Nanjing provisional government had to turn the personal and military relationships of the revolutionary period into offices, assigned duties, and official correspondence. Although provinces had declared support for a republic, they did not necessarily surrender control of tax revenues or military command at the same time. Following Sun Yat-sen’s inauguration, provisional agencies continued to conduct daily affairs under these constraints.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

296 Line H50 Ding Xiao He Sustains the Chu–Han War from Guanzhong — Substantial Resources Still Require Judgement▶

Xiang commentary — English rendering

When the cauldron has substance, one must be careful where one goes; although an adversary is ill, there will ultimately be no blame.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

During the Chu–Han conflict, Liu Bang’s armies at the front continually needed provisions, funds, and new soldiers. Guanzhong, which lay under his control, offered a base for transporting resources and administering the population. If local administration stalled, any short-term success gained on the battlefield would be difficult to sustain.

During the struggle between Chu and Han, Xiao He largely remained in Guanzhong, administering population registers, provisions, and the replenishment of troops so that Liu Bang’s forces at the front could receive continued support. Historical records such as the Book of Han describe this rear-area work as an important condition allowing the Han armies to keep fighting.

Xiao He stayed in Guanzhong to manage local administration and send personnel and grain to the front. After each expenditure of military resources, the rear still had to mobilize and transport supplies anew. In discussing the Han victory, records including the Book of Han also mention Xiao He’s administrative and logistical work. These responsibilities do not appear in images of pitched battles, but they were carried out between one engagement and the next. Assessments of military merit could therefore extend beyond frontline commanders.

Replenishing soldiers was not simply a matter of writing a figure into a register. It required organizing men locally, securing provisions, and delivering them to the front. Xiao He’s administrative duties were directly connected to each new battlefield demand placed upon Liu Bang, leaving the Han with men and materiel to fight again after repeated engagements.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

Xiao He’s administration of Guanzhong supplied the personnel and provisions sustaining Liu Bang’s forces. The analogy is to a cauldron containing real substance that must be used carefully; abundant resources alone cannot replace sound strategic judgement.

298 Line H50 Ding The Tumu Crisis Exposes Vulnerable Campaign Planning — An Unbearable Burden Can Harm the Public▶

九四｜

298 case_id=XCASE-H50-L4 | hexagram_no=50 | line_no=4 | global_line_no=298 | original_event_id=E23 | final_grade=A | publication_status=editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English rendering

Spilling the lord’s food raises the question of how trust can be maintained.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

In 1449, the Ming emperor Yingzong personally led troops north against the Oirats. A vast marching force required coordination of provisions, transport, and orders. Neither the advance northward nor the return journey could succeed on troop numbers alone. If deployments during the return were obstructed, losses at the front could directly affect the central government.

Emperor Yingzong led the army north against the Oirats, but during the return it suffered a devastating defeat near Tumu and the emperor was captured. The court faced a severe crisis. The episode involved decisions, movement, logistics, and command, and the defense of Beijing subsequently had to be reorganized.

The Ming army was struck heavily near Tumu and Yingzong was captured. On receiving the news, officials in Beijing had to reorganize military defense and affairs connected with the imperial succession to prevent a battlefield defeat from spreading into a wider catastrophe. Historical sources differ on troop numbers and the responsibility of some individuals, but the sequence is clear: departure on campaign, difficulties on the return, capture of the emperor, and emergency measures in the capital. Beijing’s defense had to begin while the emperor was still a prisoner.

The capture of the emperor immediately had consequences beyond an ordinary military retreat. Officials had to decide how the court would continue to exercise authority, and troops defending the city needed to know whose orders to follow. The capital’s emergency defense was organized with incomplete information from the front. Information carried from the Tumu battlefield to the capital tightly linked the military disaster to political decisions in Beijing.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The catastrophic defeat at Tumu and the capture of Emperor Yingzong illustrate how inadequate arrangements for a great responsibility can harm the wider polity. The spilled food in the line is a metaphor for public responsibility, not an actual accident involving a vessel during the campaign.

300 Line H50 Ding The Song–Liao Chanyuan Treaty Ends the Immediate War — Durable Settlements Balance Strength and Restraint▶

300 case_id=XCASE-H50-L6 | hexagram_no=50 | line_no=6 | global_line_no=300 | original_event_id=E06 | final_grade=B | publication_status=editorial_review

The jade carrying-ring above represents restraint that balances firmness and yielding.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

After Liao forces marched south, the Song court had to decide whether fighting on the frontier should expand further. Emperor Zhenzong reached Chanzhou, confronting decision-makers directly with conditions at the front and enabling envoys from both states to travel back and forth over ceasefire terms. Both Song and Liao possessed military forces; neither could dispense with subsequent practical arrangements simply by saying that the two sides were now reconciled.

After the Liao advance and Emperor Zhenzong’s arrival at Chanzhou, negotiations led to the Treaty of Chanyuan in 1005. Song undertook to provide annual payments to Liao, while each government retained its authority and an established order along the frontier. The arrangement carried a fiscal cost, but it also reduced large-scale warfare for a considerable period thereafter.

The negotiations culminated in the Treaty of Chanyuan: both states kept their own governments and Song undertook annual payments. After the agreement, the major campaign then under way ceased and the border had a framework both sides could invoke; the annual payments simultaneously became a recurring item of court expenditure. Warfare on a comparable scale was avoided for a long period, but diplomatic negotiations and frontier friction did not vanish. Military and fiscal consequences of the treaty both persisted.

The treaty settled the immediate fighting and also provided agreed terms that subsequent envoys could cite. Once the armies halted their advance, the court still had to prepare the annual payments on schedule; people in frontier communities meanwhile lived under the new arrangements. The direct benefits of the ceasefire and the continuing costs were not the same for every participant.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The Chanyuan Treaty combined military confrontation, negotiation, and sustained implementation. It can illustrate a measured balance between strength and accommodation; it does not imply that concessions alone invariably preserve peace.

301 Line H51 Zhen The July 7 Incident Escalates the War Crisis — Establish Order after a Shock▶

初九｜

301 case_id=XCASE-H51-L1 | hexagram_no=51 | line_no=1 | global_line_no=301 | original_event_id=E51 | final_grade=B | publication_status=editorial_review

Xiang commentary — English rendering

Thunder comes with fear, which may bring good fortune through caution; laughter follows when proper order is established.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

In July 1937, Japanese troops and Chinese defenders clashed around the Marco Polo Bridge and Wanping. Relations between China and Japan had already been tense for years. Local forces in northern China had to respond immediately to attacks and maintain communications, while a further expansion of fighting threatened other regions.

He waited until the enemy encountered difficulties obtaining provisions and then exploited the moment of its retreat. Liang meanwhile endured pressure, making this deployment politically contentious.

Zhou Yafu maintained his own positions while dispatching other forces to interrupt the Wu–Chu supply routes. The danger facing Liang did not disappear, and Zhou was criticized politically for failing to come to its immediate rescue. Only after the enemy’s provisions were disrupted and its offensive became unsustainable did he strike during its withdrawal. Both the victory over the rebels and the risks borne by Liang belong to the outcome. This campaign illustrates how interference with supplies in the rear could alter conditions on the battlefield.

Zhou Yafu’s decision meant that Liang could not immediately receive comprehensive support, much to the displeasure of the Liang court. At the same time, the Han army still had to defend its own positions and prevent the enemy from readily redirecting its attack. Cutting supply lines was not passive observation: it was intended to make the offensive previously sustainable for the Wu–Chu forces progressively harder to maintain.

The document set out aims concerning peaceful nation-building, but the fundamental questions of military forces and local authority remained unsettled. After publication, disputes over effective control and military clashes continued to develop. Talks, an agreed text, and the implementation of that text are three related stages that do not take place simultaneously. Issuing the agreement must not be described as if peace had already been secured.

What could be written at the negotiating table did not necessarily correspond to territories already controlled by the respective armies. After representatives published the agreement, their organizations still had to communicate the commitments internally and decide whether to implement them. The difficulty of sustaining peace after the war must also be understood through the sequence of, and gaps between, these practical actions.

The Chongqing negotiations produced written commitments concerning peace and reconstruction while leaving important military and local-government questions unresolved. This illustrates measured and responsible speech; the agreement still required mechanisms for implementation and oversight.

Establishing a military demarcation line did not settle every territorial or sovereignty dispute. The armistice thus had a distinct practical achievement and equally distinct limits.

Historical event — complete four-paragraph narrative

During the Sui and Tang periods, the selection of officials gradually changed. Scholars could seek appointment through examinations, while recommendations and other routes continued. Families had unequal access to education; a new system did not immediately give everyone an equal starting point.

Examination-based selection developed gradually; categories such as the jinshi became routes into official service. Opportunities expanded for some scholars, but family background, education, recommendations, and other routes remained important.

Candidates prepared and sat examinations, but passing still required subsequent appointment. Historians differ about when the system began or matured. Sui–Tang practices should not be equated with every later examination rule; access to office remained shaped by family conditions.

Candidates needed literacy and opportunities to study, and successful candidates still needed positions. Examinations were not immediately the only recruitment method. Rules changed across dynasties, so Sui–Tang arrangements were not identical to the later mature system.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial translation

The Sui–Tang examinations offered some scholars new routes into office, while unequal education, family background, and other channels remained influential. This illustrates the risks faced by beginners, not proof that every hardship was undeserved or that all entrants had identical experiences.

He had to weigh both Liang’s immediate peril and the supply situation of the principal rebel army. If the Han army reacted immediately to every enemy movement, it might be forced to fight under conditions chosen by its opponent.

After the rebellion began, Zhou Yafu did not constantly seek a direct, decisive engagement. He held his position and sent troops to cut the Wu–Chu army’s supply lines. He waited until the enemy encountered difficulties obtaining provisions and then exploited the moment of its retreat. Liang meanwhile endured pressure, making this deployment politically contentious.

Zhou Yafu maintained his own positions while dispatching other forces to interrupt the Wu–Chu supply routes. The danger facing Liang did not disappear, and Zhou was criticized politically for failing to come to its immediate rescue. Only after the enemy’s provisions were disrupted and its offensive became unsustainable did he strike during its withdrawal. Both the victory over the rebels and the risks borne by Liang belong to the outcome. This campaign illustrates how interference with supplies in the rear could alter conditions on the battlefield.

Zhou Yafu’s decision meant that Liang could not immediately receive comprehensive support, much to the displeasure of the Liang court. At the same time, the Han army still had to defend its own positions and prevent the enemy from readily redirecting its attack. Cutting supply lines was not passive observation: it was intended to make the offensive previously sustainable for the Wu–Chu forces progressively harder to maintain.

Zhou Yafu waited rather than immediately attack during the Rebellion of the Seven States, choosing a supply-line strategy. His delay was purposeful and conditional, not a general rule that postponement is always best.

Xiao He’s administrative duties were directly connected to each new battlefield demand placed upon Liu Bang, leaving the Han with men and materiel to fight again after repeated engagements.

Whether fighting began would affect the disposition of the troops and the losses that residents and buildings might suffer.

During the Pingjin campaign, Fu Zuoyi’s representatives negotiated with the People’s Liberation Army. The Beiping garrison agreed to leave the city and undergo reorganization, and authority was transferred in January 1949. The arrangement reduced the destruction that large-scale fighting within the city might have caused, but the negotiations took place under unmistakable military pressure.

The two sides negotiated how the defending troops would leave, be reorganized, and hand over the city. Fu’s side accepted an agreement, and the main transfer of authority in Beiping was completed in January 1949 without a large-scale urban battle. Negotiations were driven by substantial military pressure; they should not be described as an unconditional, friendly reconciliation. Encirclement, agreement on the troops’ future, and actual takeover formed successive stages of implementation.

Once the garrison accepted reorganization, troops had to leave their former positions as agreed, while the incoming authorities had to keep transportation, public order, and government offices functioning. One meeting could not replace these concrete handover tasks. Arrangements for the troops’ movements and the sequence of entry helped prevent the large-scale fighting within Beiping that might otherwise have occurred.

The negotiated transfer of Beiping illustrates seeking alternatives before destruction expands. Its outcome depended on a particular military balance and cannot simply be replicated in every besieged city.

Once the garrison accepted reorganization, troops had to leave their former positions as agreed, while the incoming authorities had to keep transportation, public order, and government offices functioning. One meeting could not replace these concrete handover tasks. Arrangements for the troops’ movements and the sequence of entry helped prevent the large-scale fighting within Beiping that might otherwise have occurred.

Xiang interpretation — editorial English

Distinguish What Can and Cannot Be Done. This is a retrospective interpretive lesson; the classical wording is preserved in the bilingual verification file.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

In 154 BCE, seven kingdoms raised forces against the Han, and the armies of Wu and Chu advanced, leaving the kingdom of Liang in urgent need of relief. The court sent Zhou Yafu to command its army. He had to weigh both Liang’s immediate peril and the supply situation of the principal rebel army. If the Han army reacted immediately to every enemy movement, it might be forced to fight under conditions chosen by its opponent.

After the rebellion began, Zhou Yafu did not constantly seek a direct, decisive engagement. He held his position and sent troops to cut the Wu–Chu army’s supply lines. He waited until the enemy encountered difficulties obtaining provisions and then exploited the moment of its retreat. Liang meanwhile endured pressure, making this deployment politically contentious.

Zhou Yafu maintained his own positions while dispatching other forces to interrupt the Wu–Chu supply routes. The danger facing Liang did not disappear, and Zhou was criticized politically for failing to come to its immediate rescue. Only after the enemy’s provisions were disrupted and its offensive became unsustainable did he strike during its withdrawal. Both the victory over the rebels and the risks borne by Liang belong to the outcome. This campaign illustrates how interference with supplies in the rear could alter conditions on the battlefield.

Zhou Yafu’s decision meant that Liang could not immediately receive comprehensive support, much to the displeasure of the Liang court. At the same time, the Han army still had to defend its own positions and prevent the enemy from readily redirecting its attack. Cutting supply lines was not passive observation: it was intended to make the offensive previously sustainable for the Wu–Chu forces progressively harder to maintain.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial rendering

Zhou Yafu’s deliberate deployment illustrates recognizing when an advance is inadvisable. The value lay in judgment and timing, not in immobility for its own sake.

The Records of the Grand Historian recounts that when Emperor Wen inspected Zhou Yafu’s Xiliu camp, he could not enter directly as he had at other camps, but had to follow the camp’s notification procedures. After entering, his carriage also observed the rule against traveling quickly. The emperor consequently acknowledged Zhou Yafu’s ability to command troops.

After notice was given, the carriage entered Xiliu and proceeded slowly as the military orders required. Zhou Yafu received the emperor with military courtesies, and after leaving Emperor Wen praised the army’s discipline. The Records of the Grand Historian sets out the sequence of the gate, notification, speed of the carriage, and meeting, as well as the emperor’s assessment in comparison with other camps. The gate guards’ verification of arrivals, the carriage’s speed inside the camp, and Zhou Yafu’s reception of the emperor were details observed in succession during this visit. If only Emperor Wen’s final words of praise are retained, the different procedures he encountered at Xiliu before speaking those words become invisible.

359 Line H60 Jie Taiwan Ends the Period of National Mobilization in 1991 — Limit Extraordinary Powers and Restore Normality▶

九五｜

359 case_id=XCASE-H60-L5 | hexagram_no=60 | line_no=5 | global_line_no=359 | original_event_id=E60 | final_grade=B | publication_status=editorial_review

Xiang interpretation — editorial English

Limit Extraordinary Powers and Restore Normality. This is a retrospective interpretive lesson; the classical wording is preserved in the bilingual verification file.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

After the government of the Republic of China relocated to Taiwan, the Period of National Mobilization for Suppression of the Communist Rebellion and the Temporary Provisions continued to affect the powers of central institutions for many years. As Taiwan’s political environment changed, whether the old emergency arrangements should continue became a question that constitutional reform had to address.

In 1991 the President of the Republic of China announced that the Period of National Mobilization for Suppression of the Communist Rebellion would end on May 1, and the relevant Temporary Provisions were abolished. This was one step in Taiwan’s constitutional reform, ending part of the emergency-period framework while requiring further institutional adjustment.

The presidential announcement set May 1, 1991 as the end of the mobilization period, and the Temporary Provisions were repealed. Leaving the emergency framework also required later constitutional amendments and institutional changes to establish new distributions of authority. This was a separate milestone from the lifting of martial law in 1987; neither did the 1991 announcement complete every democratic reform on a single day. The sequence ran from long application to formal repeal and then further institutional change.

After repeal of the Temporary Provisions, central powers formerly exercised under emergency arrangements had to be redefined within a new constitutional framework. Subsequent elections and amendments had their own timetables and procedures. The announcement had a definite date, but the implementation of reform could not all be compressed into May 1.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial rendering

The 1991 end of the mobilization period illustrates the adjustment of exceptional powers and a return toward constitutional normality. It did not complete every democratic reform in one act.

Suitability and source limitations

Allied forces resisted Cao's army at Red Cliffs, but after the battle each side continued to consider its own territory and interests. The alliance was not free from friction thereafter.

Zhang Yaozuo’s rise through palace connections drew objections from Bao Zheng and other remonstrance officials. They presented memorials and argued with the court, asking the emperor to reconsider the appointment. The central issue is how officials attempted to place checks on the power to make personnel decisions.

Bao Zheng and others submitted memorials stating their objections and asking the emperor to reconsider Zhang Yaozuo’s appointments. The court disputed the respective roles of appointment authority and the right to remonstrate, and opinions were conveyed through formal documents and court audiences. This episode belonged to the procedure of appointing officials; it must not be recast as the fictional Judge Bao conducting a criminal trial of Zhang Yaozuo. The issues were who should hold office, on what grounds, and how the emperor should answer officials’ objections.

Remonstrance officials could not directly appoint or dismiss officials in the emperor’s place. They could submit opinions and continue making their case at court. Zhang Yaozuo’s appointments also have to be distinguished by post and date, rather than collapsing every dispute into a simple accusation that a palace relative was criminally guilty. He had to weigh both Liang’s immediate peril and the supply situation of the principal rebel army. If the Han army reacted immediately to every enemy movement, it might be forced to fight under conditions chosen by its opponent.

Liang meanwhile endured pressure, making this deployment politically contentious.

Zhou Yafu maintained his own positions while dispatching other forces to interrupt the Wu–Chu supply routes. The danger facing Liang did not disappear, and Zhou was criticized politically for failing to come to its immediate rescue. Only after the enemy’s provisions were disrupted and its offensive became unsustainable did he strike during its withdrawal. Both the victory over the rebels and the risks borne by Liang belong to the outcome. This campaign illustrates how interference with supplies in the rear could alter conditions on the battlefield.

Zhou Yafu’s decision meant that Liang could not immediately receive comprehensive support, much to the displeasure of the Liang court. At the same time, the Han army still had to defend its own positions and prevent the enemy from readily redirecting its attack. Cutting supply lines was not passive observation: it was intended to make the offensive previously sustainable for the Wu–Chu forces progressively harder to maintain.

His extensive realm could mobilize armies, but forces drawn from different backgrounds still had to act together during a distant expedition. Eastern Jin faced the pressure of a powerful advance in the Huai River and Yangtze regions.

Ancient histories contain dramatic battlefield accounts, and troop figures cannot always be verified precisely. The clear sequence is large-scale mobilization, defeat at Fei River, and diminished Former Qin control.

Before the southward campaign, Former Qin had to supply its expedition with provisions and orders; in defeat it also had to maintain retreat routes for forces of different origins. The collapse at Fei River quickly affected the political structure. Groups that had previously accepted Fu Jian’s command began making other choices as the military situation changed.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial rendering

Fu Jian’s failed invasion illustrates the danger of committing inadequately consolidated power to an oversized goal. Numbers and outward momentum alone do not establish readiness.

382 Line H64 Wei Ji On Protracted War Proposes a Staged Strategy of Resistance — Long-Term Goals Require Adaptable Persistence▶

九四｜

382 case_id=XCASE-H64-L4 | hexagram_no=64 | line_no=4 | global_line_no=382 | original_event_id=E32 | final_grade=B | publication_status=editorial_review

Xiang interpretation — editorial English

Long-Term Goals Require Adaptable Persistence. This is a retrospective interpretive lesson; the classical wording is preserved in the bilingual verification file.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

In 1938 the war between China and Japan was still under way. Victories and defeats on different fronts, together with popular mobilization, led to differing judgments about the war’s prospects. Mao Zedong wrote On Protracted War at that time to address whether resistance could continue, whether the balance of forces might change, and how operations should be arranged in successive stages.

In On Protracted War (1938), Mao Zedong analyzed the conditions of the Sino-Japanese War and proposed a strategy of prolonged resistance developing through stages. This was a strategic argument about the situation as it then stood, considering time, changing relative strength, and organized mobilization together.

The work examined the strength of both sides and the conditions imposed by time, setting out a staged conception of warfare. When it appeared, the subsequent course of the war had not yet unfolded. Later developments were also affected by different battlefields, political forces, and international circumstances. The eventual victory must not be read backward as proof that the essay had solved every specific military problem. Starting with the questions of 1938 shows which conditions the author chose to address at the time.

After the work was made public, its readers and military units still faced continually changing front-line conditions. The stages offered a framework for thinking about time, while individual forces still had to manage their own supply, command, and intelligence about the enemy. The strategic assessment in the essay and concrete outcomes many years later should not be collapsed into a single decision.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial rendering

The argument for protracted war illustrates sustaining a direction amid difficulties. Resolute purpose does not mean every operational step must remain unchanged or that setbacks will disappear.

383 Line H64 Wei Ji Liu Xiu Establishes the Eastern Han and Restores Administration — Build Trustworthy Results through Effective Governance▶

九五｜

383 case_id=XCASE-H64-L5 | hexagram_no=64 | line_no=5 | global_line_no=383 | original_event_id=E24 | final_grade=B | publication_status=editorial_review

Xiang interpretation — editorial English

Build Trustworthy Results through Effective Governance. This is a retrospective interpretive lesson; the classical wording is preserved in the bilingual verification file.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

After Wang Mang’s government collapsed, armed groups competed across the empire. Liu Xiu gradually won military and local support, established his own claim to political authority, and continued fighting forces that had not submitted. Even before the wars ended, his new government had to sustain officials and ordinary life in the territories it controlled.

Following the collapse of Wang Mang’s regime, Liu Xiu founded the Eastern Han amid rival warlords and gradually brought the principal regions under his rule. He then reorganized officials, household registers, taxes, and labor obligations. Rebuilding the state meant both fighting wars and restoring routine government and production.

Liu Xiu took the imperial title in AD 25 and subsequently extended control over the principal regions. After armies secured a district, local officials had to restore household registration, tax and labor administration, and agricultural production. Restoring the name Han marked a clear political turning point, but the pace of recovery varied from place to place. The transition from fragmentation to the new dynasty’s wider control took many years.

If population records remained inaccurate after fighting, the government could neither allocate levies reliably nor know how many soldiers were available. As Liu Xiu gained territory, officials had to bring registration and production back to recently pacified districts. Unification and civil administration overlapped in time; they were not both accomplished suddenly in a single year.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial rendering

Liu Xiu’s restoration of administration illustrates leadership becoming credible through results over time. The image of a noble person’s radiance is value language, not unconditional praise for every policy.

384 Line H64 Wei Ji Late-Tianbao Prosperity Gives Way to the An Lushan Rebellion — Apparent Stability Is No License for Excess▶

上九｜

384 case_id=XCASE-H64-L6 | hexagram_no=64 | line_no=6 | global_line_no=384 | original_event_id=E55 | final_grade=B | publication_status=editorial_review

Xiang interpretation — editorial English

Apparent Stability Is No License for Excess. This is a retrospective interpretive lesson; the classical wording is preserved in the bilingual verification file.

Historical event — four narrative paragraphs

Under Emperor Xuanzong, the Tang court had enjoyed prosperity and governed an extensive territory, while military strength under regional frontier commanders gradually increased. An Lushan controlled frontier troops, and political tensions between the center and the regions became harder to manage as power accumulated.

The Xuanzong era saw prosperity and expansion, but difficulties involving frontier military commands and central politics continued to build. In 755 An Lushan rose in rebellion, breaking the court’s control of the situation. The ensuing warfare had long-lasting effects on population, public finance, and regional authority.

When An Lushan rebelled in 755, the existing Tang order was shaken and Emperor Xuanzong left Chang’an. The war lasted for years, affecting population movements, fiscal revenues, and local military and political power. The uprising had a specific starting date, but the relations between regional commands and the center had developed over a much longer period. A narrative confined to palace anecdotes cannot explain why prolonged warfare changed the way the Tang was governed.

Regional military governors controlled troops and local resources; prosperity at court did not by itself guarantee control over the frontier commands. After the rebellion began, armies advanced and the court had to decide how to defend positions and when to withdraw. The long war also increased the extent to which regions handled their own finances and military affairs, with consequences extending far beyond 755.

Line-specific historical comparison — English editorial rendering

The transition from late-Tianbao prosperity to rebellion illustrates the need for restraint after apparent success. The wine-drinking image is neither the sole cause of the war nor direct evidence of an actual decision.
